units.title: How programs get made
units.summary: What computers and programs are made of, how source code becomes an executable, the parts of a C++ program, the programming process, and how to plan with pseudocode, flowcharts and hierarchy charts.

lessons.title: Hardware and software
lessons.html:
The picture to hold in mind: a clerk at a desk

Hardware means the physical parts of a computer, the parts you could touch. To keep them straight, picture an office clerk who follows written instructions. The clerk works at a desk, keeps everything long-term in a filing cabinet, receives new work through an in-tray and passes finished work out through an out-tray. Every major part of a computer plays one of those roles.

In the officeIn the computerIts job
The clerkCPUCarries out instructions, one at a time.
The deskMain memory (RAM)Holds the program that is running and the data it is using right now. Quick to reach, limited space, cleared when the power goes off.
The filing cabinetSecondary storageKeeps programs and files for the long term.
The in-trayInput devicesBring data in: keyboard, mouse, microphone.
The out-trayOutput devicesSend results out: screen, printer, speakers.

Those five, the CPU, main memory, secondary storage, input devices and output devices, are the five major hardware parts of a computer system. The rest of this lesson takes them one at a time, then turns to software.

Why one machine can do so many jobs

A kitchen timer is built for one job. A computer is not. Right now it runs a game, a minute later a spreadsheet, then a web browser. The hardware stays the same. Only the instructions change.

The instructions that tell the computer how to do one job make up a program. Because a computer does whatever job its program describes, it is called programmable. In the picture: the clerk stays the same, and you hand over different instructions.

Main memory: the desk

Main memory is usually called RAM, short for random-access memory. "Random access" means the CPU can go straight to any spot in it, without reading through everything in front of it. While a program runs, its instructions and the data it is working on sit in RAM.

Bits and bytes. The smallest piece of memory is a bit, short for binary digit. A bit is a tiny switch that is either on or off, written 1 or 0. Eight bits in a row make a byte. A byte has 256 possible on and off patterns, which is enough to stand for one character. For example, the letter A is stored as the pattern 01000001. Memory is divided into bytes.

Addresses. Every byte has its own number, called its address. The numbers run in order, like numbered post office boxes along a wall. When the CPU needs something it asks for it by address: "give me what is in byte 1000".

address:   1000      1001      1002      1003
contents:  01000001  00000111  00101010  00000000
           (each box is one byte of 8 bits)

Notice what has an address: each byte, not each bit. Later in the course, when you write int total;, the computer sets aside some bytes for total, and the name stands for their address. You use the name. The computer uses the address.

Volatile. RAM keeps its contents only while it has power. Switch the computer off and everything in RAM is gone. Memory that loses its contents without power is called volatile. This is why a document you never saved is lost in a power cut: it only ever lived in RAM. In the picture, the desk is cleared every night.

Secondary storage: the filing cabinet

Secondary storage holds programs and files for the long term. Examples are hard disk drives, solid-state drives (SSDs) and USB flash drives. It is nonvolatile: it keeps its data with the power off.

It is much larger and cheaper per byte than RAM, but much slower. That is why a computer has both: RAM is the fast work area, secondary storage is the permanent store. Follow one program from start to finish:

StepWhere things are
Before you start itThe program file sits on the SSD (secondary storage).
You open itA copy of the program is loaded into RAM.
It runsThe CPU takes its instructions from RAM, one at a time.
You type a documentYour text is held in RAM only.
You press SaveThe document is copied from RAM to the SSD, where it survives a power cut.

The CPU never runs a program straight from the disk. The program is copied into RAM first.

The CPU: the clerk

The CPU, or central processing unit, is the part that carries out program instructions. Today a CPU is a single small chip called a microprocessor. It has two main parts:

  • The control unit is the clerk reading the instructions and directing the work. It works out which instruction comes next, gets it from memory, works out what it asks for, and sends signals to the part that will do it. It coordinates everything the computer does.
  • The arithmetic and logic unit, or ALU, is the clerk's calculator. It does arithmetic (add, subtract, multiply, divide) and comparisons (is 7 greater than 5? are these two values equal?). "Logic" here means comparing and testing.

The CPU handles every instruction with the same three steps, called the fetch/decode/execute cycle:

  1. Fetch. The control unit gets the next instruction from main memory.
  2. Decode. An instruction is stored as a number. The control unit works out which operation that number stands for and produces the signals for it.
  3. Execute. The signals go to the part that does the work, for example the ALU for an addition, and that part carries out the operation.

Then it starts again with the next instruction. A modern CPU repeats this billions of times a second. Here is one pass, for an instruction that says "add 7 and 5":

StepWhat happens
FetchThe control unit copies the instruction from RAM into the CPU.
DecodeIt sees a number and works out that this number means "add".
ExecuteIt signals the ALU. The ALU adds 7 and 5 and the result, 12, is stored.
NextThe control unit fetches the instruction after this one.

The order is forced: the CPU cannot work out an instruction it has not fetched yet, and it cannot carry out an instruction it has not worked out.

Input and output devices

An input device sends data into the computer: keyboard, mouse, touchscreen, microphone, scanner, camera. An output device sends data out of it: monitor, printer, speakers. Some devices do both. A disk or USB drive is an input device when the computer reads a file from it, and an output device when the computer saves a file to it.

Software

Software means programs: the instructions that tell the hardware what to do. There are two general kinds.

System software controls and looks after the computer itself. It comes in three kinds:

  • The operating system is the core set of programs that manages the hardware, memory and files, and starts and stops other programs. Windows, macOS, Linux and Android are operating systems.
  • Utility programs do one specialized job that keeps the computer running well or protects its data: virus scanners, file-compression programs, backup programs.
  • Software development tools are the programs programmers use to build software: text editors, compilers, debuggers. The next lesson covers them.

Application software does a job for the user: word processors, spreadsheets, email programs, web browsers, games.

To sort a program, ask who it works for. If its job is to run or protect the computer, it is system software. If its job is a task the user wants done, such as writing a letter or browsing the web, it is application software. Two traps follow from this:

  • A web browser runs on top of the operating system, but that does not make it system software. Its job is the user's task, so it is application software.
  • A virus scanner is something you install, much like an app, but its job is protecting the computer. It is a utility program, so it counts as system software.

Mistakes students make

  • Saying RAM keeps its data with the power off. RAM is volatile. Secondary storage is the nonvolatile one.
  • Mixing up the two parts of the CPU. The control unit fetches, decodes and directs. The ALU calculates and compares.
  • Putting the cycle in the wrong order. It is always fetch, then decode, then execute.
  • Thinking each bit has an address. Addresses belong to bytes, and a byte is 8 bits.
  • Thinking the CPU runs a program from the disk. It is copied into RAM first.
  • Calling a browser or word processor system software. It does the user's work, so it is application software.
  • Calling a virus scanner or backup program application software. Utility programs are system software.

What to remember for the test

  • Five hardware parts: CPU, main memory, secondary storage, input devices, output devices.
  • A computer is programmable: the same hardware does whatever job its program describes.
  • CPU = control unit (fetches and decodes instructions, coordinates everything) + ALU (arithmetic and comparisons).
  • Every instruction goes through fetch, decode, execute, in that order.
  • RAM: volatile, divided into bytes of 8 bits, and every byte has a unique address.
  • Secondary storage: nonvolatile, bigger, cheaper, slower. Programs are copied from it into RAM to run.
  • System software = operating system, utility programs, development tools. Application software = programs that do the user's tasks.

lessons.title: Programs, languages, compiling and linking
lessons.html:
The problem: a CPU only understands numbers

A program is a list of instructions that a computer carries out to do a job. Before anyone writes a program, someone works out the steps: an algorithm is a finite set of precise, ordered steps that solves a problem. A program is an algorithm written in a language a computer can be made to run.

That last part is the catch. The last lesson showed that the CPU runs instructions stored as numbers. The only language a CPU can run directly is machine language: instructions written as binary numbers, each one a tiny operation. For example, on the kind of chip inside most PCs, these two bytes are one instruction:

10110000 00000101    put the number 5 into a storage
                     spot inside the CPU called AL

Writing a whole program like that is slow and error-prone. This lesson is about how we avoid it: we write in a language people can read, and other programs translate it into machine language for us.

Low-level and high-level languages

KindWhat "put 5 somewhere" looks like
Machine language10110000 00000101
Assembly languagemov al, 5
High-level language (C++)x = 5;
  • Machine language is binary. Each kind of CPU has its own: the chip in a PC and the chip in a phone use different instruction numbers. A machine-language program for one kind of CPU will not run on another.
  • Assembly language is the same instructions with short names instead of numbers. It still matches one kind of CPU, instruction for instruction.
  • Both are low-level languages: close to the hardware and tied to one kind of CPU.
  • A high-level language, such as C++, Python or Java, uses statements that look like English words and ordinary math, for example total = price * qty;. It does not depend on any one CPU. One high-level statement often becomes many machine instructions.

Because a high-level program is not tied to one CPU, you can take the same source code to a different kind of computer and translate it there, usually with few or no changes. A language like that is called portable. C++ is portable. Machine language is not.

Source code and the trip to an executable

The C++ text you type is source code. You save it in a source file, whose name ends in .cpp, using a text editor (a program for typing and changing plain text). The CPU cannot run source code, so it must be turned into machine language. In C++ that takes three programs, always in the same order. Picture an assembly line, where each station takes what the last one produced:

ship.cpp        source file: the C++ you typed
  |  PREPROCESSOR   handles the lines that start
  |                 with #, pastes in the files
  v                 they name
expanded source still C++ text, just longer
  |  COMPILER       translates it all into machine
  v                 language, checks the rules
ship.o          object file: machine code for
  |             your own statements only
  |  LINKER         joins in prewritten library
  v                 code, such as the code for cout
ship            executable file: a complete
                program, ready to run

Take the stations one at a time, using this program as ship.cpp:

#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

int main()
{
    cout << "Hello" << endl;
    return 0;
}

1. The preprocessor reads the source file first. It looks only at lines that begin with #. These lines are called preprocessor directives. #include <iostream> tells it: paste the contents of the file named iostream in here. The result is still C++ source text, just much longer. With the g++ compiler, this 8-line file grows to tens of thousands of lines. The preprocessor does not translate anything. (If you know Python, notice the difference: in Python # starts a comment. In C++, # at the start of a line is a directive, and comments use //.)

2. The compiler takes that expanded text and translates the whole program into machine language. It writes the result to an object file, and the machine code inside it is called object code. The compiler also checks the language's rules. If you break one, for example by leaving out a semicolon, that is a syntax error: the compiler reports it and writes no object file at all.

3. The linker. The object file is not a complete program yet. Your code uses cout, but you did not write the code that actually puts characters on the screen. That code is in the runtime library: a large collection of prewritten code that comes with C++, for common jobs such as screen output and math functions. The compiler does not copy library code into the object file. It only leaves a note that says "this program needs the code for cout". The linker reads those notes, joins the object file to the library code it needs, and writes the executable file: complete machine language that can run.

4. Running. When you start the executable, the operating system copies it from disk into RAM and the CPU runs it, as in the last lesson.

You can watch each station with g++ on the command line:

g++ -c ship.cpp       preprocess and compile: makes ship.o
g++ ship.o -o ship    link: makes the executable ship
./ship                run it: prints Hello

Try to run ship.o instead and the operating system refuses, because it is not a complete program. Usually you do all three steps at once with one command, g++ ship.cpp -o ship, which runs the preprocessor, compiler and linker in turn.

Compiler versus interpreter

A compiler translates the whole program before it runs. You get an executable file, and you can run it again and again without translating again. An interpreter works differently: it reads a program and carries it out one statement at a time, translating as it goes, and it never produces an executable file. Python is usually run this way: python3 hello.py starts running your file right away. C++ is compiled.

Integrated development environments

Typing g++ commands is one way to work. Most students use an integrated development environment, or IDE: one program that bundles a text editor, the compiler, a debugger (a tool for running a program step by step to find mistakes) and other tools under one set of menus. Visual Studio and Code::Blocks are IDEs. In an IDE, one click on Build or Run preprocesses, compiles, links and starts the program. The same three stations still run. The IDE just presses the buttons for you.

Mistakes students make

  • Saying the compiler makes the executable. The compiler makes the object file. The linker makes the executable.
  • Saying the preprocessor translates code. It only handles # lines, such as pasting in included files. The compiler translates.
  • Thinking an object file can run. It is machine code, but the library code it needs is missing until the linker adds it.
  • Getting the order wrong. Each station needs what the one before it made, so the order never changes.
  • Thinking "high-level" means harder. High-level means further from the hardware and closer to human language.
  • Mixing up a compiler (translates everything first, makes an executable) with an interpreter (translates and runs one statement at a time).
  • Calling an IDE a library or a compiler. It is a package of tools, one of which is a compiler.

What to remember for the test

  • The CPU runs only machine language directly. Machine and assembly language are low-level and tied to one kind of CPU.
  • C++ is a high-level, portable language: the same source code can be compiled for other systems with little or no change.
  • Order: source file, preprocessor, compiler, object file, linker, executable file.
  • Preprocessor: handles # directives such as #include. Compiler: translates to machine language, makes the object file, reports syntax errors. Linker: adds runtime library code, makes the executable.
  • An object file cannot run by itself.
  • An IDE bundles editor, compiler, debugger and other tools in one package.
  • An interpreter translates and runs one statement at a time and makes no executable.

lessons.title: What a C++ program is made of
lessons.html:
The idea: every program is built from a few kinds of pieces

An English sentence is made of words and punctuation, put together by grammar rules. A C++ program is the same. It is made of a handful of kinds of pieces, and once you can name each kind you can label every part of any program. Here is a complete program to take apart. It reads a weight in pounds and a price per pound, then shows the charge.

#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

int main()
{
    double pounds, price, charge;
    cin >> pounds;
    cin >> price;
    charge = pounds * price;
    cout << "Charge: " << charge << endl;
    return 0;
}

If the user types 4 and 2.5, it prints Charge: 10. Here is what each line does:

LineWhat it does
#include <iostream>A preprocessor directive (last lesson). It pastes in the iostream file, which defines cin and cout.
using namespace std;The library's names belong to a group called std. This line lets you write cout instead of std::cout.
(blank line)Ignored. It only makes the code easier to read.
int main()The start of the function called main. A function is a named group of statements. Every C++ program has exactly one main, and running the program means running main.
{ and }Mark where the body of main starts and ends.
double pounds, price, charge;Creates three variables (named storage spots in memory, explained below) that can hold numbers with a decimal part.
cin >> pounds;Reads a number the user types and stores it in pounds.
charge = pounds * price;Multiplies, then stores the result in charge.
cout << ... << endl;Shows the text Charge: , then the value of charge, then ends the line.
return 0;Ends main and tells the operating system the program finished normally.

The five kinds of program element

ElementWhat it isIn the program above
Key words, also called reserved wordsWords built into C++ with a fixed meaning. Always lowercase. You cannot use one as a name.using, namespace, int, double, return
Programmer-defined identifiersNames the programmer made up, for variables and functions.pounds, price, charge
OperatorsSymbols that do an operation on data. The values they work on are called operands.=, *, <<, >>
PunctuationCharacters that mark where a statement ends or that sit between the items of a list.; and ,
SyntaxThe rules for putting all of these together correctly. Not a piece you can point to, but the grammar for the pieces.A statement must end with ;

Key word or identifier? Two quick tests. First: could the programmer have picked a different word here? charge could be renamed cost everywhere and the program would still work, so it is an identifier. double cannot be renamed, so it is a key word. Second: key words work with no #include at all, because they are part of the language. Other common key words are if, else, while, for, char, bool, const and void.

Trap: cout, cin and endl are not key words. They are names defined in the iostream library. Remove #include <iostream> and the compiler reports that cout was not declared, while int and return still work. main is not a key word either: it is the required name of the program's starting function.

Operator or punctuation? An operator does something to values: * multiplies pounds and price, and = stores a value. Punctuation does nothing to values. It only marks structure: ; ends the statement and , separates the names in a list.

The assignment operator

The = symbol is the assignment operator. It works out the value on its right, then stores that value in the variable on its left. Read it as "gets" or "is set to", not "equals".

charge = pounds * price;
before:   pounds 4,  price 2.5,  charge (no value yet)
right:    4 * 2.5 is 10
after:    charge is 10

Testing whether two values are equal is a different operator, ==, with two equal signs. Python works the same way, so this should feel familiar.

Variables and literals

A variable is a place in memory that has a name. Recall from the first lesson that memory is a row of numbered bytes. A variable is some of those bytes with a name, so you can say charge instead of an address. Its value can change while the program runs, and storing a new value replaces the old one:

int count = 5;        count is 5
count = 8;            count is 8, the 5 is gone
count = count + 1;    count is 9

A variable definition creates a variable by giving its type and name, as in double charge;. Unlike Python, where a variable appears the first time you assign to it, C++ needs the definition before the variable is used. Two types appear in this unit: int holds whole numbers, called integers, such as 5 or -129. double holds floating-point numbers, which can have a decimal part, such as 6.7. One definition can create several variables of the same type, separated by commas, and can give them starting values: int apples = 3, pears = 4;.

A literal is a value written directly into the code: 5, 2.5, or the string literal "Charge: " in double quotes. A literal never changes. A variable is a name whose value you look up when the line runs. That is why cout << "charge"; prints the word charge, but cout << charge; prints the number stored in it.

Names are case-sensitive: Total and total are two different names. Since key words are always lowercase, Int is not a key word. And Cout is a different name from cout, so writing Cout << 5; is an error: no name Cout was ever declared.

Lines versus statements

A line is one row of text in the file. A statement is one complete instruction that makes the computer do something. In Python, one line is normally one statement. In C++ it is the semicolon, not the end of the line, that ends most statements. So the two do not match up:

CodeLinesStatements
int x = 4;11
cout << "x is "
<< x << endl;		21. The first line has no semicolon, so the statement carries on.
int a = 1; int b = 2;12
a blank line, or a comment10

To count statements in a short piece of code, count the semicolons that end statements. A semicolon inside quotes, as in "a;b", is just a character of text and does not count.

Comments

A comment is a note for people. The compiler ignores it completely. C++ has two forms:

  • // starts a comment that runs to the end of that line.
  • /* starts a comment that runs until */, even across several lines.

Code inside a comment does not run. To work out what such code prints, cross out every comment first:

cout << "a";   // cout << "b";
/* cout << "c";
   cout << "d"; */
cout << "e" << endl;

On line 1, only cout << "a"; runs, because everything after // is a comment. Lines 2 and 3 are one comment. Line 4 runs. The output is ae.

Output with cout

cout sends output to the screen. The << operator, called the stream insertion operator, sends the item on its right to cout, and one statement can chain several items. (cin >> goes the other way: it reads a value the user types into a variable.)

The big difference from Python's print: cout never adds a space or a new line by itself. Items are printed exactly next to each other, and the next cout carries on right where the last one stopped. endl ends the current line, so later output starts on a new line.

cout << "One";
cout << "Two" << endl;
cout << "Three" << endl;

Trace the screen as you go. After line 1 it shows One. Line 2 adds Two on the same line, then ends the line. Line 3 prints on the new line. Result:

OneTwo
Three

Spaces work the same way: cout << "Fruit:" << 7; prints Fruit:7. To get a space, put it inside the quotes: "Fruit: ".

Mistakes students make

  • Calling cout, cin, endl or main a key word. They are names, not reserved words.
  • Calling ; an operator. It is punctuation. It ends a statement but does nothing to any value.
  • Counting lines instead of statements. A statement ends at its semicolon, however many lines it spans.
  • Reading = as "is equal to". It stores a value. The equality test is ==.
  • Expecting cout to start a new line like Python's print. Without endl, the next output continues on the same line.
  • Running code that is inside a comment. Cross out everything after // and everything between /* and */ first.
  • Mixing up a literal and a variable: "charge" in quotes is text, charge without quotes is a variable.

What to remember for the test

  • Key words (reserved words) are lowercase, built in, and cannot be used as names. Identifiers are names the programmer chose.
  • Operators act on operands: =, *, +, <<, >>. Punctuation such as ; and , only marks structure.
  • Syntax = the rules for combining the elements.
  • = is the assignment operator: right side worked out first, then stored on the left.
  • A variable is a place in memory that has a name. A new value replaces the old one.
  • Statements end at semicolons, not at line ends. Blank lines and comments are not statements.
  • // comments to end of line, /* ... */ comments everything between. Comments never run.
  • cout adds no spaces and no new lines. endl ends the line.

lessons.title: Input, processing, output, and the programming process
lessons.html:
The idea: every program is input, processing, output

Go back to the clerk from the first lesson. Work arrives in the in-tray, the clerk does something with it, and the result goes out through the out-tray. Nearly every program has the same three parts:

  • Input is data the program receives from outside while it runs: typed on the keyboard, read from a file, or sent by a device. In C++, keyboard input uses cin.
  • Processing is what the program does with that data: calculations, comparisons, decisions. In C++ that is statements such as pay = hours * rate;.
  • Output is data the program sends out: to the screen, a printer or a file. In C++, screen output uses cout.

Here is a small program with each line labeled:

double hours, rate, pay;
cout << "Hours worked: ";        // output (a prompt)
cin >> hours;                    // input
cout << "Hourly rate: ";         // output (a prompt)
cin >> rate;                     // input
pay = hours * rate;              // processing
cout << "Pay: " << pay << endl;  // output

A prompt is a message that tells the user what to type. It is output, even though its purpose is to help with input.

To classify a step in a question, ask one thing: is data coming in, being worked on, or going out? Reading an age from the keyboard is input. Working out a birth year from it is processing. Showing the year on the screen is output. Words like compiling and linking are never the answer to this kind of question. They are steps in building a program, not things a running program does.

The programming process

Writing a program is usually taught as a process of nine steps. The point of the list is that a good program starts with a plan, not with typing. The first four steps all happen before any code exists. Follow them with the pay program as the example.

  1. Clearly define what the program must do. State exactly what problem the program must solve. You do this by naming four things: its purpose, its input, its processing and its output. For the pay program: purpose, find a worker's pay. Input, hours worked and hourly rate. Processing, multiply them. Output, the pay.
  2. Visualize the program running. Picture, or sketch, the screen the user will see, with sample input and output. Put yourself in the user's place: what will the program ask, and what will it show?
  3. Model the program with design tools. The tools are hierarchy charts, pseudocode and flowcharts, covered in the next two lessons.
  4. Check the model for logical errors. Trace the model by hand and make sure its steps give the right answer. A logical error, usually called a logic error, is a mistake in the steps themselves. The next section shows one.
  5. Type the code, then save and compile it. Only now is any C++ written.
  6. Fix the errors the compiler reports. Repeat steps 5 and 6 until the program compiles.
  7. Run the program with test data. Test data is input you choose and whose correct answer you have already worked out by hand.
  8. Correct errors found while running. Change the code, then repeat steps 5 to 8 as many times as needed.
  9. Validate the results. Check that the finished program really solves the problem you stated in step 1.

For step 2, a sketch of the pay program looks like this, with the user's typing included:

Hours worked: 40
Hourly rate: 12.5
Pay: 500

A way to hold the nine steps in your head: steps 1 to 4 plan, steps 5 and 6 build, steps 7 and 8 test, and step 9 checks against the goal. The step right before typing any code is step 4, checking the model. Defining the problem always comes first.

Logic errors and desk-checking

A logic error is a mistake in the steps themselves. The program follows the rules of C++, so it compiles and runs, but it gives the wrong result. Suppose the processing line were typed as pay = hours + rate;. With 40 hours at 12.5, the program prints Pay: 52.5 instead of Pay: 500. The compiler cannot catch this. It has no idea that you meant to multiply.

The way to catch it is desk-checking: stepping through the program by hand, on paper, and writing down each variable's value and anything displayed after every statement. Then compare the result with the answer you expected. Here is a desk-check of the correct version:

double hours = 40, rate = 12.5, pay;
pay = hours * rate;
cout << "Pay: " << pay << endl;
After statementhoursratepayScreen
14012.5?
24012.5500
34012.5500Pay: 500

Desk-checking works on a model (step 4) and on real code (step 8) alike. It is also exactly how you answer "what does this print?" questions.

Three rules the short programs in questions rely on

1. Several definitions in one statement. double hours = 40, rate = 12.5, pay; creates three variables. hours starts at 40 and rate at 12.5. pay is given no starting value, so it holds nothing meaningful until a value is stored in it. That is the ? in the table above.

2. A variable must be defined before it is used. The compiler reads the file from top to bottom. When it meets a name, it must already have seen that name's definition higher up.

total = 5;      // error: total was not declared
int total;

int total;      // correct: define first,
total = 5;      // then use

The first version does not compile. g++ reports 'total' was not declared in this scope. Python is different: there, a variable comes into being the first time you assign to it. In C++ the definition must come first.

3. How cout shows a double. By default it shows up to six significant digits and leaves off any zeros at the end, including a useless .0. So a double holding a whole number prints with no decimal point:

ValuePrinted as
500.0500
2.52.5
3.103.1
1.0 / 30.333333 (six digits)
1234567.01.23457e+06 (too many digits, so it switches to scientific notation)

So for output questions, do the arithmetic, then write the result the way cout would: 500, not 500.0 or 500.00.

Procedural and object-oriented programming

There are two main ways to organize a program.

  • Procedural programming is built around procedures. A procedure is a group of statements that does one task. In C++, procedures are called functions. The data sits in variables, separate from the procedures. The procedures are handed that data to work on, and often several procedures share the same variables.
  • Object-oriented programming (OOP) is built around objects. An object bundles some data together with the procedures that work on that data. You get an object to do something by calling one of its own functions, which is also described as sending it a message.

Example: a bank account. Done procedurally, there is a balance variable and a separate deposit function that is given the balance and an amount. Done with objects, an account object holds its own balance and has its own deposit function, and you ask the account itself to make the deposit. If you know Python, you have used objects already: in name.upper(), upper is a function that belongs to the string name. C++ supports both styles. The early part of this course is procedural, and classes come at the end.

The whole job of designing, writing, testing, debugging, documenting and maintaining programs is called software engineering.

Mistakes students make

  • Calling a calculation "output" because its result is later shown. Working out the value is processing. Showing it is output.
  • Answering "compiling" or "linking" for an input, processing or output question. Those build the program, they are not done by it.
  • Thinking the process starts with typing code. It starts with defining the problem, and four planning steps come before any code.
  • Mixing up testing (step 7, running with test data) and validating (step 9, checking the program solves the original problem).
  • Thinking the compiler finds logic errors. It only finds rule-breaking. A logic error compiles and runs, and gives a wrong answer.
  • Writing 75.0 or 75.00 for a double holding 75. cout prints 75.
  • Using a variable on a line above its definition.
  • Describing OOP as "functions that share data". That is procedural. OOP bundles the data and its functions into objects.

What to remember for the test

  • Input comes in (cin), processing works on it, output goes out (cout).
  • Defining a program means naming its purpose, input, processing and output. This is step 1.
  • Step 2: visualize the screens. Step 3: model it with design tools. Step 4: check the model for logic errors. Then type and compile.
  • Step 7 tests with data whose answer you know. Step 9 validates against the original problem.
  • Desk-checking: trace by hand, recording every variable's value and the output after each statement.
  • A variable must be defined above its first use.
  • A double holding a whole number prints with no decimal point.
  • Procedural = procedures (functions) acting on separate data. OOP = objects that bundle data with the functions that use it.

lessons.title: Algorithms, pseudocode and hierarchy charts
lessons.book: Sections 1.3 and 1.6, pages 9 and 19 to 21; design tools
lessons.html:
The idea: work out the steps before you write the code

An algorithm is a finite set of well-defined, ordered steps that solves a problem. Each word matters. Ordered: the steps happen in a set order. Well-defined: each step means exactly one thing. Finite: it comes to an end. A recipe is an everyday algorithm. A program is an algorithm written in a programming language.

Working out the steps and writing C++ are two separate jobs, and doing both at once is hard. So programmers first write the algorithm with a design tool, then translate it. This lesson covers two tools, pseudocode and hierarchy charts. The next lesson covers flowcharts.

Pseudocode

Pseudocode ("fake code") is a mix of plain English and programming-language-style statements. It is written for people only. There is no compiler for it, the computer cannot run it, and it has no official syntax: Input price and Read price are both fine. What matters is that it is precise enough to translate line by line into real code. This course uses these conventions:

PseudocodeMeaningC++
Input xGet a value from the user and store it in x.cin >> x;
Display xShow x. Each Display shows on its own line unless the step says otherwise.cout << x; (add << endl to end the line)
Set x = y + 1Work out the right side, then store it in x.x = y + 1;
If ... Else ... End IfChoose which steps run.if (...) ... else ...
While ... End WhileRepeat steps.while (...) { ... }

Indenting shows which steps are inside an If or a While.

Every algorithm is built from just three structures. Sequence: steps run one after another, in order. Selection: a test picks which steps run. Repetition, also called iteration: steps repeat while a test stays true. The sections below take them in that order.

Sequence, and how to trace it

Picture each variable as a labeled box that holds one value. A Set or Input step puts a new value in one box, and the old value in that box is gone. Every other box stays as it was. To find what an algorithm displays, keep a table with a column per variable and update it one step at a time.

Set x = 5
Set y = x + 2
Set x = y * 3
Display x
Display y
StepxyShown
Set x = 55
Set y = x + 257
Set x = y * 3217
Display x21721
Display y2177

The right side always uses the values in the boxes right now. In step 3, y is already 7, so x becomes 21 and the old 5 is gone.

Steps written in English. Some questions describe each step in a sentence. Turn each sentence into a Set step, then trace as usual. "The variable m starts with 10" is Set m = 10. "Subtract 4 from m" is Set m = m - 4, so m is 6. "Put m times 2 into n" is Set n = m * 2, so n is 12. Watch which variable each sentence stores into: that is the only box that changes.

Order of operations. Arithmetic follows the same rules as math, C++ and Python: multiplication and division are done before addition and subtraction, and parentheses override that. 2 + 3 * 4 is 2 + 12 = 14. (2 + 3) * 4 is 20.

Swapping two values needs a third box. To swap first = 4 and second = 9, this does not work:

Set first = second     first 9, second 9   the 4 is gone
Set second = first     first 9, second 9

The first step destroys the 4 before anything saved it. Save it in a spare variable first:

Set temp = first       temp 4
Set first = second     first 9
Set second = temp      second 4      swapped

A step can only use values that already exist. A classic design error puts a calculation above the Input steps it needs:

Display "Enter width"
Input width
Set area = width * height     wrong: height has no value yet
Display "Enter height"
Input height
Display area

The fix is to move Set area below Input height. The prompts are fine where they are: a prompt (a Display telling the user what to type) belongs right before the Input it describes.

Selection: If, Else If, Else

A condition is a test that is either true or false, such as score >= 90. The comparison operators are >, <, >= (greater than or equal), <=, == (equal) and != (not equal). An If ... Else runs exactly one of its two paths. A chain with Else If works like Python's elif: the tests are checked top to bottom, only the first true one runs, and the rest are skipped. Steps after End If run every time.

Set score = 85
If score >= 90
    Display "A"
Else If score >= 80
    Display "B"
Else If score >= 70
    Display "C"
Else
    Display "F"
End If
Display "end"

Trace: 85 >= 90 is false, so go to the next test. 85 >= 80 is true, so B is shown and the chain is finished. The test 85 >= 70 is also true, but it is never checked. Then end is shown. Output: B, then end.

In C++ the condition goes in parentheses, with no colon and no End If:

if (age >= 18)
    cout << "adult";
else
    cout << "minor";

Three traps when matching pseudocode to C++:

  • = is not ==. if (age = 18) does not compare. It stores 18 in age, and C++ counts any nonzero number as true, so the "adult" path runs whatever age was entered. It is still legal C++, so it compiles. At most the compiler prints a warning, which is easy to miss.
  • > is not >=. "18 or older" is age >= 18. age > 18 sends someone who is exactly 18 down the wrong path.
  • Indentation means nothing to C++. In Python, indenting decides what is inside an if. In C++, without braces, only the one statement right after if (...) belongs to it. Leave out else and the next statement is not part of the if at all, so it always runs:
if (age >= 18)
    cout << "adult";
cout << "minor";      // always runs: age 20 prints adultminor

When a path holds more than one statement, wrap them in braces { }.

Repetition: While

A While loop tests its condition. If it is true, the indented steps (the body) run, then control goes back up to the test. When the test is false, the loop ends and the step after End While runs. The test happens before every pass, including the first, so if it is false at the start the body runs zero times. Something in the body must change the tested variable, or the test never becomes false and the loop never ends. That is called an infinite loop.

Set total = 0
Set k = 2
While k <= 8
    Set total = total + k
    Set k = k + 2
End While
Display total
Testtotal afterk after
2 <= 8 true24
4 <= 8 true66
6 <= 8 true128
8 <= 8 true2010
10 <= 8 false: loop ends2010

Display total is after End While, so it runs once: 20. Notice that k = 8 still passes, because <= includes the equal case.

If a Display is inside the body, it shows a value on every pass. Here n is shown before it changes:

Set n = 1
While n < 20
    Display n
    Set n = n * 3
End While

This shows 1, 3 and 9. Then n becomes 27, the test 27 < 20 is false, and the loop ends. 27 is never shown, because the loop stops at the test before reaching Display n again.

Reading until a stop value. A loop often reads values until the user enters a special value that means "stop", such as 0. This pattern needs two Input steps: one before the loop, so the first test has a value to check, and one as the last step in the body, so each test checks a fresh value.

Set count = 0
Input num
While num != 0
    Set count = count + 1
    Input num
End While
Display count

With input 5, 8, 0: num is 5, the test passes, count is 1, num becomes 8. The test passes, count is 2, num becomes 0. The test 0 != 0 is false, so the loop ends and 2 is shown. In C++:

count = 0;
cin >> num;
while (num != 0)
{
    count = count + 1;
    cin >> num;
}
cout << count;

What goes wrong with the other versions: drop the cin inside the loop and num never changes, so if the first value is not 0 the loop never ends. Use if instead of while and the body runs at most once. Move the cout inside the braces and it shows a running count on every pass instead of one result at the end.

Hierarchy charts

A hierarchy chart shows how a program's job breaks into smaller jobs. The top box names the whole task of the program. The boxes on the level below are its major subtasks, and each of those can split again. Working this way, from the whole job down to pieces small enough to write easily, is called top-down design. In real programs the boxes often become functions.

                 +-------------------+
                 |  Find a student's |
                 |    course grade   |
                 +-------------------+
                           |
        +------------------+------------------+
        |                  |                  |
+---------------+  +---------------+  +---------------+
|    Read the   |  |  Work out the |  |  Display the  |
|     scores    |  |    average    |  |  letter grade |
+---------------+  +---------------+  +---------------+
        |
    +---+-----+
    |         |
+-------+ +-------+
|  Read | |  Read |
| tests | |  labs |
+-------+ +-------+

A hierarchy chart shows what the parts are and which part belongs to which. It does not show the order the steps run in, any decisions or loops, or the values of variables. It has no Start or End box either. Start and End belong to flowcharts, the next lesson's tool, which do show order and decisions. To pick the top box, ask what the whole program is for. Reading, calculating and displaying are always pieces on a lower level.

Mistakes students make

  • Thinking pseudocode has strict rules or is compiled. It is for people, and only needs to be clear.
  • Using an old value after a box has been overwritten. Update the table after every step.
  • Swapping with a = b then b = a. Both end up with b's value.
  • Adding before multiplying. a * a + b * b squares each first.
  • Running every true test in an Else If chain. Only the first true one runs.
  • Showing the value that made a loop's test fail. The loop stops at the test.
  • Writing = where == is meant, or > where "or more" means >=.
  • Trusting indentation in C++. Without braces, only one statement belongs to an if or while.
  • Putting a calculation before the Input steps it uses.
  • Putting Start at the top of a hierarchy chart, or reading the chart as an order of steps.

What to remember for the test

  • Algorithm: finite, well-defined, ordered steps. Pseudocode: precise English-like steps for people, never compiled.
  • Three structures: sequence, selection, repetition.
  • Trace with a table: one column per variable, update one box per step, write down every Display.
  • Else If chain: first true test wins. Steps after End If always run.
  • While: test first, body, back to the test. The Display after End While runs once.
  • Stop-value loop: Input before the loop and Input as the last step inside it.
  • Hierarchy chart: whole task at the top, subtasks below. No order, no decisions, no Start.

lessons.title: Flowcharts
lessons.book: Section 1.6 and Appendix C material (written from standard practice)
lessons.html:
The idea: a map of the path through the steps

A flowchart is a diagram of an algorithm. Each step sits inside a shape, and the shape tells you what kind of step it is. Lines with arrowheads, called flow lines, join the shapes and show the order the steps happen in. Unlike a hierarchy chart, a flowchart shows order and decisions.

To run a flowchart in your head, put your finger on Start and follow the arrows. Do what each shape says, keeping a table of variable values as in the last lesson. At a decision, answer its question and follow the exit that matches. When your finger reaches End, you are done. Everything in this lesson is that one habit.

The shapes

This page draws flowcharts with text characters, so each shape has a text form too.

ShapeNameUsed forText form here
Oval (a rectangle with rounded ends)TerminalStart and End (some books write Stop). A chart has exactly one Start.( Start )
Parallelogram (a slanted rectangle)Input/outputReading a value or displaying one. The words inside say which./ Input n /
RectangleProcessA calculation or assignment.a box: | n = n + 1 |
DiamondDecisionA yes/no (true/false) question. One line goes in, two leave, labeled Yes and No.< n > 0 ? >
Small circleConnectorContinues the chart somewhere else.(A)
Rectangle with an extra line inside each sidePredefined processA call to a module (a function) whose own steps are drawn in a separate flowchart.|| getData ||

A few more rules. Flow lines normally run top to bottom, and arrowheads (drawn v and > here) show direction where it is not obvious. A process or input/output shape has one line in and one line out. A decision has one line in and two out. As in pseudocode, each Display shape shows its value on its own line.

Connectors solve a drawing problem. When a chart is too big for the page, or a line would have to cross half the chart, the line stops at a small circle with a letter in it, say A. The flow carries on from another circle with the same letter A, at another point on the page or on another page. (Some standards draw the other-page case with a different shape, like a baseball home plate.)

To translate a chart into C++, go shape by shape: an input parallelogram becomes cin >>, an output parallelogram becomes cout <<, a rectangle becomes an assignment statement, and a diamond becomes an if or the test of a loop.

Sequence: shapes in a straight line

When there are no decisions, the shapes run straight down from Start to End, and the C++ statements come in exactly the same order:

        ( Start )
            |
   / Display "Length? " /
            |
      / Input len /
            |
   / Display "Width? " /
            |
      / Input wid /
            |
    +----------------+
    | area = len*wid |
    +----------------+
            |
     / Display area /
            |
         ( End )
cout << "Length? ";
cin >> len;
cout << "Width? ";
cin >> wid;
area = len * wid;
cout << area;

Three things to check when matching code to a chart like this. The calculation must come after both inputs, because a step can only use values that already exist. The formula must be copied exactly: a - b and b - a give different answers. And an Input shape needs cin: cout << len; would display len instead of reading it.

Selection: a diamond whose paths join again

A decision diamond splits the flow into a Yes path and a No path. Each path runs its own shapes, and then the two paths join again below and carry on down together. This is an if/else:

                / Input x /
                     |
                     v
   +---- Yes ---- < x > 0 ? > ---- No ----+
   |                                      |
   v                                      v
/ Display "pos" /           / Display "not pos" /
   |                                      |
   +------------------+-------------------+
                      |
                      v
                   ( End )
cin >> x;
if (x > 0)
    cout << "pos";
else
    cout << "not pos";

If one path has no shapes on it, the line just goes straight to the join point. That is an if with no else.

Two decisions in a row are both tested. Suppose x is 3. The chart has a diamond "x > 1?" whose Yes path displays A, the paths join, then a second diamond "x > 2?" whose Yes path displays B, and the paths join again. Follow it with your finger: after the first diamond, both of its paths lead down to the second diamond, so the second test always happens. 3 > 1 is true, so A is shown. 3 > 2 is true, so B is shown too. In C++ that is two separate if statements:

if (x > 1)
    cout << "A" << endl;
if (x > 2)
    cout << "B" << endl;     // x = 3 shows A, then B

Repetition: a line that goes back up

A loop in a flowchart is a flow line that goes back up to an earlier point, so some shapes are visited again. This is how you tell a loop from a selection: both use a diamond, but a selection's paths join below it, while a loop has a line that returns up to the diamond or above it.

Pre-test loop. The diamond comes first. Yes runs the body and a line goes back up to the diamond. No leaves the loop. This is the While from pseudocode and the C++ while loop. If the test is false the first time, the body runs zero times.

          ( Start )
              |
              v
         / Input n /
              |
              v
       +-------------+
       |  count = 1  |
       +-------------+
              |
              v
  +--> < count <= n ? > --No--> ( End )
  |           |
  |          Yes
  |           |
  |           v
  |   / Display count /
  |           |
  |           v
  |  +-----------------+
  |  | count = count+1 |
  |  +-----------------+
  |           |
  +-----------+
cin >> n;
count = 1;
while (count <= n)
{
    cout << count << endl;
    count = count + 1;
}

With n = 3, follow it: 1 <= 3 Yes, show 1, count 2. 2 <= 3 Yes, show 2, count 3. 3 <= 3 Yes, show 3, count 4. 4 <= 3 No, End. Output 1, 2, 3, each on its own line.

Post-test loop. The body comes first and the diamond comes after it, with the Yes line going back up to the top of the body. Because the test is at the bottom, the body always runs at least once, even if the test would have been false from the start. In C++ this is a do-while loop. Note the semicolon after its while (...).

          ( Start )
              |
              v
       +-------------+
       |   k = 10    |
       +-------------+
              |
              v
  +----> / Display k /
  |           |
  |           v
  |    +-------------+
  |    |  k = k * 2  |
  |    +-------------+
  |           |
  |           v
  +--Yes-- < k < 50 ? >
              |
              No
              |
              v
           ( End )
k = 10;
do
{
    cout << k << endl;
    k = k * 2;
} while (k < 50);
Shownk afterTest
102020 < 50 Yes, back up
204040 < 50 Yes, back up
408080 < 50 No, End

Now start k at 100 instead. The body runs first, shows 100 and makes k 200, and only then is 200 < 50 tested. It is false, so the chart ends, but 100 was already shown once. A pre-test loop starting at 100 would have shown nothing.

Whichever kind of loop it is, something in the body must change the value the diamond tests. Otherwise the answer never changes, the line goes back up forever, and you have an infinite loop, on paper as much as in C++.

Integer division when tracing

Charts often divide whole numbers, and C++ has a rule here that Python does not. When both values are integers, / gives a whole number: the fraction is dropped, not rounded. It works like Python's // for positive numbers. The % operator gives the remainder.

ExpressionResultWhy
7 / 233.5 with the .5 dropped
20 / 633.33... with the fraction dropped
9 / 1000.9 with the fraction dropped
20 % 626 goes into 20 three times, 2 left over
7.0 / 23.5one value is not an integer, so normal division

So halving 50 over and over with integer division gives 25, 12, 6, 3, 1. Each step drops the half.

Mistakes students make

  • Using a rectangle for input or output. Reading and displaying go in parallelograms. Rectangles are for calculations.
  • Calling the oval anything but the terminal symbol. It marks Start and End only.
  • Mixing up the circle (connector) with the oval (terminal).
  • Reading a diamond as a loop just because it is a diamond. Look for a line going back up.
  • Skipping the second of two diamonds in a row. Both are tested unless a path leads around the second one.
  • Thinking a post-test loop can run zero times. The body always runs once before the first test.
  • Keeping the fraction in integer division. 5 / 2 is 2.
  • Translating an Input shape as cout, or putting the calculation above the inputs it needs.
  • Writing if without else for a diamond that has shapes on both paths. The No-path statement would then run every time.

What to remember for the test

  • Oval = terminal (Start, End). Parallelogram = input/output. Rectangle = process. Diamond = decision, two exits. Small circle = connector. Rectangle with an extra line inside each side = predefined process, a call to a separately charted module.
  • Trace with your finger and a variable table. At each diamond, take the matching exit.
  • Selection: paths join below the diamond. Repetition: a line goes back up.
  • Diamond before the body = pre-test loop (while), may run zero times. Diamond after the body = post-test loop (do-while), runs at least once.
  • Integer / drops the fraction. % gives the remainder.

questions.prompt: Which hardware component fetches, decodes and executes program instructions?
choices: The CPU
Main memory
Secondary storage
The output device
questions.explain:
The CPU is the part that carries out instructions, and it does every one in three steps: its control unit fetches the next instruction from main memory, decodes it to see what it asks for, and then the operation is executed, often by the ALU.

The other parts only hold or move data. Main memory stores the instructions while the program runs, but it does not act on them. Secondary storage keeps files for the long term. An output device such as a screen only shows results.

questions.prompt: What happens to the contents of main memory (RAM) when the computer is switched off?
choices: They are kept, because RAM is permanent storage
They are lost, because RAM is volatile
They are automatically moved to the CPU
They are sent to the output device
questions.explain:
They are lost. RAM holds data only while it has power, and a memory that loses its contents without power is called volatile. That is why you save your work: saving copies it from RAM to secondary storage, which keeps data with the power off.

"Permanent storage" describes secondary storage, not RAM, so that choice mixes the two up. Nothing is moved to the CPU or sent to an output device when the power goes off. With no power, nothing can be moved at all.

questions.prompt: The CPU has a control unit and a second unit that performs math and comparisons. Name it.
questions.explain: The arithmetic and logic unit, or ALU. It is the CPU's calculator: it does arithmetic such as adding and multiplying, and comparisons such as "is 7 greater than 5?". The other part, the control unit, fetches and decodes each instruction and tells the ALU when to work. For example, when a program works out `price * qty`, the multiplication itself happens in the ALU.

questions.prompt: Which of these is system software?
choices: A spreadsheet program
An email program
The operating system
A web browser
questions.explain:
The operating system. Ask who the program works for. The operating system looks after the computer itself: it manages the hardware, memory and files, and starts and stops other programs. That makes it system software.

A spreadsheet, an email program and a web browser each do a task the user wants done, so they are application software. Running on top of the operating system does not turn them into system software.

questions.prompt: Secondary storage such as a solid-state drive keeps its data when the power is off.
questions.explain:
True. Secondary storage, such as a solid-state drive, hard disk or USB flash drive, is nonvolatile: it keeps its data with the power off. That is its whole purpose, to be the long-term store.

RAM is the opposite: it is volatile and loses everything when the power goes off. Secondary storage is much slower than RAM, which is why a program is copied from the drive into RAM before the CPU runs it.

questions.prompt: What does a compiler do?
choices: Combines object files with library code
Handles lines that begin with #
Runs the program one statement at a time
Translates source code into machine language (object code)
questions.explain:
A compiler translates source code into machine language. It works on the whole program and writes the result, the object code, to an object file. It also reports syntax errors.

Each wrong choice describes a different tool. Combining object files with library code is the linker's job, and it happens after compiling. Handling lines that begin with `#`, such as `#include`, is the preprocessor's job, before compiling. Running a program one statement at a time describes an interpreter, which is how Python is usually run, not how C++ is built.

questions.prompt: Which program combines your object file with library code to create the executable file?
choices: The linker
The preprocessor
The compiler
The editor
questions.explain:
The linker. Your object file contains machine code for your own statements, plus notes saying which library pieces it needs, such as the code behind `cout`. The linker joins the object file to that runtime library code and writes the executable file.

The preprocessor runs first and only handles `#` lines. The compiler translates your code but stops at the object file. An editor is just where you type the source code. None of these produces the executable.

questions.prompt: Lines that begin with # (such as #include) are handled by the ___ before the compiler sees the code.
questions.explain: The preprocessor. Lines that start with `#` are preprocessor directives, and the preprocessor deals with them before the compiler sees the program. For example, `#include <iostream>` makes it paste the contents of the iostream file into your source at that spot. Its output is still C++ text, which then goes to the compiler. If you know Python, note that `#` does not start a comment in C++.

questions.prompt: Which pair of statements about languages is correct?
choices: C++ is low-level because it is compiled; machine language is portable
C++ is high-level and portable; machine language is low-level and specific to one kind of CPU
Both C++ and machine language are high-level but only C++ needs a compiler
C++ must be rewritten for each CPU; machine language runs on all CPUs
questions.explain:
C++ is high-level: its statements look like words and math, and it is not tied to one CPU, so the same source can be compiled for different machines. That makes it portable. Machine language is low-level: binary instructions for one kind of CPU, which will not run on another kind.

The wrong pairs each flip a fact. Being compiled does not make a language low-level, and machine language is not portable at all, since it runs only on the kind of CPU it was written for. Machine language is the lowest level, not high-level, and it needs no compiler because it is already what the CPU runs. C++ does not need rewriting for each CPU, and machine language does not run on every CPU.

questions.prompt: Machine language is the only language a CPU can execute directly.
questions.explain: True. A CPU's circuits recognize only its own instruction numbers, which is what machine language is. Everything else must be translated into machine language before the CPU can run it: assembly language by a translating program called an assembler, C++ by the compiler and linker, Python by an interpreter as it goes. Even the "Hello" program you write in C++ runs as machine code in the end.

questions.prompt: Which is the correct order for turning a C++ program into a running program?
choices: source file, compiler, preprocessor, linker, object file, executable file
source file, linker, object file, compiler, executable file
source file, preprocessor, compiler, object file, linker, executable file
source file, preprocessor, linker, compiler, executable file, object file
questions.explain:
Each station needs what the station before it produced:
```
source file    the C++ you typed
preprocessor   pastes in #include files, output is still C++
compiler       translates to machine code
object file    what the compiler writes
linker         adds the library code
executable     the finished, runnable program
```
The other orders break that chain. The compiler cannot run before the preprocessor, because it needs the pasted-in text. The linker cannot run before the compiler, because there is no object file yet to link. And the executable is the final product, so the object file cannot come after it.

questions.prompt: In the statement `int total = 5;` which item is a programmer-defined identifier?
questions.code: int total = 5;
choices: int
total
questions.explain:
`total` is the programmer-defined identifier: a name someone made up for this variable. A quick test is to ask whether the programmer could have chosen a different word. They could call it `sum` or `amount` and the program would work the same, so it is an identifier.

The others are different kinds of element. `int` is a key word, built into C++, and cannot be renamed. `=` is the assignment operator. `5` is a literal, a value written straight into the code.

questions.prompt: Which of these is NOT a C++ key word?
choices: cout
return
int
while
questions.explain:
`cout` is not a key word. It is a name defined in the iostream library, which is why programs need `#include <iostream>` before they can use it. Leave that line out and the compiler says `cout` was not declared.

`return`, `int` and `while` are key words: they are part of the language itself, always lowercase, work with no `#include`, and cannot be used as names. Many students guess `cout` is a key word because it appears in every program, but appearing often is not what makes a word reserved.

questions.prompt: In the statement `charge = pounds * price;` the = symbol is called the ___ operator.
questions.code: charge = pounds * price;
questions.explain: Assignment. The `=` symbol is the assignment operator: it works out the value on its right, then stores it in the variable on its left. If `pounds` is 4 and `price` is 2.5, the right side is 10, and 10 is stored in `charge`. Read it as "charge gets pounds times price". It does not test whether two things are equal. That test is written `==`.

questions.prompt: How many statements are in this code?
questions.explain:
Count the semicolons that end statements, not the lines.
```
int x = 4;               semicolon: statement 1 ends
cout << "x is "          no semicolon, the statement continues
     << x << endl;       semicolon: statement 2 ends
```
The `cout` statement is split across two lines, but it is still one statement because it only ends at its semicolon. So there are 2 statements. Three is the count of lines, which is the usual mistake. One would treat the whole block as a single instruction, and four does not match anything in the code.

questions.prompt: Every line of a C++ source file is exactly one statement.
questions.explain: False. In C++ a statement ends at its semicolon, not at the end of a line, so lines and statements do not match up. One statement can run over several lines, as when a long `cout` chain is split in two. One line can hold several statements, as in `int a = 1; int b = 2;`. And some lines are not statements at all: blank lines and comments. If you know Python, this is a real difference, since there one line is normally one statement.

questions.prompt: What does this code print? Assume the code is inside main(), with iostream included and using namespace std; in effect.
questions.explain:
`cout` never starts a new line by itself. Only `endl` does. Trace what is on the screen after each statement:
```
cout << "A";            screen: A
cout << "B" << endl;    screen: AB, then the line ends
cout << "C";            C goes on the new line
```
So the output is AB on the first line and C on the second. Printing A, B and C on three separate lines is the Python `print` habit, but `cout` adds no line break after A. Printing ABC on one line forgets the `endl` after B.

questions.prompt: What does this code print? Assume the code is inside main(), with iostream included and using namespace std; in effect.
questions.explain:
Cross out every comment first, then run what is left.
```
cout << "x"; // cout << "y";   only cout << "x"; runs
/* cout << "w"; */             all comment, nothing runs
cout << "z" << endl;           runs
```
Everything after `//` to the end of that line is ignored, so the `y` is never printed. Everything between `/*` and `*/` is ignored, so `w` is never printed. The two statements that run print x and then z with no space, so the output is `xz`.

questions.prompt: The rules that say how key words, operators and punctuation may be combined in a language are called its ___.
questions.explain: Syntax. A language's syntax is its grammar: the rules for how key words, identifiers, operators and punctuation may be put together. For example, a C++ statement must end with a semicolon, so `int total = 0` with no semicolon breaks the syntax. The compiler checks every line against these rules and reports a syntax error when one is broken.

questions.prompt: A program asks the user for an age, works out the birth year, and shows the result on the screen. The step that takes the age from the keyboard is which of a program's three basic activities?
choices: Processing
Output
Input
Linking
questions.explain:
Input. Taking the age from the keyboard means data is coming into the program from outside, and that is what input means. In C++ it would be a `cin` statement.

The other steps in the same program are the other activities: working out the birth year is processing, and showing it on the screen is output. Linking is not one of a running program's activities at all. It is a step in building the program, done before it ever runs.

questions.prompt: According to the steps of the programming process, what comes first?
choices: Type the code and compile it
Run the program with test data
Check the results for validity
State exactly what problem the program must solve
questions.explain:
Step 1 is to state exactly what problem the program must solve: its purpose, input, processing and output. You cannot plan, write or test a program until you know what it is supposed to do.

Typing and compiling the code is step 5, after four planning steps. Running with test data is step 7, and checking the results for validity is step 9, the very last step. Starting with typing is the habit the process is designed to break.

questions.prompt: A program reads a radius, calculates the area of a circle and displays it. Calculating the area is which activity?
choices: Processing
Input
Output
Compiling
questions.explain:
Processing. Calculating the area means doing something with the data the program already has: it takes the radius and works out a new value from it. That is processing.

Reading the radius is input, because data comes in from outside. Displaying the area is output, because data goes out. Compiling is not something a running program does. It is part of building the program before it runs.

questions.prompt: What does this code print? Assume the code is inside main(), with iostream included and using namespace std; in effect.
questions.explain:
Desk-check it one statement at a time.
```
double hours = 6, rate = 12.5, pay;   hours 6, rate 12.5, pay unset
pay = hours * rate;                   6 * 12.5 is 75, so pay is 75
cout << "Pay: " << pay << endl;       prints Pay: then 75
```
`pay` is a `double`, but `cout` drops a useless `.0`, so a double holding 75 prints as `75` with no decimal point. The output is `Pay: 75`. Writing `Pay: 75.0` or `Pay: 75.00` is the common mistake.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes object-oriented programming compared with procedural programming?
choices: OOP is centered on functions that share data with each other
OOP is centered on objects that combine data with the functions that work on that data
OOP requires every program to have no variables
OOP means the program is designed with flowcharts only
questions.explain:
Object-oriented programming is built around objects, and each object bundles its data together with the functions that work on that data. A bank account object, for example, holds its own balance and has its own deposit function.

"Functions that share data with each other" describes procedural programming, where the data sits apart from the procedures. OOP does not ban variables, since objects are full of data. And OOP has nothing to do with which design tool you draw with.

questions.prompt: What is desk-checking?
choices: Running the program on a very large input
Compiling the program on a second computer
Stepping through a program by hand, recording variable values and output after each statement
Asking the compiler to list all warnings
questions.explain:
Desk-checking means tracing a program by hand: you go through it one statement at a time and write down each variable's value and anything displayed after every statement. Then you compare the result with the answer you expected, which is how logic errors get caught.

It is done with paper and a pencil, not a computer, so it is not running a large input, not compiling on another machine, and not asking the compiler for warnings. The compiler cannot find logic errors anyway.

questions.prompt: A program's first line inside `main` is `total = 5;`, and the definition `int total;` appears two lines later. True or false: the compiler accepts this code.
questions.explain:
False. The compiler reads the code from top to bottom, and when it meets the name `total` in `total = 5;` it has not yet seen any definition of it. It reports an error such as "'total' was not declared in this scope", and the program does not compile.

A variable must be defined, with its type, on a line above its first use: `int total;` then `total = 5;`. Python lets a variable appear the first time you assign to it, but C++ does not.

questions.prompt: A set of well-defined, ordered steps for solving a problem is called an ___.
questions.explain: Algorithm. An algorithm is a finite set of precise steps, done in a set order, that solves a problem. A recipe is an everyday example: do this, then this, then this, and you are finished. A program is an algorithm written in a programming language so a computer can carry it out. Pseudocode and flowcharts are ways to write an algorithm down before writing the code.

questions.prompt: Pseudocode must follow strict syntax rules because the compiler checks it.
questions.explain: False. Pseudocode is written for people, not for a computer. No compiler ever reads it, it cannot be run, and there is no official syntax: `Input price` and `Read price` are both acceptable. Its one job is to describe the steps clearly and precisely enough that someone can translate them line by line into real C++. Strict syntax rules belong to the programming language, checked when the C++ code is compiled.

questions.prompt: What does a hierarchy chart show?
choices: The exact order in which statements execute, with decisions
The values stored in each variable
The machine language produced by the compiler
The overall task broken down into subtasks, level by level
questions.explain:
A hierarchy chart shows the program's overall task at the top and the subtasks it breaks into on the levels below, which is top-down design drawn as boxes.

It deliberately leaves out order and decisions: those are shown by a flowchart or by pseudocode. The values stored in variables are what you record in a desk-check table. Machine language is what the compiler produces, and no design chart shows it.

questions.prompt: This pseudocode is run. What is displayed?
questions.code:
Set total = 0
Set i = 1
While i <= 5
    Set total = total + i
    Set i = i + 1
End While
Display total
questions.explain:
Trace the loop one pass at a time. The test happens before each pass.
```
test       total   i
1 <= 5     1       2
2 <= 5     3       3
3 <= 5     6       4
4 <= 5     10      5
5 <= 5     15      6
6 <= 5     false, the loop ends
```
The loop adds 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5. `Display total` is after `End While`, so it runs once, and the output is `15`. If you got 10, you stopped one pass early: `i <= 5` is still true when i is 5.

questions.prompt: This pseudocode is run. What is displayed?
questions.code:
Set a = 3
Set b = 8
Set temp = a
Set a = b
Set b = temp
Display a
Display b
questions.explain:
This is the swap pattern. Trace each box:
```
Set a = 3       a 3
Set b = 8       a 3, b 8
Set temp = a    temp 3      the 3 is saved
Set a = b       a 8         the old 3 in a is gone, but temp has it
Set b = temp    b 3
```
a is 8 and b is 3, and each Display shows on its own line: 8, then 3. Without temp, `Set a = b` would destroy the 3, and both variables would end up 8.

questions.prompt: Which C++ code matches this pseudocode?
questions.code:
Input age
If age >= 18
    Display "adult"
Else
    Display "minor"
End If
questions.explain:
The pseudocode tests "age is 18 or more" and has an Else, so the match is `if (age >= 18)` with `cout << "adult";`, then `else` with `cout << "minor";`.

`if (age = 18)` uses one equals sign, which stores 18 in age instead of comparing, so "adult" prints for every age. `age > 18` leaves out 18 itself, so an 18-year-old would see "minor". The version with no `else` has `cout << "minor";` as a separate statement after the `if`, so it always runs: an adult would see adultminor.

questions.prompt: In a flowchart, the oval shape is used for the start and end points. What is it called?
questions.explain: Terminal. The terminal symbol is an oval, a rectangle with rounded ends, and it marks the two ends of a flowchart: one at the top saying Start and one at the bottom saying End or Stop. A flowchart has exactly one Start. Every other step sits in a different shape, such as a rectangle for a calculation or a parallelogram for input and output.

questions.prompt: In a flowchart, a parallelogram stands for a calculation (process).
questions.explain: False. A parallelogram is the input/output symbol: it holds steps like `Input price` or `Display tax`. Calculations and assignments are processes, and a process is drawn as a plain rectangle, for example a box holding `tax = price * rate`. A quick check: if the step moves data in or out of the program, it is a parallelogram. If it works something out inside the program, it is a rectangle.

questions.prompt: Which flowchart shape asks a yes/no question and has two exit lines?
choices: Rectangle
Diamond
Oval
Parallelogram
questions.explain:
The diamond is the decision symbol. It holds a yes/no question, such as "x > 0?", and it is the only basic shape with two exit lines, one labeled Yes and one labeled No. Diamonds are used both for if/else choices and for the test of a loop.

The other shapes have only one line out. A rectangle holds a calculation, an oval marks Start or End, and a parallelogram holds input or output.

questions.prompt: What is the small circle in a flowchart for?
choices: Start and end
Displaying output
A connector that continues the flow at another point or page
Making a calculation
questions.explain:
It is a connector. When a chart is too big for the space, or a line would have to cross the whole chart, the flow line ends at a small circle with a label, say A. The flow continues from another circle with the same label A, somewhere else. The circle is not a step. It only joins two parts of the chart.

Start and end use the oval, which is larger. Displaying output uses a parallelogram, and a calculation uses a rectangle.

questions.prompt: A flowchart reads: Start; Set n = 1; Diamond "n <= 3?"; Yes: Display n * n, Set n = n + 1, flow line back to the diamond; No: End. What does it display?
questions.code:
Start
Set n = 1
n <= 3 ?
  Yes: Display n * n
       Set n = n + 1
       (back to the test)
  No: End
questions.explain:
The diamond comes before the body, so this is a pre-test loop. Follow the arrows:
```
n    test       shown
1    1 <= 3     1 * 1 = 1
2    2 <= 3     2 * 2 = 4
3    3 <= 3     3 * 3 = 9
4    4 <= 3     No, so End
```
The loop shows 1, 4 and 9, each on its own line. When n is 3 the test still passes, because `<=` includes equal. A common slip is to display n instead of n * n, or to stop after n = 2.

questions.prompt: A flowchart reads: Start; Set x = 10; Diamond "x > 5?" Yes: Display "big"; No: skip. Both paths join. Diamond "x > 12?" Yes: Display "huge"; No: skip. Both paths join; End. What is displayed?
questions.code:
Start
Set x = 10
x > 5 ?   Yes: Display "big"
(paths join)
x > 12 ?  Yes: Display "huge"
(paths join)
End
questions.explain:
The two diamonds are separate decisions, one after the other. After the first one, both of its paths join and lead down to the second, so both tests are made.
```
x > 5 ?    10 > 5 is true, so big is shown
           paths join
x > 12 ?   10 > 12 is false, so nothing is shown
           paths join, End
```
The only output is `big`. huge would need x to be more than 12.

questions.prompt: A flowchart reads: Start; Input x (parallelogram); Diamond "x > 0?"; Yes: Display "positive"; No: Display "not positive"; End. Which C++ matches?
questions.explain:
