Go shape by shape. Input x is a parallelogram for reading, so it becomes `cin >> x;`. The diamond has a shape on both its Yes and No paths, so it is an if with an else: `if (x > 0) cout << "positive"; else cout << "not positive";`.

The version without `else` makes `cout << "not positive";` a separate statement that always runs, so a positive number shows both messages. `cout << x;` displays x instead of reading it. And `while` makes a loop, but no line in this chart goes back up. With a positive x, that `while` would print positive forever, since x never changes.

questions.prompt: A flowchart reads: Start; Set n = 20; Set count = 0; Diamond "n > 1?"; Yes: Set n = n / 2 (integer division), Set count = count + 1, back to the diamond; No: Display count; End. What is displayed?
questions.code:
Start
Set n = 20
Set count = 0
n > 1 ?
  Yes: Set n = n / 2   (integer division)
       Set count = count + 1
       (back to the test)
  No: Display count
End
questions.explain:
n and count are integers, so `n / 2` drops any fraction. Follow the loop:
```
test     n after    count after
20 > 1   10         1
10 > 1   5          2
5 > 1    2          3       5 / 2 is 2, not 2.5
2 > 1    1          4
1 > 1    No, Display count
```
The display is `4`. If you kept the fraction, n would go 10, 5, 2.5, 1.25, 0.625 and you would count 5 passes, which is the usual wrong result.

questions.prompt: This program is written as English statements. What would it display if it were a real program?
questions.code:
The variable p starts with the value 4.
The variable q starts with the value 7.
Add 3 to p.
Store the value of p times q in q.
Subtract p from q, and store the result in q.
Display the value in q.
questions.explain:
Turn each sentence into a Set step and trace it.
```
p starts with 4                  p 4
q starts with 7                  q 7
Add 3 to p                       p = 4 + 3 = 7
Store p times q in q             q = 7 * 7 = 49
Subtract p from q, store in q    q = 49 - 7 = 42
```
Each step uses the values left by the step before it. By the time q is calculated, p is already 7, not 4. The display is `42`. A common slip is using p = 4 in the multiplication, which gives 28 and then 24.

questions.prompt: This program is written as English statements. What would it display if it were a real program?
questions.code:
Create three variables: a = 2, b = 9, c = 0.
Compute a plus b and put the answer in c.
Put c multiplied by 2 into a.
Put a plus c into b.
Show a, b and c on one line, separated by spaces.
questions.explain:
Track all three boxes. Each step changes only the variable it stores into.
```
start           a 2,  b 9,  c 0
c = a + b       c 11        (2 + 9)
a = c * 2       a 22        (the old 2 is gone)
b = a + c       b 33        (22 + 11, the old 9 is gone)
```
Shown on one line with spaces: `22 33 11`. The usual slip is using the starting values in later steps, for example b = 2 + 11.

questions.prompt: This pseudocode should ask for a ticket price and a quantity, then display the total cost. What is the error?
questions.code:
Set cost = price * quantity
Display "Enter the ticket price"
Input price
Display "Enter the quantity"
Input quantity
Display cost
choices: Every Display must come after all of the Input steps
The multiplication should be an addition
cost is calculated before price and quantity have been input
Pseudocode lines must end with semicolons
questions.explain:
The error is that cost is calculated before price and quantity have been input. When the Set step runs, those boxes hold nothing yet, so it multiplies values that do not exist. The Set cost step must move below both Input steps, just before Display cost.

The other choices are not errors. Each prompt belongs right before the Input it describes, so Display steps do not all have to come after the inputs. Price times quantity is the right calculation for a total cost. And pseudocode has no syntax rules, so it needs no semicolons.

questions.prompt: A flowchart reads: Start; Display "Card value? " (parallelogram); Input value (parallelogram); Display "Amount spent? " (parallelogram); Input spent (parallelogram); Set remain = value - spent (rectangle); Display remain (parallelogram); End. Which C++ matches?
questions.explain:
Translate the shapes in order, top to bottom: prompt, read value, prompt, read spent, then the rectangle `remain = value - spent`, then display remain. The match has `cin >> value;` and `cin >> spent;` before `remain = value - spent;`.

The other versions each break one thing. Putting the calculation first uses value and spent before they have been read. `remain = spent - value` reverses the subtraction, so a 50 card with 20 spent would show -30 instead of 30. And `cout << value;` displays value rather than reading it, so nothing is ever input.

questions.prompt: This pseudocode is run. What is displayed?
questions.code:
Set temp = 68
If temp > 80
    Display "hot"
Else If temp > 60
    Display "mild"
Else
    Display "cold"
End If
Display "done"
questions.explain:
In an Else If chain, the tests are checked top to bottom and only the first true one runs.
```
68 > 80    false, go to the next test
68 > 60    true, display mild, skip the rest of the chain
End If     always continue here
Display "done"
```
The output is mild, then done on the next line. "cold" is never considered, because the chain stopped at the first true test. "done" sits after End If, so it is shown whatever temp is.

questions.prompt: This pseudocode is run. What is displayed?
questions.code:
Set n = 10
While n > 0
    Display n
    Set n = n - 3
End While
questions.explain:
The Display is inside the loop, before n changes, so each pass shows n and then lowers it.
```
test      shown   n after
10 > 0    10      7
7 > 0     7       4
4 > 0     4       1
1 > 0     1       -2
-2 > 0    false, the loop ends
```
Each Display is on its own line: 10, 7, 4, 1. The -2 is never shown, because the loop stops at the test before it reaches Display again.

questions.prompt: A flowchart reads: Start; Set k = 5; Display k; Set k = k + 1; Diamond "k < 5?"; Yes: flow line back up to Display k; No: End. What is displayed?
questions.code:
Start
Set k = 5
Display k        <-----+
Set k = k + 1          |
k < 5 ?   Yes ---------+
  No: End
questions.explain:
The diamond comes after the body, so this is a post-test loop, a do-while in C++. The body runs before anything is tested.
```
Display k      shows 5
Set k = k + 1  k is 6
k < 5 ?        6 < 5 is false, so No, End
```
The output is `5`. The tempting answer is nothing at all, which is how a pre-test loop would behave, since 5 < 5 is false from the start. But here the test only happens after the body has already run once.

questions.prompt: Which C++ code matches this pseudocode?
questions.code:
Set sum = 0
Input num
While num != 0
    Set sum = sum + num
    Input num
End While
Display sum
questions.explain:
The pattern needs two Input steps: one before the loop, so the first test has a value, and one as the last step inside the loop, so each test checks a new value. Display sum comes after End While. The match is the `while` loop whose braces hold `sum = sum + num;` and `cin >> num;`, with `cout << sum;` after the closing brace.

The other versions each break one part. Without the `cin` inside the loop, num never changes, so if the first number is not 0 the loop never ends. With `if` instead of `while`, the body runs at most once. With `cout` inside the braces, a running total appears on every pass instead of one result at the end.

questions.prompt: This pseudocode is run and the user types 3 and then 4. What is displayed?
questions.code:
Input a
Input b
Set c = a * a + b * b
Display c
questions.explain:
Input stores 3 in a and 4 in b. Then multiplication is done before addition, just as in ordinary math and in C++:
```
c = a * a + b * b
  = 3 * 3 + 4 * 4
  = 9 + 16
  = 25
```
The display is `25`. Working strictly left to right would give a wrong answer: 3 * 3 is 9, plus 4 is 13, times 4 is 52.

questions.prompt: In a flowchart, a diamond's Yes path runs some boxes and then a flow line goes back up to the same diamond. Which structure is this?
choices: Sequence
Selection
A connector
Repetition (a loop)
questions.explain:
Repetition, a loop. The line that goes back up to the diamond sends the flow through the same shapes again, and it keeps doing so until the answer is No.

Selection also uses a diamond, but its two paths join again below it and carry on down, never back up. Sequence has no diamond at all, just shapes in a straight line. A connector is the small circle that joins separate parts of a chart.

questions.prompt: You are drawing the flowchart for a program that reads a price and a tax rate, calculates the tax, and displays it. Which shape holds the step `tax = price * rate`?
choices: Parallelogram
Rectangle
Diamond
Oval
questions.explain:
A rectangle. `tax = price * rate` works out a value and stores it, which is a process, and processes are drawn as rectangles.

Reading the price and rate and displaying the tax are input and output, so those steps go in parallelograms. A diamond is for a yes/no decision, and nothing is being decided here. An oval only marks Start and End.

questions.prompt: A program reads a starting balance, the total of deposits, the total of withdrawals and a monthly interest rate, then calculates and displays the current balance. In its hierarchy chart, which box belongs at the very top?
choices: Read the total of deposits
Display the balance
Start
Find the current account balance
questions.explain:
The top box of a hierarchy chart names the whole task of the program. This program's whole job is to find the current account balance, so that is the top box.

Reading the total of deposits and displaying the balance are pieces of that job, so they go in boxes on a lower level. Start is a flowchart symbol, the oval that marks where the steps begin. A hierarchy chart shows how the job divides into parts, not the order of steps, so it has no Start box.

questions.prompt: In standard flowcharting, what does a rectangle with an extra vertical line just inside each side stand for?
choices: A predefined process: a call to a module or function that is charted separately
An input step
Two calculations done at the same time
The end of the program
questions.explain:
It is the predefined process symbol. It stands for a call to a module, such as a function, whose own steps are drawn in a separate flowchart. It lets the main chart say "do this whole job here" in one shape, without drawing every step of that job.

It is not an input step, which is a parallelogram, and not the end of the program, which is an oval. It does not mean two calculations at once. A flowchart shows one step at a time.

questions.prompt: One computer can run a game, a spreadsheet and a browser because its behavior is set by whatever instructions it is given: it is ___ (one word).
questions.explain: Programmable. A computer's hardware is not built for one fixed job. What it does at any moment depends on the program it is running: load a game and it plays the game, load a spreadsheet and it works with tables of numbers. The machine stays the same and only the instructions change. A device built for one job, like a kitchen timer, is the opposite of this.

questions.prompt: Which statement about main memory is correct?
choices: Each byte has a unique address, and each byte is made of eight bits
Bytes have no addresses; the CPU searches memory for the data it needs
Each bit has its own address, and a byte is two bits
A byte is sixteen bits, and only the first byte has an address
questions.explain:
Main memory is divided into bytes, each byte is 8 bits, and every byte has its own number, its address. The CPU uses the address to go straight to the byte it wants, the way a mail carrier goes straight to box 1000.

The wrong statements each break one of those facts. The CPU does not search memory, because it already knows the address. Addresses belong to bytes, not bits, and a byte is 8 bits, not 2 or 16. Every byte has an address, not just the first one.

questions.prompt: Each byte of main memory is identified by a unique number called its ___.
questions.explain: Address. Each byte of memory has a unique number, and the numbers run in order like post office boxes along a wall: 1000, 1001, 1002 and so on. The CPU finds data by asking for "the byte at address 1000". Later, when you define a variable such as `int total;`, the computer sets aside bytes for it and the name `total` stands for their address.

questions.prompt: A virus scanner, a file-compression program and a backup program are all examples of which kind of software?
choices: Application software
Operating systems
Software development tools
Utility programs, a kind of system software
questions.explain:
Utility programs, which count as system software. Each one does a specialized job that keeps the computer running well or protects its data: scanning for viruses, compressing files to save space, making backups. Their job is looking after the computer, not doing a task for the user.

They are not application software, because they do not do the user's own work like writing a letter. They are not operating systems, which are the core programs that manage the hardware and run everything else. Development tools are compilers, editors and debuggers, used to build programs.

questions.prompt: Source code written in a high-level language can usually be recompiled for a different kind of CPU with little or no editing. That property is called being ___.
questions.explain: Portable. A high-level language such as C++ is not written for one kind of CPU, so the same `.cpp` file can be taken to another kind of computer and compiled there, usually with few or no changes. For example, one source file can be compiled on a Windows PC and again on a Mac. Machine language is not portable: a program in one CPU's machine language will not run on a different kind of CPU.

questions.prompt: An object file can be run by itself, because the compiler has already translated it into machine language.
questions.explain: False. The object file does hold machine code, but only for your own statements. Code you call but did not write, such as the code behind `cout`, lives in the runtime library, and the compiler does not copy it in. It just leaves a note that it is needed. Until the linker adds that library code and writes the executable file, the program is incomplete. If you try to run an object file, the operating system refuses.

questions.prompt: Words such as int, double and return have a special meaning in C++ and may be used only for that purpose. They are called key words or ___ words.
questions.explain: Reserved. Key words such as `int`, `double` and `return` are reserved for the language: each has one fixed meaning, and you cannot use one as a name for your own variable. For example, `int return = 5;` will not compile. Key words are always lowercase, so `Int` is not one. Names like `cout` and `main` are not reserved words either.

questions.prompt: In the statement `total = price * qty;` which symbols are operators?
choices: ; and =
only *
= and *
* and ;
questions.explain:
`=` and `*`. An operator does something to values, called its operands. `*` multiplies `price` by `qty`, and `=` stores the result in `total`.

The semicolon is punctuation, not an operator. It does nothing to any value: it only marks where the statement ends. So any choice that includes `;` is wrong, and "only `*`" leaves out the assignment operator `=`.

questions.prompt: A named storage location in memory, whose value can change while the program runs, is a ___.
questions.explain: Variable. A variable is a storage location in memory that has a name, so the program can use the name instead of a memory address. Its value can change while the program runs, and each new value replaces the old one. For example, after `int count = 5;` then `count = 8;`, the variable holds 8 and the 5 is gone.

questions.prompt: In the nine-step programming process, which step comes right before typing the code?
choices: Run the program with test data
Check the model for logical errors
Validate the results
Correct errors found while running
questions.explain:
Checking the model for logical errors. The steps run: define the problem, visualize it running, build a model with design tools, check that model for logic errors, and only then type, save and compile the code. Fixing a mistake on paper is cheaper than fixing it in code.

The other choices all come after the code exists. Running with test data is step 7, correcting errors found while running is step 8, and validating the results is step 9.

questions.prompt: When you clearly define what a program is to do, which four items do you identify?
choices: Purpose, input, processing and output
Sequence, selection, repetition and hierarchy
Source code, object code, library and executable
Variables, constants, functions and objects
questions.explain:
Purpose, input, processing and output. To define a program you say what it is for, what data goes in, what is done to that data, and what comes out. For a pay program: purpose, find the pay. Input, hours and rate. Processing, multiply them. Output, the pay.

Sequence, selection and repetition are the ways steps can be arranged, covered in the next lesson, and a hierarchy chart is a design tool used at step 3. Source code, object code, the library and the executable belong to building the program, which comes later. Variables, constants, functions and objects are parts of code, which does not exist yet at step 1.

questions.prompt: Visualizing a program running means picturing, or sketching, its screens with sample input and output before you write the code.
questions.explain: True. Step 2 of the programming process is to visualize the program running: you put yourself in the user's place and picture or sketch each screen, with sample input and the output it should produce. Doing this before writing code settles what the program will ask for and what it will show. For a pay program the sketch might read `Hours worked: 40`, `Hourly rate: 12.5`, `Pay: 500`.

questions.prompt: What is an integrated development environment (IDE)?
choices: A collection of prewritten library code that the linker adds
The part of the operating system that loads programs into memory
A program that translates and runs one statement at a time
One package that combines a text editor, compiler, debugger and other tools under a single set of menus
questions.explain:
An IDE, or integrated development environment, is one package that brings together a text editor, a compiler, a debugger and other tools behind one set of menus. One click on Build or Run preprocesses, compiles, links and starts the program. Visual Studio is an example.

The other descriptions name different things. The collection of prewritten code that the linker adds is the runtime library. Loading programs into memory is a job of the operating system. Translating and running one statement at a time is what an interpreter does.

questions.prompt: The large collection of prewritten C++ code for jobs like screen output and math functions, which the linker joins to your object code, is called the ___ library.
questions.explain: Runtime. The runtime library is the large collection of prewritten code that comes with C++, for jobs such as screen output and math functions. When your program uses `cout`, you are using library code you did not write. The compiler does not put that code into your object file. The linker joins the pieces your program needs to your object code and writes the executable.

questions.prompt: Which part of the CPU coordinates the computer's operations and determines where to get the next instruction?
choices: The arithmetic and logic unit
Main memory
The control unit
Secondary storage
questions.explain:
The control unit. It is the director inside the CPU: it works out which instruction comes next, fetches it from memory, decodes it, and sends signals telling the other parts what to do.

The arithmetic and logic unit only does the arithmetic and comparisons it is told to do. It does not decide what happens next. Main memory and secondary storage are not parts of the CPU at all. They store instructions and data but do not coordinate anything.

questions.prompt: In what order does the CPU handle each instruction of a program?
choices: Fetch, decode, execute
Execute, decode, fetch
Fetch, execute, decode
Decode, fetch, execute
questions.explain:
Fetch, decode, execute. The control unit first fetches the next instruction from main memory. It then decodes it, working out which operation the stored number stands for. Finally the operation is executed by the right part, such as the ALU. Then the cycle repeats.

The order cannot change: the CPU cannot decode an instruction it has not fetched yet, and it cannot execute one it has not decoded. Every other order puts a step before the step it depends on.

units.title: Testing and debugging
units.summary: Kinds of errors, hand tracing, choosing test data, the classic C++ bug patterns, and stubs and drivers.

lessons.title: Kinds of errors and what the compiler tells you
lessons.book: Sections 1.6 and 3.10, pages 21 and 133; general debugging
lessons.html:
The one question that sorts every error: when does it show up?

A mistake in a program is called a bug. Debugging means finding and fixing bugs. Before you can fix a bug it helps to know what kind it is, and the kind depends on one thing: at what point the mistake shows up.

Recall from unit 1 the trip your code takes before it runs:

source file (.cpp)
   |  preprocessor   handles the # lines, such as #include
   |  compiler       checks the rules, writes an object file
   |  linker         joins your code to library code,
   v                 writes the executable file
executable  ->  you run it  ->  output on the screen

An object file is your code translated into machine language but not yet joined to library code, so it cannot run on its own. Think of each step as a checkpoint. Each checkpoint catches a different kind of mistake, and one kind slips past all of them. Two terms first: compile time means while the program is being built, and run time means while the finished program is running.

KindWho catches itWhenExecutable made?
Syntax errorthe compilercompile timeNo
Linker errorthe linkerend of the buildNo
Run-time errornobody, until it happensrun time: the program crashesYes
Logic erroronly you, by testing and tracingafter the run, when you check the answerYes

So to name an error, ask three questions in order. Did it build? Did it crash? Was the answer wrong?

Syntax errors: the compiler refuses

Every language has grammar rules, called its syntax. In C++ a statement ends with a semicolon, braces come in pairs, and every name must be declared before it is used. A syntax error is code that breaks those rules. The compiler cannot translate it, so it prints an error message and makes no object file and no executable. You cannot run the program at all until you fix it.

  • a missing semicolon: int total = 0
  • a misspelled key word or name: retrun 0; or cot << x;
  • a name that was never declared, such as using count with no int count; before it
  • a brace, parenthesis or quote mark with no partner
  • the wrong capital letter. C++ is case-sensitive: cout and Cout are two different names. Only cout exists, so Cout << "Total"; is an error. The compiler does not forgive it as a typo.

Intro courses call every error the compiler reports a syntax error or a compile error, including an undeclared name. Unlike Python, which reports a misspelled name only when that line runs, a C++ compiler checks every name in the file before the program can start.

Reading a compiler message

Here line 6 is missing its semicolon:

5  {
6      int total = 0
7      cout << total << endl;

g++ reports:

semi.cpp:7:5: error: expected ',' or ';' before 'cout'

Read it from the left: file semi.cpp, line 7, column 5, an error (not a warning), then the description. The line number is 7, not 6. The compiler cannot know the statement on line 6 is unfinished until it meets the next word, cout, on line 7. So when the line named in a message looks fine, check the end of the line above it.

One mistake, many messages

6      int a = 5, b = 2        // the only mistake: no ;
7      int sum = a + b;
8      cout << sum << endl;

g++ reports two errors for this one slip:

line 7: error: expected ',' or ';' before 'int'
line 8: error: 'sum' was not declared in this scope

The second message is a side effect of the first. Line 6 never ended, so the compiler could not make sense of line 7 and never created sum. Line 8 then seems to use a name that does not exist. Add the one semicolon and both errors disappear. A missing brace can produce dozens of messages this way.

The rule: fix the first error, then compile again, and see what is left. Do not start at the bottom of the list, and do not delete lines just because a message mentions them.

Warnings: legal, but probably wrong

Besides errors, a compiler can print warnings. A warning means the code follows the rules, so the compiler still builds the program, but something looks like a mistake.

  • An error stops the build. There is no executable.
  • A warning does not stop the build. You get an executable, possibly with a logic error inside it.
int x = 3;
int unused = 7;        // never used again
int sum;               // no starting value
sum += x;              // uses sum before it has a value
if (x = 5)             // = stores 5. == would compare.
    cout << "five" << endl;

Compiled with g++ and the option -Wall ("all warnings"), this code builds and runs, but g++ prints three warnings: the variable unused is never used, sum is used before it has a value, and "suggest parentheses around assignment used as truth value", which is g++ asking whether you meant ==. Without -Wall, g++ prints nothing for this code. IDEs such as Visual Studio have a warning level setting for the same job.

Two facts that get tested. A warning on its own does not stop the executable from being made. The g++ option -Werror treats every warning as an error, so with it the build does stop. Read every warning: many are logic errors caught early.

Linker errors: a promise with nothing behind it

From the functions unit: a prototype such as double computeTotal(double); tells the compiler a function's name, the type it returns and the types of its parameters. The definition is the header plus the body, the code in braces that does the work.

The compiler checks each call against the prototype. That is all it needs, so it accepts the call and writes the object file. Connecting each call to the function's actual code is the linker's job. If no definition was ever written, the linker has nothing to connect the call to:

double computeTotal(double);    // prototype only

int main()
{
    cout << computeTotal(50.0) << endl;
    return 0;
}
compile step:  succeeds, object file made
link step:     undefined reference to `computeTotal(double)'
result:        no executable

The words undefined reference (Visual Studio says unresolved external symbol) mark a linker error. The usual cause is a function that is declared and called but never defined, or defined with a different name or different parameter types than the prototype. Misspelling main, for example int mian(), gives the same kind of error: undefined reference to main.

Run-time errors: it builds, then crashes

A run-time error happens while the program is running. The program built and started, then tried to do something impossible and stopped abnormally. That is called a crash. The classic example is dividing an integer by zero:

int total, count;
cin >> total >> count;
cout << "Computing" << endl;
cout << total / count << endl;
cout << "Done" << endl;
input 90 3:   Computing
              30
              Done
input 90 0:   Computing
              (the program is stopped here. Done never appears.)

The compiler cannot catch this. total / count follows every rule, and the value of count does not exist until the user types it. C++ does not say what must happen on integer division by zero. It is undefined behavior: the language makes no promise. On most computers the operating system stops the program (on Linux with the confusing message "Floating point exception"). Python would stop with a clear ZeroDivisionError. C++ gives no such help, so careful programs check a divisor before dividing.

Logic errors: it runs, and the answer is wrong

A logic error is a mistake in the program's reasoning. The code follows every rule, so it compiles and links. It runs to the end without crashing. It just gives the wrong result.

int a = 4, b = 6;
double average = a + b / 2;      // meant (a + b) / 2
cout << "Average: " << average << endl;
b / 2        division happens first: 6 / 2 is 3
a + 3        4 + 3 is 7
prints       Average: 7        the correct average is 5

Nothing complained. The compiler checks the rules of the language, not what you meant. It has no idea you wanted an average. Other typical logic errors: < where <= was needed, = where == was meant, a loop that runs one time too few. A program with zero errors and zero warnings can still print the wrong answer. Only testing with inputs whose answers you already know, tracing by hand and careful reading find logic errors. The rest of this unit teaches those skills.

What does "runtime error" mean?

The textbook uses runtime error in a broad sense: any mistake that shows itself only once the finished program is running, as opposed to a syntax error, which the compiler finds. The book adds that most runtime errors are logic errors, such as a math mistake. In that broad sense, both the crash and the wrong average above are runtime errors. A statement like "a mistake that shows up only while the program is executing is called a runtime error" is true.

When a question offers logic error and run-time error as separate choices, use the narrow meanings:

  • It will not compile: syntax error.
  • It compiles but will not link ("undefined reference"): linker error.
  • It stops abnormally while running: run-time error.
  • It runs to the end with wrong output: logic error.

Mistakes students make

  • Calling a wrong answer a syntax error. If the program compiled and ran, it has no syntax error.
  • Thinking the compiler would have caught a logic error. It checks rules, not intent.
  • Starting with the last message in a long error list. Fix the first, then recompile.
  • Looking only at the line in the message. A missing semicolon is usually reported on the next line.
  • Ignoring warnings because the program still built. A warning often marks a logic error.
  • Thinking a warning stops the build. Only errors do, unless -Werror is used.
  • Blaming the compiler for "undefined reference". That message comes from the linker: a function was declared and called, but its body was never written.
  • Expecting the compiler to catch division by zero. When the divisor is a variable, its value is not known until the program runs.

What to remember for the test

  • Syntax error: breaks the language rules. The compiler reports it, and no executable is made. Examples: missing ;, a misspelled or wrongly capitalized name such as Cout, an unmatched brace.
  • Linker error: "undefined reference". A function has a prototype and is called but was never defined. No executable.
  • Run-time error: builds and starts, then crashes. Example: integer division by zero.
  • Logic error: builds, runs to the end, gives the wrong result. Only testing and tracing find it.
  • Warning: legal but suspicious code. The build still finishes. -Wall turns on more warnings, and -Werror turns warnings into errors.
  • One slip can cause many messages: fix the first one and recompile.
  • In the book's broad sense, any error that shows up only while the program runs is a "runtime error".

lessons.title: Hand tracing and desk-checking
lessons.html:
The idea: you play the computer

Hand tracing means running a program yourself, on paper. You pretend to be the computer. You carry out one statement at a time, exactly as it is written, and you write down every variable's value as it changes and everything the program prints. Unit 1 called the same activity desk-checking: stepping through a program or an algorithm on paper, at your desk. The two names mean the same skill.

Why do it when you could just run the program? Three reasons.

  • It finds logic errors, the bugs the compiler cannot see, because you compare what the code really does with what it should do.
  • You can check a flowchart or pseudocode before any code exists. That is step 4 of the programming process: check the model for logical errors.
  • Every "what does this print" exam question is a hand trace, with no computer allowed.

Hold one picture in mind. A variable is a box that holds exactly one value. An assignment such as x = y + 1; works in two steps: first work out the right side using the values in the boxes right now, then put the result in the box on the left. The value that was in that box before is gone. It is not saved anywhere.

The trace table

A trace table has one column per variable, a column for output if you need one, and one row for every statement the program carries out. A value you do not know yet is written as ?.

  1. Choose sample input and work out, by hand, the answer the program should give.
  2. Go one statement at a time. Work out the right side using the latest values in the table.
  3. Write the new value in that variable's column. Every other variable keeps its value until a statement changes it.
  4. When a statement prints, write down exactly what it prints.
  5. Compare the result with the answer you expected. If they differ, the first row where a value goes wrong points to the bug.

Here is a program that is meant to average three numbers:

double n1, n2, n3, avg;
n1 = 10; n2 = 20; n3 = 30;
avg = n1 + n2 + n3 / 3;
cout << avg << endl;
aftern1n2n3avg
n1 = 1010???
n2 = 201020??
n3 = 30102030?
avg = ...10203040

The average of 10, 20 and 30 should be 20. The table shows 40, so the last row is where it goes wrong. Look hard at that statement. Division has higher precedence than addition, which means it is done first. So only n3 was divided:

n3 / 3          30 / 3 is 10      (done first)
n1 + n2 + 10    10 + 20 + 10 is 40

The fix is parentheses: avg = (n1 + n2 + n3) / 3; gives 20. Note also how the result prints. avg is a double holding 40.0, and cout prints a double that has no fractional part without a decimal point. The screen shows 40, not 40.0.

The value that disappears: a failed swap

This code is meant to swap a and b:

int a = 3, b = 8;
a = b;
b = a;
cout << a << " " << b << endl;
afterabnote
start38
a = b88the 3 is gone
b = a88copies 8 back into b

It prints 8 8. Once a = b has run, no box holds 3 any more, so nothing can put it back. A swap needs a third variable to keep the old value safe:

int temp = a;    // temp 3, a 3, b 8
a = b;           // temp 3, a 8, b 8
b = temp;        // temp 3, a 8, b 3

Now it prints 8 3.

Tracing a for loop

A loop runs the same lines many times, so the table gets one row per pass (one run of the loop body), not one row per line of code. Recall how for (int i = 1; i <= 3; i++) works. It sets i to 1 once. It tests i <= 3 before every pass. If the test is true it runs the body, then adds 1 to i. When the test is false the loop ends and the body does not run. Write the test in the table too, including the final one that fails.

int x = 0;
for (int i = 1; i <= 3; i++)
    x = x * 10 + i;
cout << x << endl;
ii <= 3?x = x * 10 + ix
start0
1true0 * 10 + 11
2true1 * 10 + 212
3true12 * 10 + 3123
4falseloop ends123

It prints 123. Each pass uses the x from the row above, not the starting 0.

Counting passes: a loop that starts i at 1 and runs while i <= 4 makes 4 passes (1, 2, 3, 4). With i < 4 it makes only 3 (1, 2, 3). In general, from a up to b with <= is b - a + 1 passes.

Tracing a while loop with a decision inside

Two operators you will meet in traces. % gives the remainder of a division: 7 % 2 is 1 and 6 % 2 is 0, so n % 2 == 0 is true exactly when n is even. And / on two int values drops the fraction: 7 / 2 is 3.

int n = 7, steps = 0;
while (n > 1)
{
    if (n % 2 == 0)
        n = n / 2;
    else
        n = n - 1;
    steps++;
}
n > 1?n even?new nsteps
start: 70
7 > 1 trueno7 - 1 = 61
6 > 1 trueyes6 / 2 = 32
3 > 1 trueno3 - 1 = 23
2 > 1 trueyes2 / 2 = 14
1 > 1 falseloop ends4

The body ran 4 times, so steps is 4. Watch the trap: n held the values 7, 6, 3, 2 and 1. That is five values but only four passes, because 7 was there before the loop started. Count the rows where the body ran, not the values in the list.

Tracing input: a loop that stops at a sentinel

When code reads input, each cin >> num takes the next value the user typed, in order. Cross each value off as it is used. Many loops read until a special value called a sentinel, which means "no more data". The sentinel is not data, so it must not be counted or added.

int num, total = 0, count = 0;
cin >> num;
while (num != -1)
{
    total += num;
    count++;
    cin >> num;
}
cout << count << " " << total << endl;

The user types 6 2 9 -1. (!= means "not equal", and total += num means total = total + num.)

stepnumcounttotal
first cin600
6 != -1, pass 1216
2 != -1, pass 2928
9 != -1, pass 3-1317
-1 != -1 is false-1317

It prints 3 17. The program reads one value before the loop and the next value at the end of each pass. So the test always sees a new value before it is processed, and when -1 arrives the loop ends without adding it. Four values were read, but only three were counted.

A related pattern keeps the largest value seen so far: if (num > big) big = num;. With big starting at 0 and the same input: 6 is bigger than 0, so big becomes 6. 2 is not bigger than 6, so nothing changes. 9 is bigger than 6, so big becomes 9. Each value is compared with the current big, not with the value just before it.

Mistakes students make

  • Using a value after it has been replaced, or a new value before the statement that sets it. Always use the latest row.
  • Thinking a = b; b = a; swaps two variables. Both end up with b's old value.
  • Doing the additions before the division. *, / and % are done before + and -.
  • Counting the values a variable took instead of the passes the loop made.
  • Running the body one extra time. When the test is false, the body does not run.
  • Adding or counting the sentinel.
  • Writing 40.0 when cout prints a whole-number double as 40.
  • Skipping step 1. If you do not know the expected answer first, a trace cannot show you a bug.

What to remember for the test

  • Hand tracing and desk-checking are the same thing: run the code on paper, one statement at a time, with a column per variable, writing down what is printed.
  • Assignment: right side first with the current values, then store. The old value is lost.
  • A swap needs a third variable.
  • For a loop: one row per pass, and record each test, including the last one, which is false.
  • i from 1 while i <= n is n passes. While i < n it is n - 1 passes.
  • A sentinel ends the loop and is never processed.
  • The first row that differs from what you expected points to the bug.

lessons.title: Choosing test data
lessons.book: Section 1.6 (pages 21 and 22) and 3.10, plus general testing practice
lessons.html:
The idea: a test is a question whose answer you already know

Testing means running a program with chosen input and checking whether the output is right. The key word is checking. You can only check an answer if you know what it should be. So a test case has two parts:

  • the input you will give the program, and
  • the expected output: the correct answer, worked out by hand from the problem before you run the program.

Then you run the program and compare. If the actual output matches the expected output, the test passes. If not, you have found a bug. If you have written Python tests with assert, it is the same idea.

Why work out the answer first? Suppose you run the program, then copy what it printed into your "expected" column. Now the test agrees with the program by definition. A wrong answer becomes the expected answer, and the test can never fail. That is not a test at all.

Bugs live at the edges

Most programs make decisions at cut-off values: 60 or more passes, a score must be 0 to 100. Each cut-off is one comparison in the code, and the most common slip is getting it off by one: > where >= was meant, or 59 where 60 was meant. A slip like that changes the answer only for values right at the cut-off. Values far from it come out right either way. So the values worth testing are the ones at and next to every edge.

Here is a correct program. (|| means "or": the condition is true if either side is true.)

int score;
cin >> score;
if (score < 0 || score > 100)
    cout << "invalid" << endl;
else if (score >= 60)
    cout << "pass" << endl;
else
    cout << "fail" << endl;

Now suppose the programmer had written score > 60 by mistake. Here is what three tests show:

inputexpectedbuggy programresult
40failfailtest passes
90passpasstest passes
60passfailbug found

40 and 90 sit far from the cut-off, so they pass even though the code is wrong. Only 60, the value exactly on the boundary, catches it: 60 is not greater than 60, so the program says fail.

One test at the cut-off is not enough, though. Suppose instead the programmer wrote score >= 59. Now 60 gives pass, which is correct, so the test at 60 passes. Only 59 catches this bug, because the program passes a 59 that should fail. That is why boundary tests sit on both sides of each cut-off: 59 and 60, and 61 if you want one more just inside.

Three kinds of test data

  • Normal data (also called typical data): ordinary values well inside the allowed range, such as 75 or 30 for a score from 0 to 100. They check the everyday path.
  • Boundary data: values at the edges of a range or at a cut-off, and right next to them. For a range of 0 to 100 that means 0 and 100 (the edges) and 1 and 99 (just inside). For the pass mark, 59 and 60.
  • Invalid data: input the program should reject or handle safely, such as a score of -5, letters where a number is expected, or 0 when the value will be used as a divisor. It checks that bad input neither crashes the program nor slips through as if it were good.

The values just outside a range, -1 and 101 here, are both things at once: they are invalid, and they sit right at the boundary. They check that the edge of the valid range is in the right place. So a strong set for "0 to 100 inclusive" (inclusive means 0 and 100 themselves are allowed) is:

-1   0   1   50   99   100   101

It has invalid values on both sides, both edges, their neighbors just inside, and one normal value. Written as a test plan for the score program:

inputkindexpected
75, 30normalpass, fail
59, 60boundary (pass mark)fail, pass
0, 100boundary (range edges)fail, pass
-1, 101invalid, just outsideinvalid, invalid

"Random data" is not one of the kinds. Numbers picked at random almost never land exactly on an edge or a cut-off, which is exactly where bugs hide.

A decision with several branches

Each cut-off between two branches is its own boundary, and each needs a test on both sides. This program prints cold below 50, mild for 50 to 79, and hot for 80 and over:

if (t < 50)
    cout << "cold" << endl;
else if (t < 80)
    cout << "mild" << endl;
else
    cout << "hot" << endl;

Its cut-offs are between 49 and 50, and between 79 and 80. So the boundary tests are 49 and 50, then 79 and 80, expecting cold, mild, mild, hot. Normal values such as 30, 65 and 95 run each branch once, which is worth doing, but they would not notice t <= 50 written where t < 50 belongs. Testing only 50 and 80, one side of each cut-off, would miss a cut-off placed one too low, such as t < 49.

Cover every path

A path is one route a program can take through its decisions. Good tests make every path run at least once.

  • For an if with an else, test at least one input that makes the condition true and one that makes it false.
  • For a chain of four branches, you need at least four inputs, one per branch, plus the boundary pairs between them.
  • For a loop, test it running zero times, once, and many times. Zero and one are the boundaries of a loop.

Here is why the loop rule matters. This program averages n numbers:

int n, num, total = 0;
cin >> n;
for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++)
{
    cin >> num;
    total += num;
}
cout << "Average: " << total / n << endl;
inputexpectedprogram does
n = 3: 4 5 6Average: 5Average: 5
n = 1: 7Average: 7Average: 7
n = 0a message, no crashcrashes: integer division by zero

The typical value 3 works, and so does 1. Only n = 0 shows that the program crashes when there is nothing to average. And if the loop had been written i < n by mistake, n = 1 would make it plain: the loop would not run at all, and the program would print Average: 0 instead of 7.

Other special cases worth a test: an empty list, all values equal, the largest and smallest values allowed, and a negative number where only positive ones make sense.

What testing can and cannot prove

Passing one test proves very little. Even passing many tests does not prove a program correct, because you cannot try every possible input: on most systems an int alone has over four billion values. Testing can show that bugs exist. It can never prove that none remain. Choosing test data at the edges makes it far more likely that the bugs that do exist are found.

The last step of the programming process is to validate the results: check that the finished program solves the original problem, not just that it matches your own design. If the problem said "60 or more passes" and your design said "more than 60", tests built from your design would all pass, and the program would still be wrong.

Mistakes students make

  • Running the program first and using its output as the expected result.
  • Testing only normal values. They miss off-by-one bugs at the cut-offs.
  • Testing only the cut-off value and not the value just across it.
  • Testing only valid input. Invalid input is where many crashes come from.
  • Forgetting the zero-pass and one-pass cases of a loop.
  • Believing that a program which passes one test, or many tests, is proven correct.
  • Calling -1 or 101 normal data for a 0 to 100 range. They are invalid values that sit at the boundary.

What to remember for the test

  • A test case is an input plus the expected output, worked out by hand before running.
  • Normal data: well inside the range. Boundary data: at and next to each edge or cut-off. Invalid data: input that should be rejected.
  • For a range of 0 to 100: -1, 0, 1, 50, 99, 100, 101.
  • For each cut-off, test both sides: 59 and 60 for "60 or more passes".
  • Make every branch run at least once. Test loops with 0, 1 and many passes.
  • Testing shows that bugs exist. It never proves that none remain.
  • Validate: does the program solve the original problem?

lessons.html:
The idea: legal code that means something else

The bugs in this lesson have one thing in common: the code is legal. It compiles, so nothing stops you, but it means something different from what the programmer intended. C++ does exactly what you wrote, not what you meant. Most of these are logic errors. To spot them, read code the way the compiler does: by its symbols, never by its indentation or what the variable names suggest. Each bug below shows the wrong version, a trace of what really happens, and the fix.

1. = where == was meant

== compares two values. = assigns: it stores a value in a variable. In C++ an assignment also has a value, the value just stored. And a condition treats any nonzero number as true and 0 as false. So an assignment inside an if compiles, and it does two things: it changes the variable, and it picks the branch by the number it stored.

int x = 8;
if (x = 2)               // meant: if (x == 2)
    cout << "two ";
cout << x << endl;
x = 2      stores 2 in x. The condition's value is 2.
2          nonzero, so true: prints "two "
cout x     x is now 2: prints 2
output:    two 2

With if (y = 0) the stored value is 0, which is false, so the else branch runs, and y is now 0 whatever it held before. Python rejects if x = 2: outright. C++ accepts it, though g++ with -Wall warns "suggest parentheses around assignment used as truth value".

2. A stray semicolon

A semicolon on its own is a complete statement that does nothing, called an empty statement. An if, while or for controls exactly one statement: the one right after its parentheses. Put a semicolon there and the empty statement becomes the thing it controls.

int n = 1;
if (n > 10);             // the ; is the whole if body
    cout << "large";     // not part of the if: always runs

This prints large even though 1 is not greater than 10. The if decided whether to do nothing, and then the cout ran as the next ordinary statement. On a while the result is worse:

int k = 5;
while (k > 0);           // the body is the empty statement
{
    cout << k << " ";
    k--;
}

k > 0 is true. The empty body runs and changes nothing, so the test is true again, and again, forever. The braced block is a separate block that would run only after the loop ended, and the loop never ends. In practice the program hangs, printing nothing, until someone stops it. On a for, for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++); makes three passes of nothing, and the statement after it then runs once.

3. Missing braces

Without braces, an if, else or loop controls only the one statement after it. Braces { } group several statements into a block, which counts as one statement. Indentation means nothing to the compiler. This is the biggest change from Python, where indentation decides what belongs to an if or a loop. In C++ only braces do.

for (int i = 1; i <= 2; i++)
    cout << i;
    cout << "!";         // looks inside the loop. It is not.
pass i = 1    prints 1
pass i = 2    prints 2
i = 3         test fails, loop ends
then          cout << "!" runs once
output:       12!

With braces around both lines the output is 1!2!. The same goes for if: when two indented lines follow if (m < 0) with no braces, the second one runs every time. g++ -Wall warns "this 'for' clause does not guard..." when indentation is misleading.

4. A missing break in a switch

A switch jumps to the case label that matches, then runs statements downward until it reaches a break or the closing brace. Other case labels do not stop it. Running on into the next case is called falling through. default is where it jumps when no case matches.

switch (code)
{
    case 1: cout << "red ";
    case 2: cout << "green ";
            break;
    case 3: cout << "blue ";
    default: cout << "none";
}
codeoutputwhy
1red greenstarts at case 1, falls into case 2, stops at break
2greenstarts at case 2, stops at break
3blue noneno break after case 3, so it falls into default
4noneno case matches, so default runs

5. Integer division

When both sides of / are integers, C++ does integer division and throws the fraction away: 7 / 2 is 3. Python 3's / would give 3.5. For positive numbers, C++ behaves like Python's // here. The type of the variable that receives the result does not help, because the division happens first.

int total = 9, count = 2;
double a1 = total / count;                       // 4
double a2 = static_cast<double>(total) / count;  // 4.5
double a3 = static_cast<double>(total / count);  // 4
cout << a1 << " " << a2 << endl;               // 4 4.5

a1: 9 / 2 is 4, and only then is 4 stored as 4.0. a2: static_cast<double>(total) makes a double copy of total, and one double operand is enough to keep the fraction. a3 casts the result, which is too late: the fraction is already gone. Writing total / 2.0 also works. Note that cout prints the double 4.0 as 4. And %, the remainder, works only on integers.

6. A variable that was never given a value

A local variable declared without a value, such as int sum;, does not start at 0. It holds whatever bits were left in that memory, often called garbage. Using it is undefined behavior: C++ makes no promise about the result, and it can change from run to run.

int sum;                       // bug: unpredictable start
for (int i = 1; i <= 3; i++)
    sum += i;                  // adds to garbage

The loop is fine. The fix is the starting value: int sum = 0;. Start a running total at 0 and a running product at 1. Python stops with an error if you use a name before assigning it. C++ gives no error. g++ -Wall sometimes warns that a variable "is used uninitialized", but not always: for this loop it prints no warning at all. Do not count on one.

7. Off by one

An off-by-one error is a loop that runs one time too many or one time too few. It comes from < written where <= was needed (or the reverse), or from starting at 0 instead of 1. It is also called a fencepost error: a 10-meter fence with a post every meter needs 11 posts, not 10.

int sum = 0;
for (int i = 1; i < 4; i++)    // meant to add 1 to 4
    sum += i;
// i is 1, 2, 3. At i = 4 the test 4 < 4 is false.
// sum is 1 + 2 + 3 = 6, not 10

Count passes with this rule. Starting at 1, i <= n runs n times and i < n runs n - 1 times. Starting at 0, i < n runs n times and i <= n runs n + 1 times.

8. And versus or

&& means AND: true only when both sides are true. || means OR: true when at least one side is true. Python spells them and and or. To test that a value is outside a range you need ||:

int level = -5;
if (level < 1 && level > 10)    // meant: outside 1 to 10
    cout << "bad level";
else
    cout << "fine";

No number is below 1 and above 10 at the same time, so the && condition is always false, and this prints fine even for -5. With level < 1 || level > 10 it prints bad level. Testing for inside a range is the opposite: level >= 1 && level <= 10. Precedence causes a related slip: a + b / 2 divides only b, so an average needs (a + b) / 2.

9. Comparing doubles with ==

A double stores most decimal fractions only approximately. It works in binary, and values such as 0.1 have no exact binary form, so tiny rounding differences appear in the last digits. 0.1 + 0.2 comes out as about 0.30000000000000004, not 0.3. cout normally shows only 6 significant digits, so it prints 0.3 and hides the difference.

double t = 0.1 + 0.2;
if (t == 0.3)                  // false
    cout << "equal";
if (fabs(t - 0.3) < 0.0001)    // true
    cout << "close enough";

Python has the same problem: 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 is False there too. == on doubles is legal. It just cannot be trusted. Instead compare with a tolerance: check that the difference is smaller than some tiny amount. fabs, from <cmath>, gives the absolute value of a double (its size without the sign).

10. A loop that never ends

A loop stops only when its test becomes false, so something in the body must change what the test looks at. If nothing does, the result is an infinite loop.

int count = 10;
while (count > 0)
{
    cout << count << " ";      // count never changes
}

This prints 10 10 10 ... without end. Adding count--; inside the braces makes it print 10 down to 1 and stop. Compare the stray-semicolon while in pattern 2, which also never ends but prints nothing, because its body is empty.

Mistakes students make

  • Reading indentation instead of braces. Only braces group statements.
  • Thinking if (x = 5) will not compile. It compiles, it is always true, and it sets x to 5.
  • Forgetting that an assignment in a condition changed the variable, so a later cout << x shows the new value.
  • Thinking a switch stops at the next case label. Only break or the closing brace stops it.
  • Expecting double r = 7 / 2; to store 3.5, or casting after the division.
  • Assuming an uninitialized variable starts at 0.
  • Using && for an outside-the-range test.
  • Expecting a stray semicolon to cause a compile error. It is legal code.

What to remember for the test

  • In a condition, nonzero is true and 0 is false. if (x = 5) is always true and if (x = 0) is always false. Both change x.
  • An if, else or loop controls one statement or one braced block. A ; right after its parentheses makes the body empty.
  • A switch falls through until a break.
  • int / int drops the fraction, even when the result is stored in a double. Cast an operand before dividing.
  • Start totals at 0 and products at 1.
  • Starting at 1: <= n runs n times, < n runs n - 1 times.
  • Outside a range: ||. Inside a range: &&.
  • Compare doubles with a tolerance, such as fabs(a - b) < 0.0001.
  • A loop body must change what the loop's test checks.
