lessons.book: Section 6.16, pages 372 and 373; debugger use from general practice
lessons.html:
The idea: test one piece at a time

A program built from functions is like a machine built from parts. If you assemble the whole machine and it does not work, you cannot tell which part is broken. So you test each part on its own first. This lesson gives you two tools for that, plus two ways to watch a program while it runs.

A few words from the functions unit. The caller is the code that calls a function, often main. The arguments are the values the caller passes in. return sends a value back, and the caller can use the call as a value, as in price + getTax(price).

Every function call has two sides: the caller on the left, the function on the right.

caller (main)  --- arguments --->  function
               <--- return value ---

A stub replaces the function, so you can test the caller. A driver replaces the caller, so you can test the function. Keep that picture and the two terms never get mixed up.

Stubs: a stand-in for a function that is not ready

A stub is a dummy function used in place of a real one that is not written yet, or not yet trusted. It does not do the real work. Usually it only prints a message saying it was called, often with the argument values it received. If the real function returns a value, the stub returns a fixed test value that you choose, so the caller can carry on.

double shippingCost(double weight)    // stub
{
    cout << "shippingCost called with "
         << weight << endl;
    return 5.0;                       // fixed test value
}

int main()
{
    double weight = 12.5;
    double total = 40 + shippingCost(weight);
    cout << "Total: " << total << endl;
    return 0;
}

Trace it in the order things happen:

weight = 12.5
total = 40 + shippingCost(weight)    the call runs first
   stub prints:   shippingCost called with 12.5
   stub returns:  5.0
total = 40 + 5.0 = 45
main prints:      Total: 45

The output is two lines: shippingCost called with 12.5, then Total: 45. The stub's message comes first, because it is printed during the call, before main reaches its own cout. A stub's messages always appear at the moment each call happens, mixed in with the caller's output.

What did this run check? That main calls the function at the right moment, that it passes the right argument (12.5 shows in the message), and that it uses the returned value correctly. You chose 5, so you know the total must be 45. None of this needed a real shipping formula.

A stub must still match the function's return type. A stand-in for a function that returns an int must return an int, normally a fixed one such as return 3;. A void function returns nothing, so its stub just prints its message. Stubs are ideal for testing a menu before any of its jobs are written:

void addItem()   { cout << "addItem called" << endl; }
void showList()  { cout << "showList called" << endl; }

int main()
{
    int choice;
    cin >> choice;
    if (choice == 1)
        addItem();
    else if (choice == 2)
        showList();
    else
        cout << "Bad choice" << endl;
    return 0;
}

Input 1 prints addItem called, input 2 prints showList called, and input 7 prints Bad choice. The menu logic is tested while the two functions are still empty.

Drivers: a stand-in for the caller

A driver is a small program, often just a main, whose only job is to call one function with test data and show what comes back. The function is real. The driver tests it by itself, apart from the rest of the program. Write the expected answer next to each call, worked out by hand, exactly as in the lesson on test data.

double fToC(double f)                // the real function
{
    return (f - 32) * 5 / 9;
}

int main()                           // driver for fToC
{
    cout << fToC(212) << endl;       // expect 100
    cout << fToC(32) << endl;        // expect 0
    cout << fToC(-40) << endl;       // expect -40
    return 0;
}

It prints 100, 0 and -40, one per line, so all three tests pass. Drivers often keep the test values in an array, a numbered list of values of one type, and loop over it. In double tests[3] = {212, 32, -40}; the elements are numbered from 0, so tests[0] is 212, tests[1] is 32 and tests[2] is -40.

double tests[3] = {212, 32, -40};
for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++)
    cout << tests[i] << " -> " << fToC(tests[i]) << endl;
i = 0   tests[0] is 212   prints 212 -> 100
i = 1   tests[1] is 32    prints 32 -> 0
i = 2   tests[2] is -40   prints -40 -> -40

Each line shows the input and the result side by side, which makes a wrong result easy to spot.

Stub or driver?

ToolStands in forLets you testUse it when
Stubthe functionthe callerthe caller is ready, the function is not
Driverthe callerthe functionthe function is ready and you want to check it alone

Together they let you build a program a piece at a time. Write main with stubs and run it early. Then write one real function, check it with a driver using normal, boundary and invalid values, and swap it in for its stub. Repeat until no stubs are left, then run the whole program on full test data.

Diagnostic output: printing values while it runs

When a program gives a wrong answer and you do not know where it goes wrong, add temporary cout statements that print variable values at key points. These are diagnostic lines. In a loop, print the pass number, the value just read and the running total on every pass.

int total = 0, num;
for (int i = 1; i <= 3; i++)
{
    cin >> num;
    total = num;           // bug: should be total += num
    cout << "pass " << i << ": num " << num
         << " total " << total << endl;   // diagnostic
}

With input 4 6 5 the diagnostic lines are:

pass 1: num 4 total 4
pass 2: num 6 total 6      should be 10
pass 3: num 5 total 5

The first wrong line is pass 2, and the only statement that changes total is the bug. A single cout after the loop would show only that the final total, 5, is wrong, not where. A message such as "starting" or "done" shows that the program reached a point but says nothing about the values. Delete the diagnostic lines, or comment them out, once the bug is fixed.

The debugger: an automatic hand trace

A debugger is a tool, built into most IDEs such as Visual Studio, that runs your program under your control and lets you look inside it while it is running. Python IDEs have the same tool. The words to know:

  • Breakpoint: a line you mark. When the running program reaches it, the program pauses before carrying out that line.
  • Step: run just the next statement, then pause again. Stepping lets you go through the code one statement at a time.
  • Watch: a list of variables whose current values the debugger shows while the program is paused.

Pausing, stepping and watching is the hand-trace table again, but filled in by the computer. You see each value as it changes, not only after the program has finished.

Mistakes students make

  • Mixing up the two tools. A stub replaces the function. A driver replaces the caller.
  • Reaching for a driver when the function does not exist yet. A driver needs a real function to call. Use a stub.
  • Writing the full algorithm in a stub. Then it is not a stub, it is the real function.
  • Leaving out the return value in a stub for a function that returns a value. The caller needs a value to carry on.
  • Forgetting that the stub's message is part of the output, printed at the moment of the call.
  • Running a driver without writing the expected answers first.
  • Putting one diagnostic cout after the loop instead of inside it, or leaving diagnostic lines in the finished program.
  • Thinking a debugger shows values only after the program ends. It shows them while the program is paused.

What to remember for the test

  • Stub: a dummy function standing in for one that is not ready. It prints that it was called, often with its arguments, and returns a fixed test value if the function returns a value. It tests the caller.
  • Driver: a small program that calls a function with test data and displays the results. It tests the function.
  • Function not written yet: use a stub. Function written but untested: use a driver.
  • Diagnostic output inside a loop: pass number, value read, running total. Remove it afterwards.
  • Debugger: a breakpoint pauses at a line, step runs one statement, a watch shows current values while paused.

questions.prompt: A program has a missing semicolon at the end of a statement. What kind of error is this?
choices: Logic error
Syntax error
Run-time error
Validation error
questions.explain:
A missing semicolon breaks the grammar rules of C++, so it is a syntax error. The compiler finds it while building, prints a message with a line number (often the line after the missing semicolon), and makes no executable.

A logic error and a run-time error both need a program that has compiled and is running, and this program never gets that far. "Validation error" is not one of the kinds of error. Validating is a step in the programming process, not an error: it means checking that a finished program solves the real problem. Input validation is something else again: code you write to check what the user types.

questions.prompt: A program compiles with no messages and runs to the end, but it prints 7 where the correct answer is 5. What kind of error is it?
choices: Syntax error
Compiler warning
Logic error
Linker error
questions.explain:
Ask the three questions. Did it build? Yes. Did it crash? No. Was the answer wrong? Yes. A program that runs to the end and gives a wrong result has a logic error: the code follows the rules but does not do what was intended. For example, `a + b / 2` with a = 4 and b = 6 prints 7 instead of the average 5.

A syntax error or a linker error would have stopped the build, so there would be no program to run. A compiler warning is a message printed while building, and the question says there were no messages.

questions.prompt: A program compiles, but when run it crashes at the moment it divides an int by an int variable that holds 0. What kind of error is this?
questions.code:
int a = 10, b = 0;
cout << a / b;
choices: Syntax error
Logic error caught by the compiler
Preprocessor error
Run-time error
questions.explain:
The program built and started, then stopped abnormally in the middle of running. A failure that happens while the program runs is a run-time error.

The compiler only checks that `a / b` follows the rules, which it does. It does not work out what value `b` will hold when that line runs, so it builds the program without complaint. g++ with `-Wall` gives no warning for this code. Integer division by zero has no defined result in C++, and on most computers the operating system ends the program.

"Logic error caught by the compiler" does not fit either part. The compiler did not stop this program. It built it. And a logic error means the program runs to the end with a wrong answer, while this one stopped abnormally. A preprocessor error, such as `#include <iostrem>`, would stop the build before the program could run at all.

questions.prompt: A compiler warning, unlike a compiler error, does not by itself stop the executable file from being created.
questions.explain:
True. An error means the code breaks the rules, and the build stops with no executable. A warning means the code is legal but looks suspicious, such as an unused variable or `if (x = 5)`. The compiler reports it and still finishes the build.

The one exception is when you tell the compiler to treat warnings as errors, for example with g++'s `-Werror` option. Even when the build succeeds, read every warning, because many of them point straight at a logic error.

questions.prompt: A mistake that lets a program compile and run but produces wrong results is called a ___ error.
questions.explain:
The answer is logic error. The program follows every rule of C++, so it compiles and runs, but what it computes is not what the programmer meant.

Example: `average = a + b / 2;` divides only `b`, so with a = 4 and b = 6 it gives 7 instead of 5. The compiler checks rules, not intentions, so it cannot see this. Only testing with known answers and tracing by hand find logic errors.

questions.prompt: Hand trace this code. What does it print? Assume the code is inside main(), with iostream included and using namespace std; in effect.
questions.explain:
Division is done before addition, so only `n3` is divided.
```
n3 / 3         18 / 3 is 6       (done first)
n1 + n2 + 6    6 + 12 + 6 is 24
avg            24.0
```
`cout` prints a double with no fractional part without the decimal point, so the output is `24`.

The tempting answer is 12, the true average of 6, 12 and 18. Getting that needs parentheses: `(n1 + n2 + n3) / 3`. This is exactly how a trace exposes a logic error: you expected 12, the trace gives 24, and the difference shows up on this one line.

questions.prompt: Hand trace this code. What does it print? Assume the code is inside main(), with iostream included and using namespace std; in effect.
questions.explain:
Make a row for each pass, and always use the x from the row before.
```
i   i <= 4?   x = x * 2 + i
1   true      0 * 2 + 1  = 1
2   true      1 * 2 + 2  = 4
3   true      4 * 2 + 3  = 11
4   true      11 * 2 + 4 = 26
5   false     loop ends
```
The loop makes 4 passes, for i = 1, 2, 3 and 4. After the last pass x is 26, and that is printed. Common slips are stopping at i = 3 (getting 11) and forgetting that each pass doubles the new x, not the starting 0.

questions.prompt: The programmer meant to swap a and b. What does this print? Assume the code is inside main(), with iostream included and using namespace std; in effect.
questions.explain:
Trace the two boxes in order.
```
start     a = 5   b = 9
a = b     a = 9   b = 9    the 5 is now gone
b = a     a = 9   b = 9    copies 9 back into b
```
The output is `9 9`. The tempting answer is `9 5`, a working swap. But once `a = b` has run, no variable holds 5 any more, so the second statement can only copy 9. A swap needs a third variable to keep the old value: `int temp = a; a = b; b = temp;`.

questions.prompt: Stepping through a program by hand and writing down each variable's value after each statement is called hand tracing or ___-checking.
questions.explain: The word is desk, as in desk-checking. It means stepping through a program or an algorithm on paper, writing down each variable's value after every statement and noting what is printed. For `a = 3; b = a * 2;` a desk-check records a as 3, then b as 6. It is the same skill as hand tracing, and it finds logic errors without running the program.

questions.prompt: How many times does the body of this loop run?
questions.explain:
Trace one row per pass. `n % 2 == 0` means n is even.
```
n     even?   new n            steps
10    yes     10 / 2 = 5       1
5     no      3 * 5 + 1 = 16   2
16    yes     16 / 2 = 8       3
8     yes     8 / 2 = 4        4
4     yes     4 / 2 = 2        5
2     yes     2 / 2 = 1        6
1     test n != 1 is false, loop ends
```
The body ran 6 times. The trap is 7: n held seven values (10, 5, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1), but 10 was there before the loop, so there are only six changes. Answering 5 means stopping one pass early, missing the last change from 2 to 1. And 10 is just the starting value of n, not a count of anything.

questions.prompt: Which kind of test data is a value at the very edge of the allowed range, such as 0 or 100 when scores must be 0 to 100?
choices: Normal data
Boundary data
Invalid data
Random data
questions.explain:
Boundary data are values at the very edge of an allowed range or at a cut-off, plus their close neighbors. For scores from 0 to 100, the edges are 0 and 100. They matter because the most common slip, `<` written where `<=` was meant, changes the answer only right at an edge.

Normal data, such as 50, sits well inside the range. Invalid data is input that should be rejected, such as -5. Random data is not one of the standard kinds, and random values rarely land on an edge.

questions.prompt: A function accepts a percentage from 0 to 100 inclusive. Which set of test inputs is best?
questions.explain:
The set -1, 0, 1, 50, 99, 100, 101 covers every kind. 50 is normal. 0 and 100 are the edges, and 1 and 99 are just inside them. -1 and 101 are invalid values just outside. If the range check is off by one at either end, for example `score < 100` where `score <= 100` belongs, 0 or 100 would catch it. -1 or 101 would catch a check that lets bad values in.

Each other set misses something. 50, 51, 52, 53 and 25, 50, 75 are all normal values from the middle, where off-by-one bugs never show. 0 and 100 test the edges but have no neighbors and no invalid values.

questions.prompt: Input the program should reject, such as an age of -5, is called ___ test data.
questions.explain: The word is invalid. Invalid test data is input the program should reject or handle safely: an age of -5, letters where a number is expected, or 0 when the value will be a divisor. The test checks that the program reacts sensibly, for example by printing "invalid age" and asking again, instead of crashing or using the bad value as if it were real.

questions.prompt: If a program gives the right output for one test run, that proves the program is correct.
questions.explain:
False. One correct run shows only that the program works for that one input. A bug can still hide at a cut-off value, in invalid input, or in a loop that runs zero times. For example, a program that wrongly tests `score > 60` gives the right answer for 40 and for 90, and goes wrong only at exactly 60.

Testing can show that bugs exist, but it can never prove that none remain. Test with normal, boundary and invalid data, and make every branch run.

questions.prompt: The program should pass anyone with 60 or more. What does it print for the boundary value 60? Assume the code is inside main(), with iostream included and using namespace std; in effect.
questions.explain:
Trace it with the value 60.
```
score = 60
score > 60     60 > 60 is false (60 is not greater than itself)
else branch    prints fail
```
The output is `fail`, even though the rule says 60 or more passes. The bug is `>` where `>=` was needed. Test values such as 40 and 90 give the right answers even with this bug, so only a boundary test at exactly 60 exposes it.

questions.prompt: What does this code print? Assume the code is inside main(), with iostream included and using namespace std; in effect.
questions.explain:
The condition is `x = 5`, one equals sign, so it assigns instead of comparing.
```
x = 3
x = 5        stores 5 in x. The condition's value is 5.
5            nonzero, so true: prints "five "
cout << x    x is now 5: prints 5
```
The output is `five 5`. Two things went wrong at once: the branch is always taken, and x lost its old value. With `x == 5` the test would be false (3 is not 5), the if would print nothing, and the output would be just `3`.

questions.prompt: What does this code print? Assume the code is inside main(), with iostream included and using namespace std; in effect.
questions.explain:
The semicolon right after `if (n > 5)` is an empty statement, and it becomes the whole body of the if. So the if only decides whether to do nothing. The `cout << "big";` line is not part of the if, despite its indentation. It is the next ordinary statement, so it always runs.
```
n > 5     2 > 5 is false, so the empty statement is skipped
cout      runs anyway: prints big
```
The output is `big`. Without the stray semicolon nothing would print, because 2 is not greater than 5.

questions.prompt: What does this code print? Assume the code is inside main(), with iostream included and using namespace std; in effect.
questions.explain:
Without braces, an if controls only the one statement right after it. Unlike Python, C++ ignores indentation.
```
n > 0          -1 > 0 is false: skip cout << "a"
cout << "b"    not part of the if: always runs
```
So the only output is `b`. If both lines were inside `{ }`, the false condition would skip both and nothing would print.

questions.prompt: What does this code print? Assume the code is inside main(), with iostream included and using namespace std; in effect.
questions.explain:
A switch jumps to the matching case and then runs downward, past any later case labels, until it reaches a `break` or the closing brace.
```
choice is 2    jump to case 2: prints two
no break       falls through into case 3: prints three
break          leaves the switch. default is never reached.
```
The output is two, then three on the next line. case 1 is skipped because execution started at case 2. If choice were 1, the output would be one, two and three.

questions.prompt: What does this code print? Assume the code is inside main(), with iostream included and using namespace std; in effect.
questions.explain:
Look at the types inside each division, not the type of the variable that receives it.
```
r1 = a / b                        int / int: 7 / 2 is 3
                                  then 3 is stored as 3.0
r2 = static_cast<double>(a) / b   7.0 / 2 is 3.5
```
`cout` prints the double 3.0 as `3`, so the output is `3 3.5`. The tempting answer for r1 is 3.5, but the fraction is thrown away during the division, before anything reaches the double. Casting an operand first keeps the fraction. Casting the result, `static_cast<double>(a / b)`, would still give 3.

questions.prompt: What is the bug in this code?
choices: The loop runs one time too many
The variable i should be a double
sum should be declared after the loop
sum starts with an unpredictable value because it was never initialized
questions.explain:
`int sum;` declares a local variable with no starting value, so it holds whatever leftover bits were in that memory. `sum += i` then adds to that unknown number, and the printed result is unpredictable. The fix is `int sum = 0;`.

The other choices describe things that are fine. The loop makes exactly five passes, i = 1 to 5, which is not one too many. i counts whole numbers, so `int` is the right type. And sum must be declared before the loop, because the loop uses it.

questions.prompt: The code is meant to add 1 through 5. What does it print? Assume the code is inside main(), with iostream included and using namespace std; in effect.
questions.explain:
The test is `i < 5`, so the loop stops before i reaches 5.
```
i = 1   1 < 5 true    sum = 1
i = 2   2 < 5 true    sum = 3
i = 3   3 < 5 true    sum = 6
i = 4   4 < 5 true    sum = 10
i = 5   5 < 5 false   loop ends
```
The output is `10`, not 15. This is an off-by-one error: starting at 1, `i < n` makes n - 1 passes. Changing the test to `i <= 5` adds the 5 and gives 15.

questions.prompt: What happens when this code runs?
choices: The loop never ends and nothing is printed, because the semicolon is the loop body
It prints 0 1 2
It prints 0 1 2 3
It prints nothing and ends normally
questions.explain:
The semicolon right after `while (i < 3)` is an empty statement, and it is the entire loop body. The test `0 < 3` is true, the empty body runs, nothing changes i, so the test is true again, forever. The block in braces is not part of the loop. It would run only after the loop ended, and the loop never ends. In practice the program hangs and prints nothing.

"0 1 2" is what the code would print without the stray semicolon. "0 1 2 3" is wrong twice over: this loop never ends, and even without the semicolon the test `i < 3` fails once i is 3, so 3 would never print. "Prints nothing and ends normally" is half right: nothing prints, but the program never ends.

questions.prompt: A dummy function that stands in for a real one and usually just displays a message that it was called is a ___.
questions.explain: The word is stub. A stub is a stand-in for a function that is not written yet, or not yet trusted. It usually just prints that it was called, often with its argument values, and returns a fixed test value if the real function returns one. For example: `double getTax(double amt) { cout << "getTax called" << endl; return 10.0; }`. It lets you test the code that calls the function before the function exists.

questions.prompt: A small program that tests a function by calling it with test data and displaying the result is a ___.
questions.explain: The word is driver. A driver is a small program, often just a `main`, whose only job is to call one function with chosen test values and display what comes back. For example, a driver for `square` might print `square(3)`, `square(-2)` and `square(0)` so you can compare them with 9, 4 and 0. It tests the function by itself, apart from the rest of the program.

questions.prompt: A stub usually displays a message showing that it was called, rather than doing the real work.
questions.explain: True. A stub stands in for a function that is not finished, so it does not do the real work. Its job is to show that the caller reached it: it typically prints a message such as `calcFee called with 3`, including the argument values. If the real function returns a value, the stub also returns a fixed test value so the caller can carry on.

questions.prompt: You wrote main() with a menu but have not written the calcFee function yet. What should you use to test the menu logic?
choices: A driver for calcFee
A stub for calcFee
A second compiler
A larger set of boundary data for the menu only
questions.explain:
The menu in main is the code you want to test, and the function it calls does not exist yet. A stub fills that gap. A dummy calcFee that prints a message and returns a fixed value lets the program build and run, so you can check that each menu choice calls calcFee at the right time with the right arguments.

A driver is the opposite tool: it tests a function that already exists by calling it, and calcFee does not exist. A second compiler changes nothing. More boundary data cannot help while the program cannot even be built.

questions.prompt: This program uses a stub for getTax. What does it print? (Assume the usual includes and using namespace std;.)
questions.explain:
Follow the order in which things happen.
```
price = 200
total = price + getTax(price)   the call runs first
   stub prints:   getTax called with 200
   stub returns:  10.0
total = 200 + 10.0 = 210
main prints:      Total: 210
```
The stub's message comes first, because it is printed during the call, before main reaches its own cout. The doubles 200 and 210 print without a decimal point because they have no fractional part. So the output is getTax called with 200, then Total: 210 on the next line.

questions.prompt: This main() is a driver for the function square. What does it print? (Assume the usual includes and using namespace std;.)
questions.explain:
The driver loops over the array of test values. i takes the values 0, 1 and 2, so `tests[i]` is 3, then -2, then 0.
```
i = 0   tests[0] = 3    square(3)  = 9    prints 3 -> 9
i = 1   tests[1] = -2   square(-2) = 4    prints -2 -> 4
i = 2   tests[2] = 0    square(0)  = 0    prints 0 -> 0
```
Each line shows the test value, the arrow text, then the result. Note that -2 times -2 is positive 4. A positive, a negative and a zero make good test data, because each could expose a different bug.

questions.prompt: A stub for a function that returns an int should normally:
choices: Return nothing, so the caller notices the failure
Contain the full finished algorithm
Display a message and return a fixed test value
Call main() to test itself
questions.explain:
A function that returns an int promises its caller an int. The stub must keep that promise so the caller can carry on, so it returns a fixed test value, such as `return 5;`, and usually prints a message that it was called. Because you chose the value, you can check exactly what the caller does with it.

Returning nothing breaks the promise, and the caller gets no defined value. A stub with the full algorithm is no longer a stub, it is the real function. And a function does not call main to test itself. Testing a function from outside is the job of a driver.

questions.prompt: A program contains the prototype `double computeTotal(double);` and calls computeTotal, but the function body was never written. Compiling the .cpp file succeeds, yet building the executable fails with "undefined reference to computeTotal". Which step reported the error?
choices: The preprocessor
The linker
The running program
The compiler's syntax check
questions.explain:
The prototype `double computeTotal(double);` is a promise that the function exists somewhere. The compiler checks the call against that promise, accepts it, and writes the object file. That is why compiling succeeds.

The next step is the linker, which connects every call to the function's actual code. There is no body to connect to, so the linker stops with "undefined reference" and no executable is made.

The compiler's syntax check already passed. The preprocessor only handles `#` lines such as `#include`. And the running program never existed, because the build failed.

questions.prompt: The compiler lists 14 errors. The first one is on line 9, where a statement is missing its semicolon. What is the best next step?
choices: Fix the missing semicolon, then recompile and see which errors remain
Fix all 14 errors, starting with the last one listed
Run the program anyway, since only one line is really wrong
Delete line 9 and every other line the messages mention
questions.explain:
A missing semicolon means the statement on line 9 never ends, so the compiler reads the next line as part of it. That confusion produces follow-on errors, such as a variable reported as "not declared" because its declaration was swallowed. Many of the 14 messages may be side effects of that one slip.

So fix the semicolon, recompile, and see what is left. Starting from the last message wastes time on errors that may vanish. The program cannot be run, because a compile error means no executable exists. Deleting lines throws away code that was probably correct.

questions.prompt: A student types `Cout << "Total";` with a capital C. What happens?
choices: It runs normally, because C++ ignores capitalization
It compiles, but prints nothing at run time
It compiles and runs, but the output is wrong (a logic error)
The compiler reports an error, because C++ is case-sensitive and Cout is not defined
questions.explain:
C++ is case-sensitive, so `cout` and `Cout` are two different names. The library provides only `cout`. `Cout` was never declared, and g++ reports `'Cout' was not declared in this scope`.

That is a compile error (a syntax error in this course's terms), so no executable is made and nothing runs. The choices that describe the program running normally, printing nothing, or printing wrong output cannot happen, because there is no program to run. C++ never ignores capitalization.

questions.prompt: In the textbook's terms: a syntax error is reported by the compiler, and a mistake that shows itself only once the finished program is executing is called a runtime error.
questions.explain:
True. The textbook sorts errors by when they show up. The compiler reports a syntax error while it builds the program. Any mistake that shows itself only once the finished program is running is a runtime error in the book's broad sense. That includes a crash, such as integer division by zero, and also wrong output from a math mistake.

When a question lists logic error and run-time error as separate choices, use the narrow meanings: wrong output is a logic error, a crash is a run-time error.

questions.prompt: The code should print "out of range" for any score below 0 or above 100. What does it print when score is 150? Assume the code is inside main(), with iostream included and using namespace std; in effect.
questions.explain:
`&&` is true only when both sides are true.
```
score < 0        150 < 0 is false
score > 100      150 > 100 is true
false && true    false
```
The condition is false, so the else branch prints `ok`. In fact no number is below 0 and above 100 at the same time, so this test can never be true. An outside-the-range test needs `||`: `score < 0 || score > 100` would be true for 150 and print out of range.

questions.prompt: After `double total = 0.1 + 0.2;` a program tests `if (total == 0.3)`. Why is this test a bug risk?
choices: == cannot be used with double values, so it is a compile error
0.1 + 0.2 is computed as an integer, giving 0
Doubles store most decimal fractions approximately, so the sum may differ from 0.3 in its last bits and the test can be false
An if statement needs braces when it compares doubles
questions.explain:
A double is stored in binary, and most decimal fractions, such as 0.1 and 0.2, have no exact binary form. Their sum comes out as 0.30000000000000004, which is not exactly 0.3, so `total == 0.3` is false. The safe test checks that the difference is tiny: `fabs(total - 0.3) < 0.0001`.

`==` on doubles does compile, so it is not a compile error. 0.1 + 0.2 is double arithmetic, not integer arithmetic, so it does not give 0. Braces have nothing to do with comparing doubles.

questions.prompt: What is wrong with this loop?
choices: It prints 1 2 3 4 5 and stops
i is never changed inside the loop, so the condition stays true and it prints 1 forever
It never runs, because i starts at 1
It runs 4 times, because of <=
questions.explain:
A while loop stops only when its test becomes false. Here the body prints i but never changes it, so `i <= 5` is checked with i = 1 every time and is true every time. The output is `1 1 1 1 ...` without end: an infinite loop. Adding `i++;` inside the braces makes it print 1 2 3 4 5 and stop.

It cannot print 1 to 5 as written, because i never reaches 2. It does run, because 1 <= 5 is true at the start. And `<=` does not make it run 4 times: with `i++` added it would run 5 times.

questions.prompt: In a debugger, what is a breakpoint?
choices: A line marked so the program pauses there, letting you examine variables before continuing
A line where the compiler found a syntax error
The point where the program crashes
A comment that tells the compiler to skip a line
questions.explain:
A breakpoint is a line you mark in the debugger. When the running program reaches that line it pauses, before carrying it out. While it is paused you can look at the current values of variables (watch them), then step through the next statements one at a time.

It is not where the compiler found an error: a debugger works on a program that already compiled. It is not the point where a program crashes, although a breakpoint just before a crash helps find the cause. And it is not a comment: comments are ignored by the compiler and never pause anything.

questions.prompt: A debugger can show you the variables' values only after the program has finished running.
questions.explain: False. The whole point of a debugger is to look inside the program while it is still running. You set a breakpoint and the program pauses there, or you step through it one statement at a time. While it is paused, the debugger shows each variable's current value. It is an automatic hand trace: the same table of values you would write on paper, filled in by the computer as the program runs.

questions.prompt: A loop that totals 10 input values gives the wrong total. Which temporary debugging statement gives the most useful information?
choices: A cout inside the loop that prints the pass number, the value just read and the running total on each pass
A cout before the loop that prints "starting"
A cout after the loop that prints the final total
A cout at the end of main that prints "done"
questions.explain:
When a total is wrong, you need to know which pass first went wrong. A cout inside the loop that prints the pass number, the value just read and the running total gives one line per pass. Suppose the loop wrongly says `total = num` and the first two inputs are 4 and 6:
```
pass 1: num 4 total 4
pass 2: num 6 total 6     should be 10: the bug is here
```
The first wrong line points to the pass and the statement that broke it. A cout after the loop shows only that the final total is wrong, not where. Messages such as "starting" and "done" show the program reached a point but say nothing about the values. Remove the diagnostic line once the bug is fixed.

questions.prompt: Hand trace this code. The user types 4 9 2 7 0. What does it print? Assume the code is inside main(), with iostream included and using namespace std; in effect.
questions.explain:
Take the input one value at a time and cross each off.
```
cin >> num   num = 4
4 != 0       4 > 0, best = 4, count = 1, read 9
9 != 0       9 > 4, best = 9, count = 2, read 2
2 != 0       2 > 9? no,        count = 3, read 7
7 != 0       7 > 9? no,        count = 4, read 0
0 != 0       false, loop ends
```
The output is `4 9`. The 0 is the sentinel that ends the loop, so it is never counted. That is why count is 4, not 5. And `best` changes only when a value beats the current best, so 7 does not replace 9.

questions.prompt: A program prints child for ages below 13, teen for 13 to 19, and adult for 20 and over. Which set of test ages checks the boundaries between the branches?
questions.explain:
The cut-offs fall between 12 and 13 (child to teen) and between 19 and 20 (teen to adult). A boundary test sits on both sides of each cut-off, so the set is 12, 13, 19, 20.

5, 15 and 40 run each branch once, which is useful, but they are far from the edges and would not notice `age <= 13` written where `age < 13` was meant. 13 and 20 test only one side of each cut-off, so a cut-off placed one too low, such as `age < 12`, would slip past. 0 and 100 are extreme ages, not the edges between these branches.

questions.prompt: A loop reads n numbers and totals them. Which values of n best test the loop?
choices: Only a typical value such as 8
Several typical values such as 7, 8 and 9
0, 1 and a typical larger value such as 8
Only the largest value the program allows
questions.explain:
A loop's own boundaries are zero passes and one pass, so test n = 0, n = 1 and a typical larger n such as 8. n = 0 checks that the program copes with no data at all. For example, if it computes an average it must not divide by zero. n = 1 is the smallest real case, where a loop that is off by one shows up plainly. The typical value checks the everyday case.

Typical values alone, even several, never touch the edges. The largest allowed value alone tests one edge and misses the zero and one cases.

questions.prompt: It is fine to run the program first and then use its output as the expected result for each test case.
questions.explain:
False. The expected output must be worked out by hand, from the problem statement, before you run the program. If you copy the program's own output into the expected column, the test agrees with the program by definition. A wrong answer simply becomes the expected one, and the test can never fail.

For example, a program that wrongly prints fail for a score of 60 would pass its own test if fail were recorded as the expected result.

questions.prompt: What does this code print? Assume the code is inside main(), with iostream included and using namespace std; in effect.
questions.explain:
The condition is `x = 0`, an assignment, not a comparison.
```
x = 5
x = 0        stores 0 in x. The condition's value is 0.
0            false, so the else branch runs: prints nonzero
cout << x    x is now 0: prints a space, then 0
```
The output is `nonzero 0`. The trap is `nonzero 5`, which forgets that the assignment changed x. With `x == 0` the else branch would still run, but x would stay 5. g++ with `-Wall` warns about an assignment used as a condition, a hint that `==` was meant.

questions.prompt: What does this code print? Assume the code is inside main(), with iostream included and using namespace std; in effect.
questions.explain:
A for loop without braces controls only the one statement right after it. The indented `cout << "x";` looks like part of the loop, but C++ ignores indentation.
```
i = 0    prints 0
i = 1    prints 1
i = 2    prints 2
i = 3    test fails, loop ends
then     cout << "x" runs once: prints x
```
The output is `012x`. With braces around both statements, it would be `0x1x2x`.

questions.prompt: A loop that runs one time too many or one time too few has an ___ error.
questions.explain: The term is off-by-one. An off-by-one error is a loop that runs one pass too many or one too few, usually because of `<` versus `<=` or a wrong starting value. For example, `for (int i = 1; i < 5; i++)`, meant to cover 1 to 5, stops after 4. It is also called a fencepost error, and boundary tests are the best way to catch it.

lessons.title: Procedural versus object-oriented programming
lessons.book: Sections 1.7 and 13.1, pages 22 to 23 and 751 to 757
lessons.html:
The problem objects solve

Every program so far in this course has been procedural. In procedural programming the program is built around procedures, which in C++ are functions. The data lives in ordinary variables, kept apart from the functions, and it is passed to each function that needs it.

double addInterest(double balance, double rate)
{
    return balance + balance * rate;
}

int main()
{
    double balance = 500.0;
    double rate = 0.02;
    balance = addInterest(balance, rate);  // balance is 510
    balance = -9000;    // a bad value, and nothing stops it
    return 0;
}

The data is in balance and rate. The function addInterest does not own that data. It receives copies as arguments. This works well for small programs. In a large program, two problems grow:

  • Nothing guards the data. Any line anywhere in the program can put a bad value in balance, as the last line does. When that bad value causes a wrong answer much later, the bug is hard to track down.
  • Changes spread. Suppose the program switches from storing dollars in a double to storing whole cents in an int. Every function that receives the balance has to change. In a program with hundreds of functions, each of those changes is a chance to add a bug.

The object-oriented idea

Object-oriented programming (OOP) builds the program around objects instead. An object is one unit that holds some data and the functions that work on that data.

Picture a bank account object. It carries its own balance and interest rate inside it. It also carries its own functions for making a deposit and for reporting the balance. Code outside the object does not reach in and change the balance. It asks the object to do it.

Part of the objectGeneral nameC++ nameAccount example
The data it holdsattributesmember variablesbalance, rate
The things it can domethodsmember functionsdeposit, getBalance

So an object's attributes are its data, and C++ calls them member variables. The procedures an object performs are its member functions. Many other languages, Python included, call them methods. All of these words appear on tests.

If you know Python, you have used objects already. In names.append("Ann") the list names is an object, and append is a method that changes the data inside that one list. C++ uses the same shape: object, dot, function.

Encapsulation and data hiding: two different ideas

Tests ask about these two terms separately, so keep them apart.

  • Encapsulation means bundling: putting the data and the functions that work on it together inside one object.
  • Data hiding means restricting access: code outside the object cannot reach the object's data directly. Only the object's own member functions can. Outside code has to go through those functions.

The functions that outside code is allowed to call form the object's interface. A car is the usual example. You drive it with the pedals, the steering wheel and the gear lever. That is the car's interface. The engine, the wiring and the brake lines are hidden under the hood, and you never handle them directly.

Data hiding fixes both problems from the start of this lesson:

  • Protection. Outside code can change the balance only by calling a member function such as deposit. The author of deposit can make it refuse a negative amount, so the data cannot be corrupted by accident.
  • Freedom to change the inside. A car maker can redesign the engine and you still drive the same way. In the same way, the author of an object can change how its data is stored, and the programs that use the object keep working, because they only ever used the interface.

Python bundles data and methods too, but it mostly hides data by a naming habit: a leading underscore means "please do not touch". C++ enforces the hiding. The compiler refuses to build a program in which outside code touches hidden data. The next lesson shows how you mark data as hidden.

Class versus object

Before you can make an object, you need a description of it. A class is code that describes which member variables and member functions a particular kind of object will have. It is a blueprint. A blueprint of a house is not a house: nobody can live in it. In the same way, writing a class creates no data values at all.

An object is built from a class, and it holds real values. Each object built from a class is an instance of that class. One class can produce many instances, and each one has its own copy of the member variables:

Object (an instance of class Account)balancerate
savings500.000.02
checking75.500.00

Both objects have the same member functions, because they come from the same class. Their data is separate. A deposit into savings does not change checking, just as painting one house does not paint the house next door, even though both were built from one blueprint.

A quick check that you have the direction right: the class is the general description, and the object is the particular thing. "An object is an instance of a class" is correct. "A class is an instance of an object" is backwards.

You already use objects: string

string is a class that comes with C++. When you write string word = "tree"; you create an object named word, an instance of the string class. cin and cout are objects too, made from classes in the iostream library.

To ask an object to run one of its member functions, write the object's name, a dot, the function's name, and parentheses holding any arguments. Trace this code:

string word = "tree";   // word holds tree       4 characters
word.append("house");   // word holds treehouse  9 characters
cout << word << " " << word.length() << endl;
// prints: treehouse 9
  • word.append("house") runs append on the data inside word. It adds house to the end, so the stored text changes.
  • word.length() runs length on word. It changes nothing. It hands back the number of characters, 9. The parentheses are required even though nothing goes inside them.

A member function always works on the object named before the dot. If a second string b holds sun, then b.length() is 3, and word.append("house") leaves b alone.

Notice what you never needed to know: how a string stores its characters in memory. That part is hidden from you. You used only the interface (append and length). That is data hiding at work.

Reusability

An object is not a program by itself. It is a part that programs use. Because outside code depends only on the interface, one well-written class can be reused in many different programs. The people who wrote string, cin and cout never saw your programs, yet your programs use their classes every day.

C++ supports both styles. Everything you wrote in earlier units was procedural, and it is still valid C++. One program can mix plain functions with objects. Object-oriented code still uses functions. They simply live inside classes, as member functions.

Mistakes students make

  • Swapping the two terms. Encapsulation is bundling data with its functions. Data hiding is keeping outside code away from that data.
  • Saying a class is an instance of an object. It is the other way round: an object is an instance of a class.
  • Thinking a class holds values. Only objects hold values. A class only describes what each object will hold.
  • Thinking procedural programs have no data, or that object-oriented programs have no functions. Both have both. The difference is whether the data is kept apart from the functions or bundled with them.
  • Thinking data hiding means the data is hidden from everything. The object's own member functions use it freely. It is hidden only from code outside the object.
  • Writing word.length without parentheses. A member function call always needs ().

What to remember for the test

  • Procedural programming: built around functions. The data is kept in separate variables that are passed to those functions.
  • Object-oriented programming: built around objects. Each object bundles data with the functions that act on it.
  • Attributes = member variables (the data). Member functions = methods (what the object can do).
  • Encapsulation = bundling. Data hiding = outside code cannot touch the data directly, only through member functions.
  • Interface = the member functions that outside code is allowed to call.
  • Class = blueprint. Object = an instance of a class. One class, many objects, each with its own data.
  • Call a member function with object, dot, function: word.append("house"), word.length().

lessons.title: Declaring a class
lessons.html:
Writing the blueprint

The last lesson said a class is a blueprint for objects. This lesson is about writing that blueprint in C++. The code that does it is called a class declaration. It creates a brand new type. After it, the class name can be used the way you use int or string: to make variables, which for a class are called objects.

Here is a class for a bank account. Read the comments first, then the parts are explained one at a time.

class Account               // key word class, then the name
{
private:                    // members below are hidden
    double balance;         // member variables
    double rate;
public:                     // members below anyone may use
    void setBalance(double b);    // member function
    void setRate(double r);       // prototypes
    double getBalance() const;
    double getInterest() const;
};                          // a semicolon after the brace

The parts, one at a time

  • The header is the key word class in lowercase, then the class name. Nothing else goes after the name: no colon, no parentheses. (The opening brace may sit on the same line or on the next one.) By convention a class name starts with a capital letter (Account, Lamp), which makes it easy to tell apart from a variable.
  • The body, inside braces, lists the members. Member variables are declared like ordinary variables. Member functions are listed as prototypes, which you met in the functions unit: return type, name, parameter list, semicolon.
  • Every member function needs a return type, void if it returns nothing. The only exceptions are two special kinds you will meet later in this unit: constructors, which set up a new object, and destructors, which clean up when an object is destroyed. Those have no return type.
  • The closing brace is followed by a semicolon. This one gets its own section next.

The semicolon after the closing brace

A function body needs no semicolon after its closing brace. A class declaration does. Forget it and the program will not compile:

class Pet
{
public:
    int age;
}               // missing ;

int main()
{
    return 0;
}

g++ reports expected ';' after class definition. Some compilers notice the problem only when they reach the next line, so they point at int main(), which looks perfectly fine. When an error points at a line with nothing wrong on it, look at the line above it for a missing semicolon.

Access specifiers: private and public

The words private: and public: are access specifiers. Each one controls who may use the members listed below it, up to the next specifier. Each one ends with a colon.

  • A private member can be used only by the member functions of the same class. Code outside the class, such as main, cannot touch it.
  • A public member can be used by any code.

This is how C++ does the data hiding from the last lesson. The usual design is: member variables private, member functions public. The public member functions are the class's interface. If main has an Account object named acct, then:

acct.setBalance(1000);   // fine: setBalance is public
acct.balance = 4;        // error: balance is private

(acct.setBalance(1000) means "run setBalance on the object acct". The next lesson covers that in detail.) g++ rejects the second line with 'double Account::balance' is private within this context.

Rules about access specifiers that tests ask about:

  • The default is private. Members listed before any specifier in a class are private. Here both members are private, even though the word never appears: 
    class Gadget
{
    int level;       // private
    void reset();    // private
};
    Writing private: anyway is good style, because it makes the intent obvious.
  • struct is the same, except for the default. C++ has a second key word, struct, that declares a type in exactly the same way. With no specifier written, the members of a struct are public. That default is the only difference you need for this course. Programmers tend to use struct for a simple group of data and class for an object whose data is hidden.
  • Any order, any number of times. Private and public sections may come in any order and may repeat. Putting the private data first and the public functions after it is a habit, not a rule.
  • There is a third specifier, protected. It only matters for inheritance, a topic for a later course. It is never the default, and it does not mean "visible to all code".

Starting values inside the class

Since the C++11 standard (the 2011 edition of the C++ language rules), a member variable may be given a starting value right where it is declared. This is called in-place initialization:

class Account
{
private:
    double balance = 0.0;
    double rate = 0.05;
    ...

Every Account object then starts with a balance of 0.0 and a rate of 0.05. Without a starting value, a member variable of an object created inside a function holds leftover garbage until something stores a value in it. Older code sets starting values in a constructor instead, which is covered later in this unit.

Defining the member functions

The prototypes in the class say which member functions exist. Their bodies have to be written somewhere. There are two places.

Inside the class. Replace the prototype's semicolon with the body. Short functions are often written this way. (Lesson 6 calls these inline member functions.)

double getBalance() const { return balance; }

Outside the class, usually after it. Then the function's name must be preceded by the class name and ::, the scope resolution operator. It tells the compiler which class the function belongs to.

void Account::setBalance(double b)
{
    balance = b;
}

double Account::getInterest() const
{
    return balance * rate;
}

Read a definition header in this order:

PieceMeaning
voidthe return type
Accountthe class the function belongs to
::scope resolution: "the one belonging to"
setBalancethe function's own name
(double b)the parameter list

The general form is ReturnType ClassName::functionName(parameters), with const at the end if the prototype has it. The name before :: is always the class. The name after it is the function.

Why the class name matters. Leave out Account:: and the compiler sees an ordinary, stand-alone function that has nothing to do with the class. An ordinary function has no member variables, so a name like balance means nothing inside it:

class Scale
{
private:
    int kg;
public:
    void setKg(int);
};

void setKg(int k)    // missing Scale::
{
    kg = k;          // error: 'kg' was not declared
}

The fix is void Scale::setKg(int k). Two other wrong headers to recognise:

  • double Account.getInterest() const is wrong. The dot joins an object to a member in a call, as in acct.getInterest(). It never appears in a definition header.
  • double Account:getInterest() const is wrong. A single colon is not an operator here. It must be two: ::.

Inside a member function, use member names on their own. The body of setBalance writes balance, not acct.balance. If you know Python, this is where Python writes self.balance. C++ just writes balance, and it means the balance of whichever object the function was called for.

const member functions

Look again at double getBalance() const;. A const written after the parameter list is a promise: this function will not change any member variable of the object. The compiler holds you to it.

class Counter
{
private:
    int n;
public:
    int getN() const { return n; }   // fine: only reads n
    void bump() const { n++; }       // error: changes n
};

g++ rejects bump with increment of member 'Counter::n' in read-only object. Fix it by removing const from bump, because a function whose job is to change n should not promise not to.

  • Mark a function const when it only looks at the data, such as getBalance and getInterest.
  • Write const in both places: the prototype and the definition header. If they disagree, the compiler says the definition does not match any declaration.
  • const here says nothing about the return value or about how often the function may be called.
  • Do not confuse const with private. private limits who may use a member: outside code may not. const limits what a member function may do: read, but not change. A const member function can still read every private member of its class.

The whole thing, working

#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

class Account
{
private:
    double balance;
    double rate;
public:
    void setBalance(double b) { balance = b; }
    void setRate(double r) { rate = r; }
    double getBalance() const { return balance; }
    double getInterest() const;
};

double Account::getInterest() const
{
    return balance * rate;
}

int main()
{
    Account acct;
    acct.setBalance(1000);
    acct.setRate(0.05);
    cout << acct.getBalance() << " "
         << acct.getInterest() << endl;   // 1000 50
    return 0;
}

Three member functions are defined inside the class and one outside it with Account::. Both ways are legal and can be mixed.

Spot the errors

Examiners like a broken declaration with several mistakes in it. This one has five:

Class Fan()
{
public
    speed(int);
private:
    int rpm;
}
  1. Class must be lowercase class.
  2. No parentheses after the class name.
  3. public needs its colon: public:.
  4. speed has no return type. It needs one, such as void speed(int);.
  5. No semicolon after the closing brace.

Putting public: before private: is not an error. The corrected version:

class Fan
{
public:
    void speed(int);
private:
    int rpm;
};

Mistakes students make

  • Leaving out the semicolon after the class's closing brace.
  • Writing private or public without its colon.
  • Adding a colon or parentheses to the header, as in class Lamp: or class Lamp().
  • Giving a member function no return type. Use void when it returns nothing.
  • Defining a member function outside the class without ClassName::, which makes it an ordinary function that cannot see the members.
  • Writing Account.getInterest or Account:getInterest in a definition header instead of Account::getInterest.
  • Thinking members with no specifier are public. In a class they are private. Public is the default only for a struct.
  • Thinking private members must come first. Order is free.
  • Changing a member variable inside a const member function.

What to remember for the test

  • Shape: class Name { private: ... public: ... };. Lowercase class, a colon after each access specifier, a semicolon after the brace.
  • private: only the class's own member functions may use it. public: any code may.
  • No specifier written: class members are private, struct members are public.
  • Sections may come in any order and may repeat.
  • Since C++11: double rate = 0.05; inside the class gives a starting value (in-place initialization).
  • Outside definition: ReturnType ClassName::functionName(parameters). :: is the scope resolution operator.
  • Inside a member function, members are used by their bare names.
  • const after the parameter list: the function may read members but not change them. Write it in the prototype and in the definition.

lessons.title: Creating and using objects
lessons.html:
From blueprint to object

A class declaration describes objects, but it creates none. To get an object, you define one the same way you define a variable, with the class name as the type:

Account acct;          // one object named acct
Odometer car, van;     // two objects of class Odometer

Creating an object from a class is called instantiation, and the object made is an instance of the class. If you know Python, there you would write car = Odometer(). In C++ the class name comes first, like a type: Odometer car;.

This lesson uses one small class. An odometer counts the miles a vehicle has driven:

class Odometer
{
private:
    int miles;
public:
    void setMiles(int m) { miles = m; }
    void drive(int d) { miles += d; }
    int getMiles() const { return miles; }
};

miles += d; is shorthand for miles = miles + d;.

The picture: each object is its own box

Think of every object as a separate box that holds its own copy of every member variable. Odometer car, van; makes two boxes, and each box has its own miles. Changing one box never changes the other.

The member functions are not copied into each box. There is one copy of the code for drive, shared by every Odometer. When it runs, it works on the box of whichever object it was called for.

The dot operator

To use a public member of an object from outside the class, write the object's name, a dot, and the member. The . is called the dot operator. You can read car.drive(20) as "car, drive 20 miles".

Trace this code. A ? means no value has been stored yet.

Odometer car, van;
car.setMiles(100);
van.setMiles(500);
car.drive(20);
van.drive(5);
car.drive(30);
cout << car.getMiles() << " " << van.getMiles() << endl;
Statementcar's milesvan's miles
Odometer car, van;??
car.setMiles(100);100?
van.setMiles(500);100500
car.drive(20);120500
van.drive(5);120505
car.drive(30);150505

The output is 150 505.

The object before the dot decides whose data is used. Inside drive the code says just miles. During car.drive(20) that means car's miles. During van.drive(5) it means van's miles. Python writes self.miles for this. C++ writes the bare name miles, and the object is understood. So inside a member function you never write car.miles: the function knows nothing about a variable called car, and it has to work for every object.

Wrong ways to call a member function:

  • car::drive(20); is wrong. :: follows a class name in a definition header, as in void Odometer::drive(int d). It is not used to call a function through an object.
  • Odometer::drive(20); is wrong. It names the class but not which odometer, so there is no box for drive to change. g++ says it cannot call member function ... without object.
  • drive(car, 20); is wrong. drive is not a stand-alone function, so g++ says 'drive' was not declared in this scope.

Private members are out of reach. The dot reaches only public members from outside the class:

car.miles = 0;    // error: 'int Odometer::miles'
                  // is private within this context

Only Odometer's own member functions may touch miles. From outside, the public functions are the only way in.

State

The data an object holds at a given moment is its state. At the end of the trace, car's state is 150 miles and van's state is 505 miles. A call such as car.drive(30) changes car's state. Two objects of the same class have the same member functions, but they usually have different states.

Accessors and mutators

  • An accessor, or getter, retrieves a value from an object without changing it. Accessors are marked const, the promise from the last lesson not to change any member variable.
  • A mutator, or setter, stores a value in a member variable or otherwise changes it.

To classify a function, ask: does it change the object's data?

HeaderKindWhy
int getMiles() constaccessorreturns a value, const, changes nothing
void setMiles(int m)mutatorstores m in miles
void drive(int d)mutatorchanges miles, though its name does not start with set
Odometer()neithersame name as the class and no return type: a constructor, covered in lesson 5

Assigning one object to another

q = p; copies each member variable of p into q, one by one. After that the two objects are independent.

Odometer p, q;
p.setMiles(40);   // p: 40   q: ?
q = p;            // p: 40   q: 40   copied
p.drive(10);      // p: 50   q: 40   q is untouched
cout << p.getMiles() << " " << q.getMiles() << endl;
// prints: 50 40

This is a real difference from Python. In Python, q = p makes q a second name for the same object, so a change made through p shows up in q. In C++, p and q are two separate boxes, and = copies the values from one box into the other.

Member variables do not start at zero

Suppose Odometer car; is defined inside main and nothing stores a value in it. Then miles holds garbage: whatever bits were left in that memory. It is not 0. It is also not a compile error. The program compiles, and at best the compiler prints a warning. Calling car.getMiles() at that point could return any number.

Give every member a value before you use it. You can call a mutator first, use in-place initialization (int miles = 0; inside the class, from the last lesson), or write a constructor, which lesson 5 covers.

Do not store what you can calculate

Interest depends on the balance and the rate. Here is a class that stores the interest in its own member variable:

class BadAccount
{
private:
    double balance, rate;
    double interest;    // stored, not calculated
public:
    void setBalance(double b) { balance = b; }
    void setRate(double r)
    {
        rate = r;
        interest = balance * rate;
    }
    double getInterest() const { return interest; }
};
bad.setBalance(1000);
bad.setRate(0.05);        // interest becomes 50
bad.setBalance(2000);     // interest is still 50
cout << bad.getInterest();   // prints 50, should be 100

The stored interest was right when it was calculated and wrong as soon as the balance changed. A value that is out of date like this is called stale data. The fix is to store only balance and rate, and calculate the interest each time it is asked for:

double getInterest() const { return balance * rate; }

With that version, the same calls print 100.

Mistakes students make

  • Thinking a class declaration creates an object. Only a definition such as Odometer car; does.
  • Thinking objects of one class share their member variables. Each object has its own. Only the member function code is shared.
  • Calling a member function with :: or with the class name. A call is object, dot, function: car.drive(20);.
  • Using the dot on a private member from main, as in car.miles = 0;.
  • Writing car.miles inside a member function. Use the bare name miles.
  • Expecting member variables to start at 0.
  • Expecting q = p; to link two objects, as it would in Python. It copies, and the copies then go their own ways.
  • Thinking only functions named set... are mutators. Any member function that changes the data is a mutator.
  • Storing a value, such as interest, that can be calculated from other members.

What to remember for the test

  • ClassName objectName; creates an object. That is instantiation, and the object is an instance.
  • Each object has its own copy of every member variable. The member function code is shared.
  • The dot operator, object.member, reaches public members from outside the class.
  • The object before the dot decides whose data a member function uses. Inside the function, members are written by bare name.
  • State = the values in an object's member variables at a given moment.
  • Accessor: returns a value, changes nothing, marked const. Mutator: stores or changes a value.
  • q = p; copies member by member. The two objects stay independent afterwards.
  • Members with no starting value hold unpredictable garbage. It compiles anyway.
  • Calculate values that depend on other members in a member function, so they never go stale.

lessons.title: Why have private members?
lessons.html:
Why not make everything public?

The last two lessons put the member variables under private: and then wrote public functions just to read and change them. That can look like extra work. Why not make the data public and let main use it directly? This lesson answers that, and it is a favourite exam question.

Start with what happens when the data is public:

class Person
{
public:
    int age;
};

Person p;
p.age = -5;    // compiles. Nothing can stop it.

Any line anywhere in the program can put any value in age, including nonsense such as a negative age, or a width of 0 that later causes a divide by zero. The person who wrote the class has no say in what the data holds. If a wrong value turns up, it could have come from any line of the program.

The fix: private data behind a public interface

Make the member variables private. Then the only way for outside code to read or change them is through the public member functions that the class author wrote. Those public functions are the class's interface: the controls outside code is allowed to use. Think of a car again. The pedals and the steering wheel are the interface. The engine is private, and you cannot reach in and turn a valve.

Because every change now passes through a mutator, the mutator can check the value first:

class Rectangle
{
private:
    double width = 1.0;
public:
    void setWidth(double w)
    {
        if (w > 0)
            width = w;    // store only a sensible value
    }
    double getWidth() const { return width; }
};

Trace what happens to width:

StatementTest w > 0width after
Rectangle r;none1.0
r.setWidth(4);4 > 0 is true4
r.setWidth(0);0 > 0 is false4 (unchanged)
r.setWidth(-2);-2 > 0 is false4 (unchanged)

cout << r.getWidth(); prints 4. The bad values were simply not stored. And since width is private, main cannot get around the check by writing r.width = 0;. The compiler refuses that line.

Benefit 1: protection from bad data

The check lives in one place, the mutator, and every caller is forced through it. That protects the object from accidental corruption. It also makes bugs easier to find. If width ever holds a wrong value, the cause must be inside the class's own member functions, a short list, not somewhere among thousands of lines of other code.

Benefit 2: freedom to change the inside

Outside code depends only on the interface, so the class author can change how the data is stored without breaking that code. Here are two versions of a temperature class with the same public member functions. The first stores Celsius. The second stores Fahrenheit.

// Version 1
class Temp
{
private:
    double celsius;
public:
    void setCelsius(double c) { celsius = c; }
    double getCelsius() const { return celsius; }
    double getFahrenheit() const
    { return celsius * 9 / 5 + 32; }
};
// Version 2
class Temp
{
private:
    double fahrenheit;
public:
    void setCelsius(double c)
    { fahrenheit = c * 9 / 5 + 32; }
    double getCelsius() const
    { return (fahrenheit - 32) * 5 / 9; }
    double getFahrenheit() const { return fahrenheit; }
};

This main works with either version, and it prints 100 212 with both:

int main()
{
    Temp t;
    t.setCelsius(100);
    cout << t.getCelsius() << " "
         << t.getFahrenheit() << endl;
    return 0;
}

Now suppose the data had been public, and main had written t.celsius = 30;. Version 2 has no member named celsius, so that program would stop compiling the moment the class changed. Public data ties every program to the way the class stores its data. Private data plus a public interface removes that tie.

What private does not do

  • It does not make the program run faster or use less memory. private is a rule the compiler checks while it builds the program. The running program is no quicker and no smaller for it.
  • It does not remove the need for member functions. It is the reason you need them, because member functions are the only way in from outside.
  • It does not hide anything from the class itself. The class's own member functions use private members freely.

Member functions can be private too. A helper function that only the class itself needs, such as one that does part of a calculation, is made private so that outside code cannot call it. Lesson 6 shows an example.

If you know Python: Python mostly relies on a naming habit, a leading underscore, to say "please do not touch". A Python programmer can still change p._age directly. In C++ the compiler enforces private, so the protection is real.

The exam answer

"Why should member variables be private?" The best answer has two parts. First, outside code can then change the data only through the class's member functions, and those functions can check (validate) every value before storing it. Second, the way the data is stored is hidden, so it can be redesigned without breaking the code that uses the class.

Mistakes students make

  • Saying private members make a program faster or smaller. They change nothing at run time.
  • Thinking private data is hidden from the class's own member functions. It is hidden only from outside code.
  • Writing a mutator that stores any value it is given. Then the data is private but still unprotected. The protection comes from the check.
  • Expecting a rejected value to be stored anyway. If the mutator's test fails, the member keeps its old value.
  • Thinking the interface means the member variables. The interface is the public member functions.

What to remember for the test

  • Usual design: member variables private, member functions public.
  • The public member functions are the class's interface.
  • Protection: a mutator can validate a value and refuse a bad one. Outside code cannot get around it.
  • Freedom to change: the storage inside a class can be redesigned without changing the code that calls its public functions.
  • When a mutator refuses a value, the member keeps the value it had before.
  • Private has no effect on speed or memory.
  • Helper functions that only the class needs can be private too.

lessons.title: Constructors and the default constructor
lessons.html:
The problem constructors solve

Lesson 3 showed that a new object's member variables hold garbage until something stores values in them. You could call mutators straight after creating every object, but it is easy to forget one. A constructor makes C++ do the setting up for you, every time.

A constructor is a member function that runs automatically at the moment an object is created. Its job is to set up the new object, which usually means giving its member variables their starting values. If you know Python, it plays the role of __init__.

Writing a constructor

class Room
{
private:
    double length, width;
public:
    Room()              // a constructor
    {
        length = 10;
        width = 10;
    }
    double getArea() const { return length * width; }
};

Three rules make a function a constructor:

  • Its name is exactly the class name, with the same capital letters: Room, not room.
  • It has no return type, not even void. Nothing is written before the name.
  • It is normally public, so that code such as main can create objects.

Now Room hall; creates hall and immediately runs Room() on it. Length and width are both 10, so hall.getArea() is 100. No garbage, no forgotten setter.

Like any member function, a constructor can be defined outside the class. The header then names the class twice, once as the class and once as the function, and still has no return type:

Room::Room()
{
    length = 10;
    width = 10;
}

When it runs

A constructor runs once for each object, at the exact moment that object is defined. You never call it yourself: hall.Room(); is a compile error. Defining the object is what runs it. This class prints a word from its constructor, only so that you can see when it runs:

class Bell
{
public:
    Bell() { cout << "ding" << endl; }
};

int main()
{
    cout << "one" << endl;
    Bell a;                  // constructor runs here
    cout << "two" << endl;
    Bell b;                  // and again here
    cout << "three" << endl;
    return 0;
}

Output, one item per line: one, ding, two, ding, three. Each ding appears exactly where an object is defined.

Constructors with parameters

A constructor can take parameters, so that each object can start with different values. Put the arguments in parentheses after the object's name:

Room(double l, double w)    // inside the class
{
    length = l;
    width = w;
}

Room kitchen(12, 15);       // in main: length 12, width 15

In Python this would be kitchen = Room(12, 15). In C++ the arguments go straight after the object's name.

More than one constructor

A class may have several constructors, as long as their parameter lists differ. This is the function overloading you met in the functions unit. The arguments written in each object definition decide which constructor runs.

class Room
{
private:
    double length, width;
public:
    Room();                     // no parameters
    Room(double l, double w);   // two parameters
    double getArea() const { return length * width; }
};

Room::Room()
{
    length = 10;
    width = 10;
    cout << "Room() runs" << endl;
}

Room::Room(double l, double w)
{
    length = l;
    width = w;
    cout << "Room(double, double) runs" << endl;
}

int main()
{
    cout << "start" << endl;
    Room hall;
    Room kitchen(12, 15);
    cout << hall.getArea() << " "
         << kitchen.getArea() << endl;
    return 0;
}
LineArgumentsConstructor that runsResult
Room hall;noneRoom()10 by 10
Room kitchen(12, 15);twoRoom(double, double)12 by 15

The program prints start, then Room() runs, then Room(double, double) runs, and last 100 180.

The default constructor

A default constructor is any constructor that can be called with no arguments. That means either it has no parameters, like Room(), or every one of its parameters has a default value. It is the constructor used by a definition with no arguments, such as Room hall;. Four rules about it are tested often.

1. Write no constructor, and the compiler supplies one. If a class has no constructors at all, the compiler quietly adds a default constructor that does nothing useful to the member variables. Unless they have in-place starting values, they still hold garbage. That is why Account acct; compiled in earlier lessons.

2. Write any constructor, and the compiler supplies none. Suppose Room has only Room(double l, double w):

Room r;      // error: no matching function
             // for call to 'Room::Room()'

Room r; needs a constructor that takes no arguments, and there is none. Writing your own constructor switched off the free one. To fix it, add a Room() constructor, or give the parameters default values.

3. Default arguments let one constructor do several jobs. You met default arguments in the functions unit. Missing arguments are filled in from the end of the parameter list:

Room(double l = 10, double w = 10)
{
    length = l;
    width = w;
}
Definitionlw
Room a;10 (default)10 (default)
Room b(12);1210 (default)
Room c(12, 15);1215
