A single argument always goes to the first parameter. It never skips ahead to the second. You can call this constructor with no arguments, and that makes it a default constructor.

4. Only one default constructor. If a class has both Room() and Room(double l = 5, double w = 5), both can be called with no arguments. Then Room a; fails: g++ says call of overloaded 'Room()' is ambiguous, because it cannot choose. The error appears on the line that needs a default constructor. Room a(8); still compiles, because only the second constructor can take one argument. The rule to remember: a class should have only one default constructor.

Trap: empty parentheses

Room a();    // NOT an object
Room a;      // an object, made with the default constructor

With empty parentheses, C++ reads the line as a declaration of a function named a that returns a Room. No object is created, and a later a.getArea() fails to compile. To use the default constructor, write no parentheses at all.

Member initialization list

A constructor can set members in a different place: after a colon, between the parameter list and the body.

Room() : length(10), width(10) { }
Room(double l, double w) : length(l), width(w) { }

This is a member initialization list. Each entry is a member name with its starting value in parentheses, and the entries are separated by commas. The list runs before the body, so the body is often just empty braces, { }. Empty braces do not mean nothing happens: the list already did the work. For the classes in this course the effect is the same as assigning in the body. These two constructors give the same results as before: 100 180.

Which constructor headers are valid?

Inside class AccountValid?Why
Account(double b);yesclass's exact name, no return type
void Account(double b);noa constructor cannot have a return type, not even void
account(double b);nolowercase name does not match, so the compiler sees an ordinary function with no return type
Account(double b) const;noa const member function promises not to change the members, but a constructor's whole job is to set them

Mistakes students make

  • Giving a constructor a return type, usually void.
  • Spelling the constructor's name differently from the class, even by one capital letter.
  • Writing Room a(); to use the default constructor. That declares a function.
  • Adding a constructor with parameters and then writing Room r;, forgetting that the free default constructor is gone.
  • Writing both Room() and a constructor whose parameters all have defaults, then defining Room a;.
  • Thinking a single argument can go to the second parameter. It always fills the first.
  • Thinking a constructor with an empty body { } sets nothing, when it has a member initialization list.
  • Expecting a constructor to run when the class is declared. It runs when each object is defined, once per object.

What to remember for the test

  • A constructor runs automatically when an object is created, once per object, at the line that defines it.
  • Name = the class name exactly. No return type, not even void. Not const. Usually public.
  • Arguments go after the object's name: Room kitchen(12, 15);. They decide which constructor runs.
  • Default constructor = callable with no arguments: no parameters, or all parameters have defaults.
  • No constructors written: the compiler supplies a default one. Any constructor written: it supplies none.
  • Two constructors that can both be called with no arguments make Room a; ambiguous.
  • Room a(); declares a function. Use Room a;.
  • Member initialization list: Room() : length(10), width(10) { } sets members before the body runs.

lessons.title: More class features (first look)
lessons.html:
What this lesson covers

This lesson is a first look at seven more class topics: inline member functions, separate files, destructors, private member functions, arrays of objects, UML diagrams, and where input and output belong. Each one is short. For each, learn the rule and the reason behind it.

1. Inline member functions

You have already seen two places to write a member function's body. When the body is written inside the class declaration, the function is called an inline member function:

class Account
{
private:
    double balance;
public:
    double getBalance() const { return balance; }  // inline
    void deposit(double amt);       // body is written outside
};

void Account::deposit(double amt)
{
    balance += amt;
}
  • An inline function needs no Account::, because it is already inside the class.
  • The name comes from inline expansion: the compiler may place a copy of the body's code at each call instead of making a real function call. That saves the small cost of a call.
  • Use it for short functions of a line or two, such as accessors. Longer bodies go outside the class with ClassName::. One class can mix both styles.

2. Putting a class in its own files

Small examples keep everything in one file. Real programs, by convention, split each class into two files named after the class:

FileNameHolds
Account.hspecification file (a header file)the class declaration
Account.cppimplementation filethe member function definitions
// Account.h  (specification file)
#ifndef ACCOUNT_H
#define ACCOUNT_H

class Account
{
private:
    double balance;
    double rate;
public:
    Account(double b, double r);
    double getInterest() const;
};

#endif
// Account.cpp  (implementation file)
#include "Account.h"

Account::Account(double b, double r)
{
    balance = b;
    rate = r;
}

double Account::getInterest() const
{
    return balance * rate;
}
// main.cpp  (a program that uses the class)
#include <iostream>
#include "Account.h"
using namespace std;

int main()
{
    Account acct(1000, 0.05);
    cout << acct.getInterest() << endl;   // 50
    return 0;
}
  • Quotes or angle brackets. #include "Account.h" uses quotes, which means "look in my own project folder first". Angle brackets, as in <iostream>, are for the standard library.
  • Both .cpp files are compiled and linked together, for example g++ main.cpp Account.cpp. The header only tells main.cpp what the class looks like. The function bodies are in Account.cpp. Compile main.cpp alone and the linker reports errors such as undefined reference to Account::getInterest() const, one for each member function main uses (the constructor too), because it cannot find their bodies.
  • The include guard. The lines #ifndef ACCOUNT_H, #define ACCOUNT_H and #endif stop the class from being declared twice if the header is included twice in one file, which would be an error. #ifndef means "if not defined". The first time through, ACCOUNT_H is not defined, so the class is read and ACCOUNT_H becomes defined. Any later time, everything up to #endif is skipped.
  • Why bother? A programmer who uses the class only needs to read the short header to see its interface. The implementation can be compiled once and reused by many programs. It is a little like a Python module that you import.

3. Destructors

A destructor is the opposite of a constructor. It is a member function that runs automatically when an object is destroyed. An object defined inside a function is destroyed when that function ends, at its closing brace.

  • Its name is a tilde, ~, followed by the class name: ~Tag().
  • Like a constructor, it has no return type, not even void.
  • Unlike a constructor, it takes no parameters. So it cannot be overloaded, and a class has only one destructor.
  • You never call it. C++ runs it for you.
  • Its job is cleanup before the object disappears, such as closing a file the object opened. In this course it is mostly used to show when objects are destroyed.
class Tag
{
private:
    string name;
public:
    Tag(string n)
    {
        name = n;
        cout << "make " << name << endl;
    }
    ~Tag() { cout << "end " << name << endl; }
};

void work()
{
    Tag t("T");
    cout << "working" << endl;
}                     // t is destroyed here

int main()
{
    Tag a("A");
    work();
    Tag b("B");
    cout << "main done" << endl;
    return 0;
}                     // b, then a, are destroyed here
What happensPrinted
a is createdmake A
work starts, t is createdmake T
work printsworking
work ends, t is destroyedend T
b is createdmake B
main printsmain done
main ends, b is destroyedend B
then a is destroyedend A

Two things to notice. t lives only while work runs. And objects in the same function are destroyed in reverse order of creation: b was made last, so it goes first.

4. Private member functions

Member functions can be private too. A private member function can be called only by other member functions of the same class. Code outside the class cannot call it, not even with an object and the dot. Make a function private when it is an internal helper that outside code should never use directly.

class Account
{
private:
    double balance = 0.0;
    bool isValid(double amt) const { return amt > 0; }
public:
    void deposit(double amt)
    {
        if (isValid(amt))      // a member function may call it
            balance += amt;
    }
    double getBalance() const { return balance; }
};

In main, a.deposit(50); then a.deposit(-10); leaves the balance at 50, because isValid(-10) is false. But a.isValid(5) written in main does not compile: g++ says 'bool Account::isValid(double) const' is private within this context.

5. Arrays of objects

The elements of an array can be objects. Defining the array creates every element, so the default constructor runs once for each element, starting with element 0:

class Dot
{
public:
    Dot() { cout << "."; }
};

Dot row[3];      // three objects: prints ...
cout << endl;

The output is ..., three dots, one from each element's constructor. When the array is destroyed, the destructor (if the class has one) also runs once for each element.

To use one element, the subscript picks the object and the dot picks the member: lamps[1].getWatts(). A loop works as it does for any array:

int total = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++)
    total += lamps[i].getWatts();

If the class has no default constructor, Lamp lamps[3]; does not compile, because there is no constructor that can build an element with no arguments. Then every element needs its own initializer:

// Lamp has only the constructor Lamp(int w)
Lamp lamps[3] = {Lamp(40), Lamp(60), Lamp(75)};
Lamp more[3] = {25, 50, 100};  // works for one-argument
                               // constructors

If you give fewer initializers than elements, the rest are built with the default constructor, so that only works when the class has one.

6. UML class diagrams

UML, the Unified Modeling Language, is a standard way to draw classes. A UML class diagram is a box divided into three parts, top to bottom: the class name, the member variables, and the member functions.

+---------------------------------+
| Account                         |
+---------------------------------+
| - balance : double              |
| - rate : double                 |
+---------------------------------+
| + Account(b : double,           |
|           r : double)           |
| + setRate(r : double) : void    |
| + getInterest() : double        |
+---------------------------------+
  • A minus sign - in front of a member means private. A plus sign + means public.
  • Types come after a colon, the reverse of C++. - balance : double is the C++ line double balance; under private:.
  • A function's return type goes after its parameter list: + getInterest() : double is double getInterest(); under public:. Parameters are written as name, colon, type.
  • Constructors and destructors show no return type, because they have none.

7. Keep cin and cout out of member functions

This member function works, but it is poor design:

void Rectangle::setWidth()
{
    cout << "Enter the width: ";
    cin >> width;
}

Every program that uses this class is now stuck with that exact prompt and with keyboard input. A program that reads widths from a file, or one that shows a window, cannot use it. The better design takes the value as a parameter, void setWidth(double w), and leaves input and output to the program that uses the class. Accessors return values instead of printing them. That keeps the class reusable. The exception is a class whose whole purpose is input or output.

Mistakes students make

  • Writing ClassName:: in front of an inline function inside the class. It is only needed for a body written outside.
  • Swapping the files: the declaration goes in Account.h, the function bodies in Account.cpp.
  • Writing #include <Account.h> for your own class. Use quotes.
  • Giving a destructor parameters or a return type, or thinking a class can have several destructors.
  • Calling a destructor yourself at the end of main. It runs automatically.
  • Thinking main can call a private member function through an object.
  • Thinking only the first element of an array of objects gets constructed. Every element does.
  • Reading UML - as public. Minus is private, plus is public.
  • Putting prompts and cout inside a class's member functions.

What to remember for the test

  • Inline member function: body written inside the class declaration. No ClassName::. Good for short functions.
  • Specification file Name.h holds the class declaration. Implementation file Name.cpp holds the member function definitions. Programs use #include "Name.h", and the .cpp files are compiled and linked together.
  • Destructor: ~ClassName(), no return type, no parameters, only one per class, runs automatically when the object is destroyed (a local object: when its function ends).
  • A private member function can be called only by the class's own member functions.
  • Dot row[3]; runs the default constructor three times, once per element. With no default constructor, every element needs an initializer.
  • UML: three parts (name, member variables, member functions). - private, + public, type after a colon.
  • Member functions should take parameters and return values, and leave cin and cout to the program.

questions.prompt: Which statement describes procedural programming?
choices: The program is built around objects that contain their own data and functions
The program has no functions, only classes
The program is built around functions, and the data is kept in separate variables passed to them
The data is always hidden from every function
questions.explain:
Procedural programming is built around functions. The data sits in its own variables, and each function receives the data it needs as arguments, as in `addInterest(balance, rate)`.

The choice about objects that contain their own data and functions describes object-oriented programming, the other approach. "No functions, only classes" is wrong twice over: a procedural program is made of functions, and classes belong to the object-oriented approach. Hiding data is an object-oriented idea, and even there the data is hidden only from outside code, never from every function.

questions.prompt: Combining data and the functions that operate on it into a single object is called ___.
questions.explain:
The term is encapsulation: bundling the data and the functions that work on it into one object. An Account object that holds `balance` and also carries `deposit` and `getBalance` is encapsulated.

Do not mix it up with data hiding. Data hiding is the separate idea of keeping code outside the object away from that bundled data.

questions.prompt: What is data hiding?
choices: Encrypting the object's data when it is stored on disk
Deleting variables that are no longer used
Giving member variables short, unclear names
Keeping an object's data out of direct reach of code outside the object, so only member functions can use it
questions.explain:
Data hiding means code outside an object cannot reach the object's data directly. Only the object's own member functions use it, so outside code must call those functions. That lets a function such as `deposit` refuse a bad value, which protects the data from accidental damage.

The other choices are unrelated ideas. Encrypting data scrambles it for security, which is not what the term means. Deleting unused variables is just cleanup. Short, unclear names make code harder to read, and they hide nothing.

questions.prompt: Which statement about classes and objects is correct?
choices: A class is a blueprint; an object is an instance made from it
A class is an instance of an object
An object is a blueprint; a class is made from it
A class holds the data values; an object only holds functions
questions.explain:
A class is the description, like a blueprint. An object is a real thing built from that description, with its own data values, and it is called an instance of the class. One `Account` class can produce `savings` and `checking`, each holding its own balance.

"A class is an instance of an object" and "an object is a blueprint" both reverse the relationship. The choice saying the class holds the data values while the object holds only functions is backwards too: each object holds its own values, and the class holds none.

questions.prompt: In OOP terms, the data in an object are its attributes and the procedures it performs are its member functions.
questions.explain:
True. An object's attributes are the data it holds, and C++ calls them member variables. The procedures the object can perform are its member functions. Many other languages, Python included, call those methods.

For an Account object, `balance` is an attribute (a member variable) and `deposit` is a member function.

questions.prompt: A class declaration contains the members below with no access specifier written. What is their access?
choices: public
private
protected, which is visible to all code in the file
None; it is a compile error
questions.explain:
In a `class`, any member listed before the first access specifier is private. No specifier is written here, so `level` and `reset` are both private. Only member functions of `Gadget` may use them, and a line in `main` such as `g.level = 3;` would not compile.

Public is the default for a `struct`, not for a class. `protected` is a real key word, but it is used with inheritance, it is never the default, and it does not mean visible to all code. Leaving out the specifier is not an error, just weaker style.

questions.prompt: The access specifier that lets code outside the class use a member is ___.
questions.explain:
The answer is `public`. Members listed after `public:` can be used by any code, for example `main` calling `acct.getBalance()`. Members listed after `private:` can be used only by the class's own member functions.

The usual design is data private and member functions public. The public member functions then form the class's interface.

questions.prompt: What does const after the parameter list of a member function mean?
questions.code: double getArea() const;
choices: The function can only be called once
The function returns a constant value
The function may not modify the object's member variables
The member variables become public
questions.explain:
A `const` after the parameter list is a promise that the function will not change any member variable of the object it is called for. If the body of `getArea` tried `width = 0;`, the compiler would reject it. Functions that only read data, such as `getArea`, are marked this way.

It does not limit how many times the function can be called. It is not about the return value: `double` is the return type, and this `const` sits after the parentheses. It does not change access either: only `public:` and `private:` do that.

questions.prompt: The compiler accepts the class declaration below, which is followed directly by `main`.
questions.explain:
False. A class declaration must end with a semicolon after its closing brace, written `};`. Here the brace after `int age;` has no semicolon, so compiling stops with an error such as `expected ';' after class definition`.

The slip is easy to make because a function body, like `main`'s, needs no semicolon after its brace. A class declaration does. Some compilers report the problem at the next line, `int main()`, so when an error points at a line that looks fine, check the line above.

questions.prompt: Which is the correct header for defining the const member function getInterest of class Account outside the class?
choices: double getInterest() const
double Account.getInterest() const
double Account:getInterest() const
double Account::getInterest() const
questions.explain:
A member function defined outside its class needs the class name and the scope resolution operator in front of the function name: `double Account::getInterest() const`. The `const` stays, because the prototype inside the class has it.

Without `Account::` the header defines an ordinary function that belongs to no class, and an ordinary function cannot be marked `const`, so it does not compile. The dot joins an object to a member in a call, as in `acct.getInterest()`, and never appears in a header. A single colon is not an operator here. It takes two.

questions.prompt: When a member function is defined outside its class, the class name is followed by the ___ operator (written ::).
questions.explain:
`::` is the scope resolution operator. In `void Account::setBalance(double b)` it says that this `setBalance` belongs to class `Account`, which is what lets its body use `balance` and the other members.

Leave out `Account::` and you have defined an ordinary function that has nothing to do with the class.

questions.prompt: Why does this class fail to compile?
choices: bump is const but modifies the member variable n
n is private so bump cannot use it
A class may not have a function named bump
The class is missing a return type for bump
questions.explain:
`bump` is marked `const`, which promises it will not change any member variable. Its body does `n++`, which changes `n`. The compiler rejects the broken promise: g++ says `increment of member 'Counter::n' in read-only object`. Removing `const` from `bump` fixes it.

`n` being private is not the problem. A class's own member functions can always use its private members. `bump` is an ordinary, legal name, and the function does have a return type: `void`.

questions.prompt: The operator used to access a member of an object, as in box.getArea(), is the ___ operator.
questions.explain:
It is the dot operator: the object's name, a `.`, then the member, as in `box.getArea()`. The dot says which object's member to use, so `box.getArea()` works on `box`'s own data.

From outside the class it reaches only public members. Do not confuse it with `::`, the scope resolution operator, which goes after a class name in a member function's definition header.

questions.prompt: What does this program print?
questions.explain:
Follow `t`'s one member variable, `count`, through each call:
```
t.setCount(5)   count = 5
t.add(3)        count = 5 + 3 = 8
t.add(4)        count = 8 + 4 = 12
t.getCount()    returns 12
```
`count += n` means `count = count + n`, so each call to `add` adds to the stored value. The program prints `12`. If you got 4, you treated `add` like `setCount`, replacing the value instead of adding to it.

questions.prompt: What does this program print?
questions.explain:
`a` and `b` are separate objects, and each has its own `width` and `height`.
```
a.setWidth(2)    a: width 2
a.setHeight(3)   a: height 3
b.setWidth(4)    b: width 4
b.setHeight(5)   b: height 5
a.getArea()      uses a's data: 2 * 3 = 6
b.getArea()      uses b's data: 4 * 5 = 20
```
The object before the dot decides whose members `getArea` uses, so the output is `6 20`. The areas are `double` values, but `cout` prints a whole-number `double` without a decimal point.

questions.prompt: A member function that stores a value in a member variable is called a(n) ___.
choices: accessor
mutator
constructor
stub
questions.explain:
A mutator, also called a setter, stores a value in a member variable or otherwise changes the object's data. `void setMiles(int m) { miles = m; }` is a typical one.

An accessor, or getter, is the opposite: it returns a value and changes nothing. A constructor is the special function that runs automatically when an object is created. A stub is a placeholder function used while testing a program.

questions.prompt: The class Account has a private member balance and public functions deposit, getBalance and setOwner. Which statement in main causes a compile error?
choices: acct.deposit(50);
cout << acct.getBalance();
acct.balance = 100;
acct.setOwner("Lee");
questions.explain:
`balance` is private, so only `Account`'s own member functions may use it. `acct.balance = 100;` is written in `main`, outside the class, so the compiler rejects it with an error such as `'double Account::balance' is private within this context`.

The other three lines call `deposit`, `getBalance` and `setOwner`. Those are public, so `main` may call them through `acct` with the dot operator. From outside, the way to change the balance is a public function such as `deposit`.

questions.prompt: What does this program print?
questions.explain:
`q = p;` copies the member variables of `p` into `q`, one by one. After that, the two objects are separate.
```
p.setCount(5)   p.count = 5   q.count = ?
q = p           p.count = 5   q.count = 5   (copied)
p.add(3)        p.count = 8   q.count = 5   (q untouched)
```
So the output is `8 5`. If you answered `8 8`, you treated `q` as another name for `p`, which is how assignment works in Python. In C++, assigning an object copies its values, and later changes to `p` do not reach `q`.

questions.prompt: Two objects of the same class share a single copy of the member variables.
questions.explain:
False. Every object gets its own copy of each member variable. That is why two `Box` objects can hold different widths, and changing one leaves the other alone.

What the objects do share is the member function code. There is one copy of `getArea`'s instructions, and the object before the dot decides whose data it works on.

questions.prompt: What is the main benefit of making member variables private and providing public mutators?
choices: The program runs faster
The variables use less memory
No member functions are needed
Mutators can check values before storing them, and the inside of the class can change without breaking other code
questions.explain:
Private data forces every change to go through the class's own member functions. A mutator can then check a value before storing it and refuse a bad one. And because outside code never touches the data directly, the class author can change how the data is stored without breaking that code.

`private` is a rule the compiler checks while building the program, so it does not make the program faster or use less memory. "No member functions are needed" is backwards: with private data, member functions are the only way in from outside.

questions.prompt: What does this program print?
questions.explain:
`setAge` stores its argument only when the argument passes the test `a >= 0`.
```
p.setAge(20)   20 >= 0 is true    age = 20
p.setAge(-5)   -5 >= 0 is false   nothing stored, age stays 20
p.getAge()     returns 20
```
The program prints `20`. The tempting answer is -5, but the second call never stores it. And because `age` is private, `main` cannot get around the check by writing `p.age = -5;`.

questions.prompt: If a class keeps its data private, its internal storage can be redesigned without changing the code that calls its public member functions.
questions.explain:
True. Outside code uses only the public member functions, never the private data. If the class author changes how the data is stored, for example keeping a temperature in Fahrenheit instead of Celsius, only the bodies of the member functions change.

As long as each public function takes the same arguments and gives the same results, every program that calls it keeps working without a single change.

questions.prompt: The public member functions through which outside code works with an object are called its ___.
questions.explain:
The answer is interface: the set of public member functions that outside code is allowed to call. Like a car's pedals and steering wheel, it lets you operate the object without touching the machinery inside.

For an `Account` class the interface might be `deposit`, `withdraw` and `getBalance`, while the `balance` member stays private behind it.

questions.prompt: A member function that is called automatically when an object is created is a ___.
questions.explain:
The answer is constructor. A constructor is a member function whose name is the class name, and it has no return type. C++ runs it automatically at the moment an object is created, once for each object, and its job is to set up the object, usually by giving the member variables their starting values.

For example, `Room hall;` runs `Room()` on `hall`. In Python the matching idea is `__init__`.

questions.prompt: Which is a valid declaration of a constructor taking one double for the class Account?
choices: Account(double b);
void Account(double b);
account(double b);
Account(double b) const;
questions.explain:
A constructor's name must match the class name exactly, and it has no return type at all. `Account(double b);` follows both rules.

`void Account(double b);` gives it a return type, which a constructor may not have, not even `void`. `account(double b);` has a lowercase a, so it does not match `Account`, and the compiler sees an ordinary member function with no return type, which is an error. `Account(double b) const;` is invalid because a `const` function promises not to change the members, and setting them is a constructor's whole job.

questions.prompt: What does this program print?
questions.explain:
The arguments in each object definition pick the constructor.
```
Box a;        no arguments: Box() runs, width 1, height 1
Box b(3, 4);  two arguments: Box(w, h) runs, width 3, height 4
a.getArea()   1 * 1 = 1
b.getArea()   3 * 4 = 12
```
So the output is `1 12`. `Box a;` with no parentheses uses the default constructor, and that constructor sets both sides to 1, so its area is 1, not 0 or garbage.

questions.prompt: What is a default constructor?
choices: The constructor that runs when the program ends
A constructor that can be called with no arguments
A constructor that has a void return type
The only constructor a class is allowed to have
questions.explain:
A default constructor is any constructor that can be called with no arguments. Either it has no parameters, like `Box()`, or every parameter has a default value, like `Box(double w = 1, double h = 1)`. It is the one that runs for a definition such as `Box a;`.

A constructor never has a return type, so a void one is impossible. A class may have several constructors with different parameter lists, so the default one is not the only one allowed. Code that runs when an object is destroyed belongs to the destructor, a different function covered in the next lesson.

questions.prompt: Why does this code fail to compile?
choices: Constructors cannot have parameters
Rect r; needs parentheses: Rect r();
The class has a constructor with parameters, so the compiler supplies no default constructor for Rect r;
The constructor must return a value
questions.explain:
`Rect` has one constructor, and it needs two arguments. `Rect r;` supplies none, so it needs a default constructor. The compiler adds a default constructor only when a class has no constructors at all. As soon as you write any constructor, that free one is gone. g++ reports `no matching function for call to 'Rect::Rect()'`. The fix is to add `Rect()`, or to give both parameters default values.

Constructors may have parameters, and they never return a value. Writing `Rect r();` would not help: it declares a function named `r`, not an object.

questions.prompt: What does this program print?
questions.explain:
The one constructor has two parameters, both with default value 0. Arguments fill the parameters from the left, and defaults fill whatever is missing.
```
Pt a;         no arguments         x = 0, y = 0
Pt b(5);      5 fills the first    x = 5, y = 0
Pt c(5, 6);   both are given       x = 5, y = 6
```
Each `show()` prints `x`, a comma, `y`, then a new line, so the output is:
```
0,0
5,0
5,6
```
The common slip is `0,5` for `Pt b(5);`. A single argument always goes to the first parameter, never the second.

questions.prompt: A constructor is declared with the return type void.
questions.explain:
False. A constructor has no return type at all, not even `void`. Its header is just the class name and the parameter list, as in `Account(double b);`.

Writing `void Account(double b);` is a compile error. g++ says `return type specification for constructor invalid`.

questions.prompt: Defining an object of a class, as in `Account acct;`, is called the ___ of the class.
questions.explain:
The term is instantiation: creating an object, called an instance, from a class. `Account acct;` instantiates the class `Account`, and `acct` is the instance.

A class declaration on its own instantiates nothing. It only describes what each `Account` object will hold.

questions.prompt: If no access specifier is written, members of a struct are public, while members of a class are private.
questions.explain:
True. When no access specifier is written, the members of a `class` are private and the members of a `struct` are public. Apart from that default, the two key words declare types the same way.

That is why programmers often use `struct` for a simple group of data that anyone may read, and `class` for an object whose data is hidden behind member functions.

questions.prompt: Look at this member function header. What is the function's name, and which class is it a member of?
questions.code: void Lamp::setWatts(int w)
choices: Name Lamp, member of class setWatts
Name void, member of class Lamp
Name Lamp::setWatts, not a member of any class
Name setWatts, member of class Lamp
questions.explain:
Read a definition header in this order: return type, class, `::`, function name, parameters.
```
void       the return type (returns nothing)
Lamp       the class the function belongs to
::         scope resolution, "the one belonging to"
setWatts   the function's own name
(int w)    the parameter list
```
So the function is `setWatts`, a member of class `Lamp`. The tempting mistake is to swap them, but the name before `::` is always the class. `void` is never a name. It is the return type.

questions.prompt: Class Lamp has a public void member function setWatts that takes an int. desk is a Lamp object. Which statement correctly calls setWatts for desk?
choices: desk.setWatts(60);
desk::setWatts(60);
Lamp::setWatts(60);
setWatts(desk, 60);
questions.explain:
A member function is called through an object: the object's name, the dot operator, the function name, then the arguments. So it is `desk.setWatts(60);`, which sets `desk`'s watts to 60.

`desk::setWatts(60);` uses `::`, which belongs after a class name in a definition header, never after an object. `Lamp::setWatts(60);` names the class but not which lamp, so there is no object's data to change. `setWatts(desk, 60);` calls it like a stand-alone function, which it is not.

questions.prompt: In a class declaration, all private members must be declared before the public members.
questions.explain:
False. `private:` and `public:` sections may come in any order, and each may appear more than once. An access specifier simply applies to every member below it, up to the next specifier.

Putting the private data first and the public functions after it is a common habit that makes a class easy to read, but the compiler does not require it.

questions.prompt: Class Thermostat has these member functions. Which one is an accessor?
choices: void setTarget(double t)
double getTarget() const
void raise(double amount)
Thermostat()
questions.explain:
An accessor returns a value from the object without changing anything. `double getTarget() const` fits: it returns a `double`, and the `const` after the parentheses promises it changes no member variable.

`void setTarget(double t)` stores a new target, so it is a mutator. `void raise(double amount)` changes the object's data too, so it is also a mutator, even though its name does not start with set. `Thermostat()` has the class's own name and no return type, so it is a constructor, which is neither.

questions.prompt: What does this program print?
questions.explain:
A constructor runs by itself at the exact moment its object is defined. Follow `main` from the top:
```
cout << "before"   prints before
Greeter g;         g is created, Greeter() runs, prints built
cout << "after"    prints after
```
So the output is `before`, `built` and `after`, on three lines. Nothing calls `Greeter()` by name. Defining `g` is what runs it, so `built` appears exactly where `g` is defined, between the other two lines.

questions.prompt: Class Account has private double members balance and rate and no constructor. Inside main, `Account acct;` is defined. What do balance and rate hold right after this statement?
choices: 0 and 0, because member variables start at zero
1 and 1
Nothing, because the statement is a compile error
Unpredictable garbage values, until something stores values in them
questions.explain:
Member variables are not set to zero automatically. `acct` is created inside `main`, and `Account` has no constructor and no starting values, so `balance` and `rate` hold leftover garbage from whatever used that memory before. Their values are unpredictable until something stores real values in them.

It is not a compile error: the definition is legal, and at most the compiler warns if the values are used. 0 and 0, or 1 and 1, are guesses that nothing in the class supports. To get known starting values, use in-place initialization such as `double rate = 0.0;`, or a constructor.

questions.prompt: Account stores balance and rate but has no interest member; getInterest() calculates balance * rate each time it is called. Why is that the better design?
choices: Multiplication is not allowed inside a member variable declaration
A stored interest figure would go stale: it would be wrong as soon as balance or rate changed
A class may not have more than two member variables
getInterest would have to be private if the interest were stored
questions.explain:
Interest depends on `balance` and `rate`. If it were stored in its own member variable, it would be right only until `balance` or `rate` changed, and then it would still hold the old figure. That out-of-date value is stale data. Calculating `balance * rate` inside `getInterest()` gives the current answer every time it is called.

The other reasons are false. Multiplication is not banned anywhere in a class, a class may have any number of member variables, and storing a value would not force `getInterest` to be private.

questions.prompt: Inside the definition of Account::getInterest, how does the code refer to the calling object's balance member?
choices: acct.balance
Account.balance
balance
getInterest.balance
questions.explain:
Inside a member function, members are written by their bare names, so the code says `balance`. It automatically means the balance of whichever object called the function: for `acct.getInterest()` it is `acct`'s balance, for `savings.getInterest()` it is `savings`'s. Python would write `self.balance` here.

`acct.balance` would tie the function to one particular object, and the class knows nothing about a variable named `acct`. `Account.balance` puts a dot after a class name, which is never valid. `getInterest.balance` treats a function as if it held data.

questions.prompt: string is a class, and word is an object of it. What does this code print? Assume the code is inside main(), with iostream and string included and using namespace std; in effect.
questions.explain:
`word` is a `string` object, and each call after the dot works on the text stored inside `word`.
```
string word = "tree"   word holds tree       (4 characters)
word.append("house")   adds house to the end, word holds treehouse
word.length()          counts t-r-e-e-h-o-u-s-e, which is 9
```
The `cout` prints the text, a space, then the length: `treehouse 9`. A common slip is 4, the length before `append`. But `append` changed the stored text, so `length` counts all 9 characters.

questions.prompt: What does this program print?
questions.explain:
Both constructors use a member initialization list: the part after the colon sets members before the body runs, and both bodies are empty.
```
Timer a;      no arguments: Timer() runs, secs(30) sets secs to 30
Timer b(90);  one int: Timer(int s) runs, secs(s) sets secs to 90
```
`a.getSecs()` returns 30 and `b.getSecs()` returns 90, so the output is `30 90`. The empty braces `{ }` do not mean nothing happens. The list after the colon already did the work.

questions.prompt: Why does `Lamp desk;` fail to compile with this class?
choices: A constructor cannot have a default argument
Both constructors can be called with no arguments, so the call is ambiguous; a class cannot have two default constructors
Lamp desk; needs empty parentheses: Lamp desk();
watts must be public for a constructor to set it
questions.explain:
`Lamp desk;` needs a constructor that can be called with no arguments, and both qualify. `Lamp()` has no parameters, and `Lamp(int w = 60)` can be called with none because `w` has a default. The compiler cannot choose, so it reports `call of overloaded 'Lamp()' is ambiguous`. That is why a class should have only one default constructor. `Lamp desk(75);` would compile, because only the second constructor takes one argument.

Default arguments in constructors are allowed. `Lamp desk();` declares a function, not an object. `watts` can stay private, because a constructor is a member function.

questions.prompt: Since C++11, a member variable may be given an initial value in its declaration inside the class, as in `double rate = 0.05;`.
questions.explain:
True. Since C++11 a member variable may be given a starting value right where it is declared inside the class, as in `double rate = 0.05;`. This is called in-place initialization. Every object of the class then starts with that value until something changes it.

Before C++11, starting values had to be set by a constructor, a special member function covered later in this unit.

questions.prompt: Which statement about a destructor is true?
choices: It is named with a tilde and the class name, has no return type and no parameters, and runs automatically when the object is destroyed
It can take any number of arguments, like a constructor
It must be called explicitly at the end of main
It returns true when the object was destroyed successfully
questions.explain:
A destructor is named with a tilde and the class name, such as `~Lamp()`. Like a constructor it has no return type. Unlike a constructor it takes no parameters. It runs by itself when the object is destroyed, which for a local object is when its function ends.

Because it takes no parameters, it cannot be overloaded, so a class has only one destructor. You never call it at the end of `main`: C++ runs it automatically. And with no return type, it cannot return true or anything else.

questions.prompt: What does this program print?
questions.explain:
`Star sky[4];` creates four `Star` objects, `sky[0]` to `sky[3]`, and the default constructor runs once for each of them, in order.
```
sky[0] is created   Star() prints *
sky[1] is created   Star() prints *
sky[2] is created   Star() prints *
sky[3] is created   Star() prints *
cout << endl        ends the line
```
The output is `****`. The tempting mistake is a single `*`, as if only the first element were built. Every element of an array of objects is a full object, so every one runs the constructor.

questions.prompt: A member function whose body is written inside the class declaration is called an ___ member function.
questions.explain:
The answer is inline. A member function whose body is written inside the class declaration is an inline member function, for example `double getBalance() const { return balance; }`. It needs no `ClassName::` because it is already inside the class.

The name comes from inline expansion: the compiler may place the body's code at each call instead of making a real call. That suits short functions such as accessors.

questions.prompt: By the usual convention, where are the declaration of class Kettle and the definitions of its member functions stored?
choices: Both in the file that contains main
The declaration in Kettle.cpp and the member function definitions in Kettle.h
The declaration in Kettle.h (the specification file) and the member function definitions in Kettle.cpp (the implementation file)
The declaration in Kettle.exe and the definitions in Kettle.obj
questions.explain:
By convention the class declaration goes in a header file named after the class, `Kettle.h`, called the specification file. The member function definitions go in `Kettle.cpp`, the implementation file. A program that uses the class writes `#include "Kettle.h"`, and `Kettle.cpp` is compiled and linked with it.

The choice with `.cpp` and `.h` the other way round swaps the two jobs. Keeping everything in the file with `main` works for small examples, but it is not the convention. `.exe` and `.obj` files are produced by the compiler and linker, not written by the programmer.

questions.prompt: In a UML class diagram, what does a minus sign (-) in front of a member name mean?
choices: The member is private
The member is public
The member is a constructor
The member returns a negative value
questions.explain:
In a UML class diagram a minus sign marks a private member and a plus sign marks a public member. So `- balance : double` is a private member variable of type `double`, and `+ getBalance() : double` is a public member function that returns a `double`.

The sign has nothing to do with constructors or with negative values. Swapping the two signs is the usual slip. One way to remember it: minus means outside code gets less access.

questions.prompt: Code in main can call a private member function of a class, as long as it uses an object and the dot operator.
questions.explain:
False. A private member function can be called only by other member functions of the same class. Code in `main` is outside the class, so a call such as `a.isValid(5)` fails to compile with an error like `is private within this context`, even though it uses an object and the dot.

Inside the class, a public function such as `deposit` may call the private helper freely. That is the point of a private helper: it does internal work that outside code should never call directly.

questions.prompt: Which list names every error in this class declaration?
choices: Only the missing semicolon after the closing brace
The colon after Lamp, the missing colons after private and public, no return type on setWatts, and no semicolon after the closing brace
watts must be public, and the key word must be written Class
The colon after Lamp and the missing semicolon; everything else is legal

questions.prompt: This code fails to compile. What is wrong?
choices: kg must be public for setKg to use it
setKg cannot take a parameter
A class may not have a member named kg
The definition header lacks Scale::, so it defines an ordinary function that cannot see kg
questions.explain:
The definition header is `void setKg(int k)`, with no `Scale::` in front of the name. So the compiler treats it as an ordinary function that happens to share the name, not as the member function of `Scale`. An ordinary function has no member called `kg`, so `kg = k;` fails with `'kg' was not declared in this scope`. The fix is `void Scale::setKg(int k)`.

`kg` does not need to be public, because the real member function may use private members. Taking a parameter is normal for a function that stores a value, and `kg` is a legal member name.

questions.prompt: Why do class designers usually avoid putting cin and cout statements inside member functions such as setWidth or getArea?
choices: cin and cout cannot be used inside a class
Member functions run before main, when the screen is not ready
The class would be tied to one way of doing input and output, making it harder to reuse; the program using the class should handle the I/O
It would make the member variables public
questions.explain:
If `setWidth` prompted with `cout` and read with `cin`, every program using the class would be stuck with that exact prompt and with keyboard input. A program that reads widths from a file, or shows a window, could not use the class. When member functions take values as parameters and return results, each program decides how to get input and show output, so the class stays reusable.

The other reasons are false. `cin` and `cout` are legal inside member functions. Member functions do not run before `main`, and using `cin` does not make anything public.

questions.prompt: What is an object's state?
choices: The data stored in its member variables at a given moment
The list of member functions its class declares
Whether its class is public or private
The file in which its class is declared
questions.explain:
An object's state is the set of values stored in its member variables at a given moment. If an `Odometer` named `car` has `miles` equal to 150, that is its state, and calling a mutator such as `car.drive(30)` changes it.

The list of member functions belongs to the class and is the same for every object, so it is not state. A class is not public or private (its members are), and the file a class is declared in says nothing about one object's data.
